OPPORTUNITY TEXT:

TITLE: Seasonal dissolved oxygen gas exchange in the California Current Upwelling System

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Ren, A.S., Rudnick, D.L., & Nicholson, D.P. (2025). Seasonal dissolved oxygen gas exchange in the California Current Upwelling System. Progress In Oceanography, 103473. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.pocean.2025.103473 Image provide by Alice Ren. Eastern boundary current systems are known for seasonal upwelling that brings water from below the mixed layer to the surface. The process deoxygenates the water column by bringing lower-dissolved oxygen water closer to the surface and oxygenates the water column by driving primary productivity due to the injection of nutrients from deep waters. Here, an observational dataset of 5 years of dissolved oxygen, temperature, and salinity measured to 500 m and from the coast to around 400 km offshore is used to study the seasonal evolution of air-sea exchange of oxygen in an upwelling region. A narrow band of coastal oxygen undersaturation drives dissolved oxygen uptake by the ocean in spring and summer, while in winter dissolved oxygen uptake predominates due to more widespread but less intense oxygen undersaturation. Oxygen outgassing occurs offshore of the nearshore uptake band in spring and summer, driven by warming and primary productivity, such that the cumulative net oxygen gas exchange integrated seaward from shore reaches zero once around one hundred kilometers from the coast. Ventilation of the upper ocean is observed as a result of shoaling isopycnals in the upwelling season. Competing factors causing uptake and outgassing and the seaward extent of the domain determine whether an upwelling zone is a net source or sink of oxygen gas.

TITLE: Research Analyzes the Role of Ocean Heat Transport and Surface Heat Exchange in Warming the Arctic Ocean and Reducing Sea Ice

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
By Randy Showstack With the Arctic Ocean warming much more rapidly than the global average over the past several decades, the extent and thickness of sea ice in the Arctic has decreased dramatically. Climate models project that these trends will accelerate even more in the future. A new analysis finds that increased ocean heat transport (OHT) into the Arctic through the Barents Sea Opening (BSO) is the primary driver of this warming, with OHT from the Fram and Bering straits also contributing to the warming. (See Figure 1 for a map of the region.) Figure 1. Map indicating the location of the Arctic gateways where the ocean heat transport is calculated. (Illustration by Natalie Renier, Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution) The analysis also finds that the projected future OHT changes are driven primarily by warmer inflowing water rather than by changes in the volume of water transported through those three Arctic gateways, according to the journal article, “The Respective Roles of Ocean Heat Transport and Surface Heat Fluxes in Driving Arctic Ocean Warming and Sea Ice Decline,” published in the American Meteorological Society’s Journal of Climate in January 2024. In addition, the analysis calculates the contributions of ocean-ice and atmosphere-ice heat fluxes to the sea ice heat budget changes (see Figure 2), and determines that the ocean is likely to become the most important source of heat for the ice and hence the most responsible for the melting. “Throughout the entire twentieth century as well as the early twenty-first century, the atmosphere is the main contributor to ice heat gain in summer, though the ocean’s role is not negligible. However, over the course of the 21st century, the ocean progressively becomes the main heat source for the ice as the ocean warms,” according to the article. Figure 2. Illustration of the factors that contribute to the ocean and sea-ice heat budgets. Credit: Natalie Renier from WHOI Graphics. “The ocean is expected to play a very important role in driving sea-ice loss in the future. In particular, the increased heat inputs from the different Arctic Ocean gateways, particularly the Barents Sea Opening, the Fram Strait, and the Bering Strait from the Pacific side of the Arctic are going to be very important for driving active ocean warming,” said journal article lead author Dylan Oldenburg, a postdoctoral investigator in physical oceanography at the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI). Co-authors are Young-Oh Kwon of WHOI; Claude Frankignoul with WHOI and Sorbonne University; and Gokhan Danabasoglu, Stephen Yeager, and Who M. Kim with the National Science Foundation’s National Center for Atmospheric Research. For their heat budget analysis, the researchers defined the Arctic Ocean as the region bounded by the Arctic Ocean gateways, which include the Barents Sea Opening as well as the Barrow, Bering, Fram, and Nares straits. The analysis uses the 100-member Large Ensemble of the state-of-the-art fully coupled Community Earth System Model, version 2 (CESM2), focusing primarily on the period between 1920 and 2100. This Large Ensemble provides researchers with the ability to separate climate change signal variations from natural internal variability. “The beauty of having so many ensemble members, or simulations, is that when you average them together, there is a lot less noise, and you can remove internal variability that shows up in each ensemble member,” said Oldenburg. “When you look at the Large Ensemble, you can isolate the response of the climate or the Arctic Ocean, for instance, to the greenhouse gas forcing without internal variability masking what is happening due to that forcing.” Although the model has some minor drawbacks, such as underestimating the Fram Strait OHT relative to
target:
SUMMARY
This article reports on a scientific analysis published in the Journal of Climate in January 2024 regarding Arctic Ocean warming and sea ice decline. Researchers found that increased ocean heat transport (OHT) through the Barents Sea Opening, alongside contributions from the Fram and Bering straits, is the primary driver of Arctic warming. Future OHT changes will be driven primarily by warmer inflowing water rather than volume changes. Furthermore, the ocean is projected to become the main heat source for sea ice over the 21st century, replacing the atmosphere. The study utilized the 100-member CESM2 Large Ensemble model covering the period from 1920 to 2100.

TITLE: WHO Global Youth Competition on Influenza & COVID-19 Prevention and Control 2026

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: September 13, 2026 Applications are invited for the WHO Global Youth Competition on Influenza & COVID-19 Prevention and Control 2026. WHO invites students and young professionals to participate in this youth competition by developing brief videos that highlight the importance of influenza and/or COVID-19 prevention and control. The videos are encouraged to be innovative, address misinformation/myths, and encourage their community to protect themselves from seasonal influenza and COVID-19. Competition theme: “How do you shield your circle from respiratory infections, like influenza and COVID-19?” Competition Prompts: The submission must include a brief video that responds to one or more of the following prompts: Prompt 1: Who needs protection from seasonal influenza/COVID-19? How can vulnerable groups protect themselves? Why is it important? Prompt 2: How do you respond to someone who has doubts about influenza and/or COVID-19 prevention and control in your community? Prompt 3: What myths about influenza and/or COVID-19 prevention and control are circulating in your community? How do you address them? Benefits There will be one global winning video and up to six videos highlighted as runners-up. The winning videos will be featured by WHO on the competition webpage. The student(s) who submitted the winning video will: Be invited to present their video on a global influenza/COVID-19 prevention and control-focused webinar in October 2026 and Receive a certificate from WHO featuring their name(s) and the video title Eligibility Participants must be students or young professionals; Between the ages of 18 and 35. Instructions for Participants Participants must address at least one of the competition prompts in their video. Students can work independently or in teams. Video can be a maximum of 90 seconds (1.5 minutes). Students can submit up to three videos. Submitted videos are encouraged to be creative. Video styles can include but are not limited to storytelling, interview, reel, animation, drawings, poem, dialogue, or other creative formats. If AI is used to generate any portion of the submission, it must be acknowledged in the submission form. The video may be in any language but must include English subtitles. Submission Criteria Submissions will be assessed on the following criteria: Video message aligns with the competition theme and responds to at least one of the competition prompts Originality and creativity Accuracy and clarity of health information Visual style and storytelling quality The video includes English subtitles Responses to the submission form questions including the: Motivation/rationale for the video Prompts selected and how they were addressed Potential impact of the video Feasibility for dissemination in the community Confirmation that all filmed individuals consented to their appearance in the video and are over the age of 18 Confirmation that the individuals submitting the video are between the ages of 18-35 years Application All submissions must be received through the designated Microsoft Forms by Sunday 13 September 2026 at 23:45 CEST. TITLE: Remote Internships vs In-Person Internships: The Honest Comparison

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Imagine this: you’ve just graduated and have no idea what your next steps are. You’ve studied for three to four years, and you’re now ready to enter the working world. So where do you begin? This blog is where all your answers will be. Internships sound like a good start. You come across two types of internships, an in-person one and a remote one, and you’re unsure of which one to apply for. Both have their advantages and disadvantages. So here’s an honest breakdown of both. In-Person Internships Some may think that an internship will consist of running up and down getting lunch orders for your superiors and barely getting hands-on experience; this is an outdated view, and a real in-person internship means the internship will focus on giving you real experience you will use to do the job to the best of your ability. You’ll be exposed to real daily work operations; you’ll be able to collaborate with your colleagues, build professional relationships and connect with people on a face-to-face level. You will be required to show up every day for work, where you’ll have your set working hours and a set time for when you leave. Once you join, you’ll be assigned to a supervisor who will oversee your work and ensure you become accustomed to the work, the office culture, and the company’s SOP (standard operating procedure). In-person internships offer you a tangible work experience. If you’re considering an in-person internship, it’s important to understand that it can lead to full-time employment. According to NACE’s 2025 Internship & Co-op Report, employers extended full-time offers to 62% of their 2024 interns. Pros of an In-person Internship Interns may find it easier to talk to people when they’re face-to-face rather than being behind a screen. They’ll find it easier to form real connections with their colleagues and meaningful relationships with their peers and mentors. An in-person internship provides a structured work environment that’s built around schedules and punctuality; these structures allow for streamlined teamwork and instant communication with each other. There’s also the possibility of receiving travel allowance for you to make your way to the office. When working on-site, you have complete access to your mentors; you’re able to receive hands-on guidance on anything you may be struggling with or have any confusion cleared up instantly. Mentors can provide you with immediate feedback. Unlike remote internships, companies will provide equipment to their interns such as laptops, headset and or phones. Cons of In-person internships In an In-person internship, there is not much room for flexibility; you have fixed hours. This means you will need to adjust your schedule accordingly. If your internship is far from where you live, this may cause some constraints for you: travelling to the office, finding the right routes to take and having to wake up early in order to arrive on time. Some interns may find the hustle and bustle of the office distracting, making it harder to focus; this could affect your work quality and your work output. Remote internships A remote internship often means you’ll be more than likely working for an overseas company. These types of internships are offered to students who either aren’t able to or simply don’t want to relocate but still want the experience that an internship overseas would give them. This means your entire internship is conducted online, through virtual meetings, emails and companywide messaging platforms. When we think of an internship, most of us might have the idea of being stuck grabbing coffee for the higher-ups, sitting in meetings taking notes or printing pages till

- Not specified

MANDATORY
- None specified

RESTRICTIONS
- None specified

TARGET GROUP
- Graduates seeking internship experience

FUNDING / BENEFITS
- None specified

APPLICATION
- None specified

OTHER IMPORTANT CONDITIONS
- None specified

SUMMARY
In-person internships offer real daily work operations, collaboration with colleagues, and face-to-face connections. They provide structured work environments, travel allowances, and immediate mentorship. However, they require fixed hours, may cause travel constraints, and can be distracting. Remote internships are conducted online and are suitable for students who cannot or do not want to relocate. They offer flexibility but may lack immediate mentorship and structured work environments.

TITLE: Demographics & Planetary Health Story Prize 2026

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: October 9, 2026 Applications are open for the Demographics & Planetary Health Story Prize 2026. The Demographic & Planetary Health Story Prize contest is designed to recognize original published journalism that connects demographic change to planetary health, whether through population dynamics, reproductive health, migration, climate, or the economic and geopolitical forces tying them together. Hosted by the Johns Hopkins Institute for Planetary Health and the Planetary Health Alliance, the Hopkins Population Center, and the William H. Gates Sr. Institute for Population and Reproductive Health at Johns Hopkins University, this prize takes a wider lens and seeks to honor all types of reporting, journalism, and content creation that reaches outside a typical sector audience. Categories Print, Podcast, Digital News, & Newsletters: This category is for journalists or reporters who take a more traditional approach to journalism, whether self-publishing or publishing for a recognized media outlet. Social Media, Blogs, & Video: This category is for content creators who utilize social networks or personally-driven content outlets to engage their audiences. Prize An award of $500 will be given in each category. Eligibility Open to journalists, freelancers, community reporters, and student journalists reporting for a digital, print or social outlet. Submissions from NGO or organizational blogs are not eligible. Submissions to the Demographic & Planetary Health Story Prize should engage substantively with the intersection of demographics and planetary health. Examples might include (but not limited to): Population trends and their environmental or health consequences Migration driven by climate or resource pressure Reproductive health access in the context of environmental change Solutions and innovations to mitigate forced migration Energy/urbanization, designing cities that meet demographic trends Impacts of rising heat levels and increased pollution on maternal health Climate impacts on marginalized populations and gender disparities Evaluation Criteria Originality and rigor: Is the reporting sourced beyond press releases and does it bring new information or framing to the topic? Clarity of the demographics–planetary health connection: Does the story make that link legible to a general audience, not just specialists? Craft: Is the writing well structured, and does it use data or visual storytelling effectively? Potential for impact: Is the piece likely to reach and inform readers who wouldn’t otherwise encounter this topic?​ Substantive power of the piece: Does the reporting surface something that moves the conversation forward? Application The Demographic & Planetary Health Story Prize accepts submissions in multiple formats, including: Published or broadcast news stories Features or op-eds Explanatory pieces Short-form documentary or audio pieces Click here to apply For more information, visit Demographics & Planetary Health Story Prize.

TITLE: Partnership for Public Good (PPG) Research Fellowship 2026

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: September 28, 2026 Applications are open for the Partnership for Public Good (PPG) Research Fellowship 2026. The PPG Research Fellowship is a six-month, project-based fellowship designed to support early career researchers interested in improving government effectiveness. Fellows will be paid to conduct policy-relevant background research, use rigorous methods to collect and analyze data, and co-author publications for one of five pre-determined high-priority topics related to public procurement and local government operations. The fellowship provides dedicated time and mentorship for researchers interested in learning about and contributing directly to PPG’s mission of helping governments deliver better outcomes for residents. Fellowship Details Over six months, fellows will work on a defined research topic under the guidance of PPG staff and alongside two other fellows. The program combines independent research with regular professional development and collaboration opportunities through coaching calls and research team meetings. Fellows will receive support translating their work into draft publications, policy briefs, and other public-facing outputs that strengthen both the evidence base for government reform and the fellows’ research portfolios. This remote opportunity is designed for early-career researchers, including graduate students, postdoctoral researchers, early-career faculty, research or policy staff, and other professionals with comparable experience. Fellows will attend one in-person research retreat. Prior to the start of the fellowship, PPG and each selected fellow will agree on work hours (with flexibility in scheduling), project goals and deliverables, and expectations regarding data access, use, rights, and ownership. Benefits Fellows will work 15–25 hours per week and be paid at a rate of $50 per hour with benefits as required by state or local law. Eligibility Applicants may be affiliated with a university, think tank, nonprofit, or other research or policy organization, and maintain affiliation during the fellowship, provided they can meet the time and deliverable commitments of the program. Applicants without such affiliation are also welcome. Application To apply, submit each of the following no later than September 28: A resume/CV (no more than 2 pages). A letter of interest that answers the following questions (no more than 2 pages) Which one or two projects are you interested in and why? (If you are interested in two projects, you may include up to 3 pages. Please specify your top choice.) Why are you qualified to take on this project? How would you approach the work? A work sample. This may be a published or under review research publication or other product that illustrates your skills and expertise. Click here to apply For more information, visit PPG Research Fellowship.

TITLE: Polyfoni Social Sciences for AI Fellowship 2026-2027

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: October 15, 2026 Applications are open for the Polyfoni Social Sciences for AI Fellowship 2026-2027. The Polyfoni Fellowship is a four-month part-time research collaboration for social scientists with fieldwork experience in regions where AI products are being deployed. Fellows join remotely from November 2026 to March 2027 and conduct a cultural audit of a real AI product in their region of expertise. Fellowship Details Fellows conduct a cultural audit: an empirical analysis of how a specific AI product encodes assumptions about the context it is deployed in, and where those assumptions break. Each audit follows Polyfoni’s Cultural Audit Method: assumption mapping, contextual failure identification, severity assessment, and recommendations. Polyfoni supervisors propose audit themes aligned with the research priorities. Fellows choose and shape their project in close collaboration with their academic and industry mentors. The output is a report written for a product team, published on Polyfoni’s Substack under the fellow’s name. The audit target should be a real AI product in a region the fellow has genuine contextual knowledge about. Your fieldwork experience is the data. You are not starting from scratch. You are applying what you already know through a structured method. Examples of audit targets: A health AI chatbot in East Africa A ocean AI tool in Southeast Asia An agricultural AI tool in West Africa An LLM deployed in a non-English-dominant market Benefits Dual mentorship from an academic collaborator and an AI industry professional Training in Polyfoni’s Cultural Audit Method Online masterclasses and monthly group sessions, supported by our partner AI Mission Lab A published research on Polyfoni’s website and Making AI Listen (open access publication) under your name Eligibility You can apply if you are interested in using your social science training to contribute to how AI products are built, evaluated, and governed. They are interested in candidates from a broad set of disciplinary backgrounds, including anthropology, sociology, STS, development studies, political science, humanities, and area studies. There are no strict degree requirements, although we expect that the most promising candidates will have fieldwork experience in a Global South context and an interest in technology careers. Prior AI experience is not required. When assessing applications, they will be looking for: Regional expertise with evidence of fieldwork: Deep contextual knowledge of a place, community, or sector where AI is being deployed. Priority regions: East Africa, South Asia, Southeast Asia, Latin America, China. Clear motivation: A specific reason for wanting to work at the intersection of social science and AI, and a concrete idea of which AI product you would audit. They expect the fellows to work on the audit 5 hours a week. Language: Comfortable working in English. Additional languages are an advantage. They select for diversity of region and discipline. Application Application is now open. The selection process has two steps: Step 1: Initial application. Submit a short application with motivation (500 words maximum). Successful candidates will be contacted for a CV review. Step 2: Interview. Final candidates will have an interview and a research discussion with the Polyfoni team. Polyfoni matches fellows with mentors based on regional expertise alignment (your fieldwork region and the mentor’s company market) and sector alignment (health, fintech, content moderation, etc.). Click here to apply For more information, visit Polyfoni Social Sciences for AI Fellowship.

TITLE: How to Create the Right Business Strategy

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Starting a new business can be exciting, but a good idea alone is rarely enough to build something that lasts. Many businesses begin with enthusiasm, energy and ambition but struggle because there is no clear strategy behind the idea. A strong business strategy helps you understand what your business is trying to achieve, who it is serving, how it will make money and what you need to prioritise in order to grow. For a new business, strategy does not have to be complicated. It simply needs to provide direction and help you make better decisions from the beginning. Start With the Problem You Want to Solve One of the first things every entrepreneur should understand is the problem the business is trying to solve. Many people begin by thinking about the product they want to sell rather than the problem customers are experiencing. However, successful businesses are usually built around real needs. Before developing your product or service, ask yourself what challenge people are facing, how they currently deal with that challenge and what is missing from the existing solutions. You should also consider whether people care enough about the problem to pay for a solution. A business becomes stronger when it is addressing a problem that is clear, specific and important to its target customers. For example, instead of simply deciding to start a food delivery business, you may discover that young professionals in a particular city struggle to find affordable and healthy meals during working hours. That insight gives the business a clearer focus. Your strategy can then be built around providing convenient, affordable and nutritious meals to this specific customer group rather than trying to serve everyone. Know Exactly Who Your Customer Is Every business needs customers, but trying to serve everybody can make it difficult to serve anyone properly. A strong business strategy identifies the specific people most likely to need and pay for what the business offers. Think about their age, location, occupation, lifestyle, income level, challenges and buying habits. You should understand where they spend their time, how they make purchasing decisions and what matters most to them when choosing a product or service. The more specific you are, the easier it becomes to make good business decisions. Instead of saying that your business serves young people, you could identify your target customers as university students between the ages of 18 and 25 who need affordable professional clothing for internships and job interviews. This level of clarity can influence your pricing, branding, marketing, communication and even the type of products you develop. Create a Clear Value Proposition Your value proposition explains why customers should choose your business. It should clearly communicate the benefit you provide and what makes your business different from the alternatives already available. New entrepreneurs sometimes assume that saying they offer good quality or excellent customer service is enough, but these are things customers already expect. Your strategy should identify something more meaningful. Perhaps your business is more affordable than competitors. Perhaps it provides faster delivery, better convenience, locally produced goods, personalised services or products designed specifically for an underserved group. Whatever makes your business valuable should be easy to explain. If customers cannot quickly understand why your business matters to them, your message may need to be clearer. Understand the Market Before You Enter It Before investing heavily in your business, take time to understand the market. Research businesses already offering similar products or services. TITLE: OpenAI’s AI & Teen Development Research Grant Program 2026

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: October 6, 2026 Applications are open for the OpenAI’s AI & Teen Development Research Grant Program 2026. OpenAI is committing $5 million to support independent research on how generative AI affects the lives and development of young people ages 13–17. Generative AI is becoming part of how teens learn, create, and seek advice. Its effects are likely to be nuanced. They may depend on what teens use AI for, how they engage with it, their individual circumstances, and the support available from families, schools, communities, and technology providers. They want to build a stronger evidence base about the way teens use AI, as well as the impacts of AI on their lives, to inform development of AI products for teens and to help answer major questions facing policymakers and regulators. For example, they aim to deepen industry-wide understanding of the nuances across age and context, efficacy of safeguards and interventions, and the ways that evidence can inform implementation and evaluation. This program will fund independent research into the opportunities and challenges associated with AI use during adolescence, with a particular focus on teens’ social and emotional development. Research Priorities They encourage submissions that relate to one or more of the following topics: Emotional development and well-being: Research on emotion regulation, resilience, identity, agency, self-esteem, and social connection. Social development and relationships: Research on friendships, family relationships, belonging, communication, empathy, social skills, and the relationship between AI and human connection. Patterns, contexts, and variance across demographics: Research on how outcomes vary by time spent, type and purpose of use, age, culture, language, socioeconomic circumstances, and other individual or contextual factors. Mitigations, age-appropriate design, and policy approaches: Research evaluating safeguards, product interventions, AI literacy, parental or educator support, and healthy-use practices. Grant They will award individual research grants up to $1 million and totaling up to $5 million. Eligibility Must be 18 or older; Must be affiliated with a research institution or organization, and/or significant experience relevant to child or adolescent development, well-being, human-computer interaction, AI impacts, or a closely related field; They are seeking to fund research rather than for-profit initiatives, so we will not prioritize for profit organizations at this time. Review Criteria Proposals will be evaluated based on: Scientific rigor: The strength and appropriateness of the research design and analysis Relevance: Examination of a topic relevant to current public discourse on AI Proposal quality: The clarity, focus, and coherence of the application Actionability: The potential to translate findings into guidance for models, products, safeguards, regulatory approaches, or future research Ethics and safeguarding: The adequacy of protections for minors and other participants Feasibility: Whether the project can be completed with the proposed resources and timeline Team expertise: The team’s ability to conduct the proposed work responsibly Inclusion and generalizability: Attention to diverse populations, contexts, cultures, and experiences Complementarity: The extent to which the work adds to existing evidence and complements OpenAI’s internal research agenda Independence and credibility: The project’s ability to produce trustworthy findings regardless of whether those findings are favorable to providers of AI products Application Applications should be formatted as a single-spaced Google doc. Applicants should submit: Project summary: A brief overview of the proposed research and its expected contribution, less than one page. Research proposal: No more than three pages, excluding references, addressing: Research questions Relevant prior research Proposed methods and analysis Study population and recruitment strategy, including evidence of feasibility or access Expected outputs Potential limitations Relevance to the program’s goals Project plan and timeline: Key activities, milestones, and expected completion date. Budget and budget justification: Requested funding, major cost categories, and any other committed

TITLE: Bloomberg Harvard Visiting Scholars Program 2027

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: October 28, 2026 Applications are open for the Bloomberg Harvard Visiting Scholars Program 2027. The Bloomberg Harvard Visiting Scholars Program supports rigorous, policy-relevant research on urban problem-solving and city leadership. The program selects a cohort of researchers whose work has the potential to make meaningful contributions both to scholarship and to real-world challenges. Individuals selected through the application process are appointed as Bloomberg Harvard Visiting Scholars. Scholars may spend either one semester or one full academic year in residence at the Bloomberg Center for Cities at Harvard University. During their residency, scholars focus primarily on advancing their research while engaging with the Center’s intellectual community. This is the inaugural year of the Bloomberg Harvard Visiting Scholars Program. The Center’s goal is to build a lasting and collaborative community of scholars whose work informs the practice of urban problem-solving and city leadership. Benefits The program provides housing near Harvard University. Financial assistance is available to enable scholars to dedicate sustained time to their proposed research project. Depending on individual circumstances, this support may be used to facilitate course buyout or other arrangements that allow scholars to step back from regular academic obligations during the residency period. Eligibility The program invites applications from researchers whose work aligns with the mission of the Bloomberg Center for Cities. Applicants may come from a range of disciplinary backgrounds and be at different career stages. Applicants must hold a doctoral degree (Ph.D. or comparable terminal research degree) and, at the time of application, hold a current faculty or research appointment at a degree-granting university or recognized research institution. Applicants should submit a proposal describing a specific research project that they will pursue during the residency. Proposals should clearly articulate: The urban problem or city leadership challenge that the research addresses The research question(s) that the project examines and the theorey/theories underpinning the work The research design and methodological approach The significance of the project for the fields of research and practice The type(s) of outputs envisioned and potential impacts Applicants may be invited to participate in an interview with members of a selection committee. Following this process, selected applicants will be formally appointed as Bloomberg Harvard Visiting Scholars. Selection Criteria Applications will be evaluated based on: Clarity and significance of the research problem Strength of the research design Potential contribution to scholarship and to the practice of urban problem-solving Alignment with the mission and thematic interests of the Bloomberg Center for Cities Application Application deadline is October 28, 2026. Notice of selection will be sent out in February 2027. Click here to apply For more information, visit Bloomberg Harvard Visiting Scholars Program.

The Open Notebook offers a paid, part-time fellowship program for early-career science journalists. Science journalists (or aspiring science journalists) must have fewer than three years of regular professional science writing experience. Internships and student work do not count toward the fewer-than-three-years requirement. Exceptions to this requirement may also be made for cases in which an applicant has more than three years of professional science writing experience but some or all of that experience is not in English. Applications, including writing samples and letters of recommendation, must be in English. Materials translated into English from another language are acceptable. However, for a successful experience in this fellowship you must have a fairly high level of proficiency in English.) OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: November 1, 2026 Applications for the Bennington College Young Scientists Awards 2026 are now open. The Bennington College Young Scientists Awards celebrate exceptional high school students in grades 9-12 who are thinking critically and creatively about STEM and whose work demonstrates originality, curiosity, and scientific inquiry. The Bennington Young Scientists Awards recognize the next generation of scientists whose work challenges conventions, explores new ideas, and reflects a distinct point of view. Whether you are curious about pollinator diversity in local gardens or the effects of drought stress on plant growth, they want to see work that demonstrates creativity, thoughtfulness, and a willingness to take risks and examine the natural world. Category: Natural Sciences Submit a visual illustration that reflects your specific and/or unique understanding of a particular aspect of the natural world. This could be an expression of a particular scientific concept, the rendering of one or more elements in nature, or a poster reflecting independent research. The goal is to present a personally crafted artifact that demonstrates your knowledge and appreciation of natural science. AI may not be used in any portion of your submission. Benefits Cash Prizes (per category) First place: $2,000 Second place: $1,000 Third place: $500 Distinguished Submissions Distinguished designation by category and grade level: $250 Particularly strong submissions of original work may be selected for this designation. While these submissions may not have been selected for the top three composition prizes, students whose quality is distinguished amongst other entries will be recognized. Scholarships First Place Winners who enroll at Bennington receive a full-tuition scholarship for four years Distinguished Designation Recipients who enroll receive a half-tuition scholarship for four years Finalists who enroll receive a $25,000 annual scholarship for four years. Publication and Showcase Winning and distinguished entries may be featured on Bennington’s website, social media channels, publications, and other showcase opportunities throughout the year. These entries will remain the property of the student. Eligibility Only one submission in this discipline award is allowed per student. Open to students in grades 9–12 worldwide. All entries must be original work and will be reviewed for authenticity. No AI should be used in any portion of your submission. Entries must be reviewed and approved by a sponsoring teacher or mentor. Grade 12 students must submit through the Common Application or Coalition Application process (no application fees required, non-binding, no supplemental essays required). Once the application is complete, they will send a follow-up email with YCA submission instructions. Since so many YCA participants also apply to Bennington, this approach allows students to submit their college and YCA applications through a single process. Students who have already graduated from high school are not eligible. Application Submissions are accepted beginning September 1 at 9:00 AM ET through November 1 at 11:59 PM ET. TITLE: How to Write a Winning Mastercard Foundation Scholarship Essay

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applying for the Mastercard Foundation Scholars Program can feel overwhelming, especially when you know that thousands of talented young people may be applying for the same opportunity. It is easy to assume that the strongest application belongs to the person with the highest grades, the biggest organisation, the most difficult life story or the longest list of achievements. That is not necessarily the case. A good application is one that helps the person reading it understand you. By the time they finish your essays, they should know where you are coming from, what matters to you, what you have already done with the opportunities available to you, what has stood in your way, what you still need to learn and what you hope to do with that learning. Your application should not feel like several unrelated essays written to answer different questions. It should feel like different parts of the same story. From my experience winning the Mastercard Foundation Scholarship, here are 24 tips to help you write a strong essay. 1. Know What You Are Applying For Before writing your essays, spend time understanding the Mastercard Foundation Scholars Program. Do not begin with the questions on the application form. Begin with the scholarship itself. The programme is interested in young people who have demonstrated academic potential, leadership and service to others, particularly those who have faced significant barriers to education. At Edinburgh, there is also a strong focus on climate justice and on the contribution scholars can make to their communities and home countries. This matters because it tells you that academic results alone will not carry an application. Neither will financial need on its own. Leadership without evidence of service is also not enough. The selectors are trying to understand the person behind the qualifications. They want to know what you care about, why you care about it and what you have done about it. 2. Find the Story That Connects Everything Before you start writing, look at your experiences and ask yourself what connects them. Perhaps you grew up in a farming community and became interested in food security because you saw what unpredictable rainfall did to families around you. Maybe your experience of struggling to stay in school led you to begin supporting other girls to continue their education. Perhaps volunteering in a health centre showed you how difficult it was for people in rural communities to access basic healthcare. There should be a reason your past experiences, current work, chosen master’s programme and future plans belong in the same application. You do not need to force every achievement you have ever had into your essays. In fact, trying to mention everything can make an application weaker because the reader finishes without knowing what really matters to you. Choose the experiences that best explain your journey. Your application should make it possible for someone to say, after reading it, “I understand why this person is doing this work, why they want this degree and what they want to do afterwards.” 3. Tell Your Story Without Writing Your Entire Life History One of the easiest mistakes to make is turning the personal essay into an autobiography. You do not need to begin with the year you were born and take the reader through primary school, secondary school, university and every organisation you have joined since then. Choose the moments that mattered. Maybe there was one experience that completely changed how you understood a problem in your community. Maybe there was a period when continuing your education became uncertain. Maybe something you witnessed pushed you to start volunteering

McCain from Arizona. The Gilman-McCain Scholarship provides awards of $5,000 for child and spousal dependents of active or activated United States military personnel during the time of application (including Air Force, Air Force Reserve, Air National Guard, Army, Army National Guard, Army Reserve, Coast Guard, Coast Guard Reserve, Marine Corps, Marine Corps Reserve, Navy, Navy Reserve, Space Force, NOAA Commissioned Corps, and USPHS Commissioned Corps) to study or intern abroad on credit-bearing programs. Award The Gilman-McCain Scholarship recipients are awarded $5,000 to be used toward the cost of study abroad or international internship programs. Eligibility To be eligible for a Gilman-McCain Scholarship, an applicant must be: A citizen or national of the United States; An undergraduate student in good standing at an accredited institution of higher education in the United States (including both two-year and four-year institutions); Dependent (child or spouse) of active or activated United States military personnel during the time of application (including Air Force, Air Force Reserve, Air National Guard, Army, Army National Guard, Army Reserve, Coast Guard, Coast Guard Reserve, Marine Corps, Marine Corps Reserve, Navy, Navy Reserve, Space Force, NOAA Commissioned Corps, and USPHS Commissioned Corps); Recipient of any type of Title IV federal financial aid during the time of application or provide proof that they will be receiving Title IV federal financial aid during their study abroad program or internship; In the process of applying to, or accepted to, a credit-bearing study abroad or internship program. Proof of program acceptance is required prior to award disbursement; Applying for credit-bearing study abroad programs in a country or location with an overall Travel Advisory Level 1 or 2, according to the U.S. Department of State’s Travel Advisory System. It is important to note that certain areas within a country or location that has an overall Travel Advisory Level 1 or 2 may be designated within the Travel Advisory as either Level 3 or Level 4; Gilman scholars will not be allowed to travel to these specific areas. Gilman Scholars are unable to participate in education abroad programs that involve an overseas institution on the Section 1286 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) List of “Foreign Institutions Engaging in Problematic Activities”. Application The Fall 2026 Application is now open for applicants whose abroad programs or internships start between December 1, 2026 to October 31, 2027. This cycle encompasses Winter or January term 2027, Spring 2027, Maymester 2027, Summer 2027, Fall 2027, and academic year 2027-2028 programs. TITLE: AGNES Intra-Africa Mobility Grants for Junior Researchers 2026 (Funded)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: October 16, 2026 Applications are open for the AGNES Intra-Africa Mobility Grants for Junior Researchers 2026. This grant is generously funded by the German Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ) and with the support of the Alexander von Humboldt Foundation (AvH). This AGNES Intra-Africa Mobility Grant for Junior Researchers aims to strengthen the scientific capacity and networking of young researchers in sub-Saharan Africa through the active cooperation of AGNES and potential AGNES members (serving as supervisors for the awardees of this grant). It further supports the alumni of the AvH Foundation in their efforts towards mentoring high potential junior researchers, helping them to access international networks of scientific excellence. AGNES is operating two Intra-Africa Mobility Grants for Junior Researchers for which application may be submitted directly by interested and qualified candidates from sub-Sahara Africa: General AGNES Intra-Africa Mobility Grants for Junior Researchers (Generally for MALE and FEMALE candidates) Special AGNES Intra-Africa Mobility Grants for Junior Researchers (For FEMALE candidates ONLY) Funding 1 Month: up to EUR 2,300 1.5 Months: up to EUR 2,650 2 Months: up to EUR 3,000 Eligibility Direct applications from junior researchers having published at least one article from their thesis work (in a non-predatory journal) will be considered for both AGNES Mobility Grants. The applicant: may be from any academic discipline but must be officially registered for a doctoral degree at a university/tertiary institute in sub-Sahara Africa at the time of application must be a national of a sub-Saharan African country, and must have, at least one already published paper from his/her earlier thesis work (in a non-predatory journal). For the avoidance of doubt, they will only consider journals that are indexed by SCOPUS and Web of Science. The applicant must clearly demonstrate that their work is relevant towards development in sub-Saharan African countries and cannot be conducted in the home country. Only applicants with an identified scientific host and mutually agreed-upon proposal/work schedule will be considered for the Grant. Application Complete applications MUST include the following: A short research/project proposal which MUST be in ENGLISH language (not more than 5 pages) from the junior scientist (applicant) with a short outline of the proposed research activity and a work schedule for achieving the aim(s) of the research project at the host institution. The scientific host must agree in writing to the proposal and time schedule. A standard CV of the applicant which MUST be in ENGLISH language (use the AGNES template). The AGNES CV template can be obtained from here: Download 2026 AGNES Intra-Africal Mobility CV-Template. Official proof of registration for the postgraduate degree (only current doctoral students are eligible). A copy of the official academic transcripts of the applicant, reflecting the grades obtained in the undergraduate and any postgraduate studies. If your transcript is in another language, supply the official explanation of the grading system in English language. TITLE: Digital Science Catalyst Grant 2026 (up to £25,000)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: October 5, 2026 Applications are open for the Digital Science Catalyst Grant 2026. The Digital Science Catalyst Grant is an international initiative to support innovation in new software tools and technologies to advance research and create meaningful change. The program supports and invests in early-stage ideas in the novel use of technology with an award of up to £25,000 for the most promising ideas that aid science and further its impact on society. AI is starting to do research, not just describe it. The next breakthroughs will come from agentic workflows, autonomous and multi-step, that researchers, institutions and funders can actually rely on. For 2026, they are backing the early-stage tools, agents and platforms making that real: AI that acts on research, embedded in the workflows it serves, with provenance, governance and accountability built in. Benefits The award is up to £25,000, but the grant’s real value is the conversations it starts. Our team comes from research and research software, with decades of experience between us. Most applicants do not win an award, but they can come away with advice, introductions and a sharper idea. We invest in the community because we come from it. Eligibility They want early-stage startups, research projects and moonshot thinkers building agentic tools that: Operate across multiple steps, planning, executing and reviewing, rather than answering a single prompt; Embed in the workflows researchers, institutions and publishers already use; Carry audit trails, governance controls and provenance, so the people who rely on them can trust them; Tackle a real problem across the research lifecycle: writing, discovery, evidence synthesis, peer review, funding decisions or research integrity. Application How to test your idea before applying: Name the research decision your agent affects, and who makes it today (who, when, how often). Say where it sits in the research lifecycle: writing, discovery, evidence synthesis, peer review, funding decisions or research integrity. If it isn’t one of these, it probably isn’t a fit this year. Name the tool or system it has to live inside, and who already uses that tool every day. They are more interested in something embedded in real work than a standalone demo. Check the work genuinely needs more than one step. If a single well-written prompt does the job, it isn’t an agentic workflow. Test where it breaks. Give it a task it should refuse, flag or escalate, and record what actually happened. Name your outcome metric, for example reviewer hours saved, time to funding decision, or duplicate work avoided. Click here to apply For more information, visit Digital Science Catalyst Grant.

The fellowship provides a unique opportunity for early-career African women lawyers to increase their strategic litigation, legal representation and advocacy skills and ultimately become the next generation of justice champions for women and children in Africa. The Programme is administered in partnership with the Legal Empowerment Fund at the Fund for Global Human Rights. The Fellowship Programme funds and places ten early-career women lawyers in diverse human rights and justice organizations in Kenya, Malawi, South Africa and The Gambia. These include legal aid providers, select universities with legal aid clinics, and government prosecution services to provide legal services for women and children at all stages of the justice process. The Programme equips fellows with the tools they need to advocate for the rights of women and children especially against child marriage and violence against women and children. Fellows receive immersive practical work experience and hands-on training and carry out a range of duties including legal research, drafting, client support and legal representation in court. In keeping with CFJ’s focus on using technology to increase access to justice through the partnership with Microsoft’s AI for Good Lab and the Oxford Institute of Technology, CFJ fellows will also be trained in and encouraged to apply innovative technological tools to advance their work. Benefits A paid work placement at a human rights organization, a university legal aid clinic, or government legal institution in Kenya, Malawi, The Gambia or South Africa carrying out groundbreaking work to end violence against women and children through legal representation and advice, strategic litigation and the innovative use of technology to inform women of their rights and make prosecutors and pro bono lawyers more efficient. TITLE: Gates Cambridge Scholarships 2027-2028 (Fully-funded)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: October 14, 2026 Applications are open for the Gates Cambridge Scholarships 2027-2028. Gates Cambridge is an international scholarship programme at the University of Cambridge for outstanding postgraduate students who share a potential for social leadership and a desire to improve the lives of others. At its heart are our values of Community, Learning, Internationality, Compassion and Change. Each year Gates Cambridge offers around 70 full-cost scholarships to outstanding applicants from countries outside the UK to pursue a postgraduate degree in any subject available at the University of Cambridge. Approximately two-thirds of these awards will be offered to PhD students, with approximately a third of awards available in the US round and the rest available in the International round. Scholarship A Gates Cambridge Scholarship covers the full cost of studying at Cambridge. It also provides additional discretionary funding. Core components the University Composition Fee at the appropriate rate* a maintenance allowance for a single student (£23,152 for 12 months at the 2026-27 rate; pro rata for courses shorter than 12 months) – for PhD scholars the award is for up to 4 years one economy single airfare at both the beginning and end of the course inbound visa costs & the cost of the Immigration Health Surcharge * The University Composition Fee varies for different types of students; applicants should see the Graduate Studies prospectus for full details about precise amounts. Where a student has been successful in gaining a fee award from public authorities (such as the UKRI) they should accept this award and the Trust will not pay their fee or may share their fee and maintenance costs. Discretionary components The Trust also considers applications for several types of additional funding on a discretionary basis: academic development funding – from up to £750 to up to £4,000, dependent on the length of your course, to attend conferences and courses. Dependent Children Allowance – up to £12,793 per annum for one child and up to £18,244 per annum for two or more children. No funding is provided for a partner. fieldwork – you may apply to keep up to your normal maintenance allowance while on fieldwork as part of your PhD (the Trust does not fund other fieldwork costs as these should be funded by the University Composition Fee). maternity/paternity funding – should you require it, you may apply to intermit your studies for up to 6 months and continue to receive your maintenance allowance during this time hardship funding – for unforeseen difficulties facing the scholar Eligibility You can apply for a Gates Cambridge Scholarship if you are: a citizen of any country outside the United Kingdom applying to pursue one of the following courses at the University of Cambridge: PhD (full-time or part-time*) MLitt (full-time) one-year postgraduate course (full-time), with some exceptions. Gates Cambridge is continuing to pilot a scheme which allows applicants to apply for funding for a part-time doctoral degree (PhD). Selection Criteria The selection criteria are: outstanding intellectual ability reasons for choice of course a commitment to improving the lives of others leadership potential Application To be considered for a Gates Cambridge Scholarship you must complete the admission to a course and a College place section and the Gates Cambridge part of the funding section. Gates Cambridge has access to the full application for admission and funding when reviewing applications. Click here to apply For more information, visit Gates Cambridge Scholarships.

TITLE: New Anglia University: An International Pathway to a Career in Medicine

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
For students considering a career in medicine, choosing a medical school is about more than where they will study. It is also about the clinical environments they will experience, the healthcare systems they will encounter, and how their education will prepare them for an increasingly international medical profession. New Anglia University is an international medical university dedicated to educating and preparing future doctors for careers in a global healthcare environment. Located in Anguilla, a British Overseas Territory in the Caribbean, the University offers a focused pathway in medical education that combines a strong scientific foundation with clinical exposure from the early stages of the program, followed by extensive supervised clinical training through a network of more than 50 hospitals and healthcare organizations across the United States and United Kingdom. A distinctive feature of New Anglia University’s approach is the international structure of its medical education. Students begin their studies at the University’s campus in Anguilla before progressing to supervised clinical training across different healthcare environments. This allows students to develop their medical knowledge within an international setting while gaining experience with different healthcare systems and learning alongside clinicians and multidisciplinary teams. The Four-Year Medical Doctor (MD) Program New Anglia University’s four-year Medical Doctor (MD) program is designed for students who have completed the appropriate prior university-level education and are ready to undertake an intensive medical curriculum. Students begin with approximately 20 months of Basic Sciences education at the University’s campus in Anguilla. During this stage, they build their understanding of the biomedical sciences and the scientific principles underlying clinical medicine. Importantly, clinical exposure begins during the Basic Sciences stage rather than only after students progress to their formal clinical rotations. Alongside lectures, laboratory work, simulation, and practical clinical skills training on campus, students have opportunities for supervised early clinical exposure in healthcare settings in Anguilla. This includes structured observation within emergency care and exposure to pathology services, including the opportunity to observe post-mortem examinations (autopsies). These experiences help students begin connecting the biomedical sciences they study in the classroom with clinical practice and patient care from an early stage of their medical education. Students subsequently progress to 72 weeks of Clinical Sciences, undertaking supervised clinical training through New Anglia University’s network of more than 50 hospitals and healthcare organizations. The clinical curriculum includes core rotations across major areas of medicine, including Internal Medicine, Surgery, Pediatrics, Obstetrics and Gynecology, Psychiatry, and Family Medicine, together with elective clinical experiences. Through these rotations, students develop their clinical knowledge, communication skills, professionalism, and understanding of patient care while learning alongside healthcare professionals in real clinical environments. An International Approach to Clinical Education For students interested in building an international medical career, exposure to different healthcare environments can be an important part of their development. New Anglia University has developed a growing clinical training network encompassing more than 50 hospitals and healthcare organizations across the United States and United Kingdom. Following their Basic Sciences education in Anguilla, students progress into supervised clinical training across this international network. This structure provides students with opportunities to experience medicine across different clinical environments, patient populations, and healthcare systems while progressing through a structured medical curriculum. Rather than limiting medical education to a single campus or healthcare system, New Anglia University’s model combines campus-based scientific education and early clinical exposure in Anguilla with extensive clinical education in international healthcare settings. Who Should Consider New Anglia University? The four-year MD program is particularly suited to students who have already completed the appropriate university-level education and are looking for a direct pathway into medical education. TITLE: Chevening British Library Coptic Collections Fellowship 2027 (Funded)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: October 27, 2026 Applications are open for the Chevening British Library Coptic Collections Fellowship 2027. The Chevening British Library Coptic Collections Fellowship is co-funded by the British Library and the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office. It is open to applications from mid-career professionals from Egypt, Palestine, and Sudan, who have a strong interest in Coptic manuscript heritage and cultural collections. The British Library holds one of the world’s most significant collections of Coptic manuscripts, comprising hundreds of complete and fragmentary codices, as well as papyrus, parchment, and paper fragments documenting more than 1,500 years of Coptic history, theology, and literary culture. This internationally important collection provides unique insights into the history of Christianity, Egypt’s cultural heritage, manuscript production, and scholarly traditions. The fellowship will take place at the British Library, where you will work closely with Dr. Michael Erdman, Head of Asian and African Studies (interim) to lead a research project. You will use your language skills, subject expertise, and professional experience to survey the British Library’s Coptic holdings, enhance catalogue records, investigate collection provenance, and develop new opportunities for public and community engagement. Benefits Each fellowship includes: 12-month period of project-based activity at the British Library Living expenses for the duration of the fellowship Return economy airfare Allowance package for fellowship-related activities Up to £1,000 for approved project-related expenses Eligibility Be citizens of Egypt, Sudan, or Palestine. Applicants should normally be resident in one of these countries, however citizens of these countries who are resident elsewhere in the Middle East and North Africa region in Chevening eligible, ODA-eligible countries (Iran, Iraq, Jordan, Lebanon, Libya, Morocco, Syria, Tunisia, Yemen) may also apply. Applicants must demonstrate a clear intention to return to and contribute to their country of citizenship following the fellowship and must return there for at least one year after the fellowship ends. Have a postgraduate level qualification (or equivalent professional training or experience in a relevant area) at the time of application. Have significant professional and/or academic research experience (at least five years). Be currently employed or enrolled as a PhD candidate (your PhD must not be with a UK/EU or USA university). Have excellent knowledge of Coptic (Sahidic or Bohairic), with knowledge of Arabic and/or Greek desirable. Have good written and spoken English, with the ability to communicate research findings effectively. Have experience of cataloguing and handling manuscript collections, with knowledge of manuscript description standards. Have experience of provenance research and documentation, or a demonstrable interest in this area. Have experience of working with heritage communities or delivering engagement activities related to cultural heritage collections. Application Applications are open until 27 October 2026, at 12:00 (UTC). The duration of this fellowship is 12 months. TITLE: Yenching Academy at Peking University 2027 – Full Scholarship for Master’s Study in China

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: November 30, 2026 Applications are open for the Yenching Academy at Peking University 2027 – Full Scholarship for Master’s Study in China. The Yenching Academy annually enrolls approximately 120 new students from both the Chinese Mainland and abroad, to study, live, and learn together. International students comprise roughly 75% of the student body. This initiative brings together young people who have demonstrated a talent for leadership and innovation. At Yenching, they are immersed in an intensive learning environment where they can explore China and its role in the world—past, present, and future. The Academy’s goal is to shape new generations of global citizens with a nuanced understanding of China. Scholarship The Yenching Academy provides a generous fellowship to all scholars, including: Tuition fees Accommodation Monthly stipend One round-trip travel fare Field study costs Eligibility Applicants should have: Minimum of a Bachelor’s degree in any field, or be currently enrolled in a Bachelor’s program with the expectation of receiving their diploma in August of the intended enrollment year*; An outstanding academic record; Strong interest in interdisciplinary study of China; A record of extracurricular achievement, community engagement, social responsibility, and leadership potential; English proficiency. *Peking University does not allow students to be enrolled in other degree programs whilst studying at the university. Application Candidates may apply through Yenching Academy’s online application portal. Each applicant will create an account on the Yenching Academy admissions portal and submit the following materials in English: Completed online application form; Personal statement (750 words or less); Statement of Research Interest (maximum 1500 words, excluding citations); Curriculum Vitae; Official transcript(s); Diploma(s) or Certificate(s) of Enrollment; Two academic letters of recommendation (Chinese or English): Peking University will only accept recommendation letters written by full professors or associate professors (or equivalent titles). Letters of recommendation must be submitted by professors in the applicant’s intended field of study. English requirements and minimum scores*: IELTS (Academic): Overall 7.0 TOEFL (iBT): Overall 100 Cambridge English Scale (Advanced): Overall 185 CET 6: Overall 600 TEM 4: Pass level of “良好” or above * International applicants whose native language is English, or have graduated from an English-taught degree program (undergraduate or above), are not required to provide an English proficiency test report. Applicants from China’s Hong Kong, Macao and Taiwan Regions (HMT) are required to provide an English proficiency test report, even if they have attended or graduated from an English-taught degree program. Without providing an English proficiency test report, candidates from these regions will need to take English as a Second Language after enrollment at Peking University. For applicants from the Chinese Mainland, an English proficiency test report is a compulsory application material. * English proficiency tests must be taken after September 1, 2025. Currently, they do not accept TOEFL MyBest Scores, TOEFL iBT Home Edition, IELTS Indicator test, IELTS Online, or IELTS One Skill Retake. * Submission of English scores: For IELTS, TOEFL, and Cambridge tests, they will only accept scores sent directly from these organizations. Make sure you choose “Yenching Academy of Peking University” as the designated recipient of your scores when you book the exam time. For TOEFL, use the institution code: C488. For more information, visit Yenching Academy at Peking University.

TITLE: Institute for AI Policy and Strategy (IAPS) AI Policy Fellowship 2027 (Fully-funded)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: September 27, 2026 Applications are open for the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy (IAPS) AI Policy Fellowship 2027. The IAPS AI Policy Fellowship is a fully funded, three-month program for professionals from varied backgrounds seeking to strengthen practical policy skills for securing a positive future in a world with powerful AI. The IAPS Policy Fellowship is designed to cultivate the talent needed to ensure AI policy can meet the magnitude of challenges emerging from the frontier. Participants embed into the live AI policy field, responding to priority policy windows, and developing the skills to further their careers at leading organizations in the field. Fellowship Tracks Two tracks are available to participants: Research Track: The Research track pairs you with an IAPS researcher (or an external supervisor at a partner organization) to produce a substantive piece of AI policy research over the course of the Fellowship. You will scope a question with your supervisor in the first weeks, then take primary ownership of the analysis and writing, with regular feedback on research direction, methods, and drafting for a policy audience. The goal is developing the ability to carry a research project from open question to evidence-based conclusions, and to produce a publishable output. Former Fellows have published reports written during their time with IAPS. Applied Track: The Applied track focuses more on hands-on policy work rather than a single research output. You will work with a supervisor on projects closer to the practice of AI policy that will require adaptability to real-life, evolving situations rather than building deep specialization on a research question. This track would suit people coming from an adjacent field (government, programs, operations, event organizing, grantmaking, etc.) who want to fast-track the conversion of existing professional skills into AI policy experience, or researchers who want to transition to practitioner roles. Former Fellows have run policy workshops, assisted in evaluating grant applications, and collaborated on policy memos. Financial Support Senior Fellows will receive $24,000 and Fellows $18,000 as a stipend to work full-time during the three-month program. Fellows on the DC or London track will also receive an additional $3,000 stipend. They can provide part-time options for exceptional candidates. They will provide financial support for travel and accommodation for the two-week D.C. event. Eligibility They are looking for people who want to develop a career in AI policy and address the lasting implications of frontier AI. They encourage applicants to familiarize themselves with IAPS’s areas of focus by checking out their research. Applicants with policy, technical, academic, and government backgrounds are strongly recommended, but they are open to a wide variety of backgrounds. Application The application takes about 45 minutes, in five sections: About you (5 min): basic details and eligibility. Your experience (5 min): where you have worked, for how long, and what you did. Your motivation (10 min): rank the AI policy issues that motivate you, then two short written answers – a research interest (up to 300 words) and your career goals (150-200 words). Communicating with stakeholders (10 min): one written reply to a policy conversation (100-200 words). Timed reasoning (15 min): logic and reasoning questions with a timer. This comes last, and you start it when you are ready. Click here to apply For more information, visit IAPS AI Policy Fellowship.

MANDATORY
- Work full-time during the three-month program (part-time available for exceptional candidates)

TARGET GROUP
- Professionals from varied backgrounds seeking to strengthen practical AI policy skills

FUNDING / BENEFITS
- Senior Fellows: $24,000 stipend
- Fellows: $18,000 stipend
- DC or London track: additional $3,000 stipend
- Financial support for travel and accommodation for the two-week D.C. event

TITLE: Fung Global Fellows Program at the Princeton Institute for International and Regional Studies (PIIRS) 2027-2028

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: November 16, 2026 Applications are open for the Fung Global Fellows Program at the Princeton Institute for International and Regional Studies (PIIRS) 2027-2028. The program will select early-career scholars from around the world to be in residence at Princeton for an academic year (10 months) and to engage in research and discussion around a common theme. The fellowships will be awarded to those employed outside the United States who have a faculty appointment or a professional research appointment, and they will be expected to return to their positions at the conclusion of the fellowship. Lastly, they must have demonstrated outstanding scholarly achievement and unusual intellectual promise. Early-career scholars will be appointed at the rank of Visiting Research Scholar. Democratic governance faces mounting pressure around the world. The rise of populist movements, declining trust in institutions, polarization, disinformation, and democratic backsliding (including in democracies once considered as consolidated) have prompted renewed debate about whether democracy’s ascendance in the late 20th century was more fragile than assumed. At the same time, democracies have proven resilient in unexpected ways—through grassroots mobilization, institutional safeguards, judicial independence, and civic renewal—raising the question of what, precisely, allows some democratic systems to weather crisis while others erode or collapse. During the 2027-28 academic year, the program theme will be “Democracy in Crisis?” They invite applications from scholars who study the challenges confronting democratic governance and/or the sources of democratic resilience. Projects might explore the drivers and dynamics of populism; the erosion of democratic norms and institutions; the role of media, technology, and disinformation in shaping political life; the relationship between economic inequality and democratic legitimacy; or the strategies through which citizens, civil society, and institutions have defended or renewed democratic practice. They are equally interested in work that interrogates the conceptual and normative foundations of democracy itself – what it means, who it serves, and how it has been imagined and contested across different political and cultural traditions. Salary The salary range is between $100,000 – $135,000. Eligibility Early-career scholars will be appointed at the rank of Visiting Research Scholar. To be eligible, applicants must have received their Ph.D. (or equivalent) generally after September 1, 2017. Candidates who are currently enrolled in a Ph.D. program or employed as postdocs are not eligible to apply. Fellowships will be awarded to those employed outside the United States who have a faculty appointment or a professional research appointment, and they will be expected to return to their positions at the conclusion of the fellowship. Should an offer be made, successful candidates will be required to submit an official letter from their current employer affirming that they would be permitted to accept the offer and to spend the academic year at Princeton University. Fellowships will be awarded to candidates who have already demonstrated outstanding scholarly achievement and exhibit unusual intellectual promise but are still at the beginning of their careers. Criteria for the fellowship include the strength of the candidate’s research projects, the relationship of those projects to the program’s theme, the candidate’s previous scholarly work, the candidate’s ability to contribute to the intellectual life and intellectual exchange of the program, and the candidate’s work experience outside the United States. The selection committee is looking to establish a cohort of fellows whose work represents any region of the world, with any disciplinary background in the humanities and social sciences. Princeton University is an Equal Opportunity Employer and all qualified applicants will receive consideration for employment without regard to age, race, color, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, national origin, disability status, protected veteran status, or any other characteristic
