TITLE: How to Use Opportunity Desk to Reach Your Desired Future

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The future you desire may feel far away, but sometimes the distance between where you are and where you want to be is simply access to the right opportunity. That is where Opportunity Desk comes in. Opportunity Desk connects young people, students, professionals, entrepreneurs and changemakers with opportunities from around the world. From scholarships and fellowships to grants, jobs, internships, competitions, conferences and leadership programmes, the platform helps you discover opportunities that can move you closer to your goals. But finding opportunities is only the first step. The real value comes from knowing how to use them intentionally. Be Clear About the Future You Want Before applying for every opportunity you come across, ask yourself where you want to be in the next three to five years. Do you want to pursue higher education? Build an international career? Grow a business or organisation? Become a leader in your field? Develop new skills? When you understand the future you are building, it becomes easier to identify the opportunities that can help you get there. Make Opportunity Desk Part of Your Routine Great opportunities often come with deadlines, and discovering them too late can mean missing out. Visit Opportunity Desk regularly, follow its updates and set aside time each week to search for opportunities relevant to your goals. Consistency can make a significant difference. Apply Strategically You do not need to apply for every opportunity. Focus on those that align with your interests, experience and long-term ambitions. A scholarship can provide access to education. A fellowship can expand your network. A grant can help you launch an idea. An internship can introduce you to an industry, while a conference can place you in rooms with people who may shape your next chapter. Think of each opportunity as a building block towards the future you want. Do Not Disqualify Yourself One mistake many people make is deciding they are not qualified before even applying. Read the eligibility requirements carefully. If you meet them, give yourself a chance. You do not have to feel completely ready before pursuing an opportunity. Sometimes the opportunities that stretch you the most are the ones that help you grow the most. Keep Improving Your Applications Every application is an opportunity to become better at telling your story. Build a strong CV. Keep records of your achievements and impact. Learn how to communicate your goals clearly. Ask for feedback and improve with every application. Not every application will be successful, but every application can prepare you for the one that eventually changes your life. Turn One Opportunity Into Many When you finally receive an opportunity, do not see it as the destination. Build relationships. Stay connected with people you meet. Share your work. Ask questions. Volunteer for responsibilities and look for opportunities to collaborate. Sometimes the greatest benefit of a fellowship, scholarship, internship or conference is not the programme itself, but the people, knowledge and possibilities it introduces into your life. Start Today Your desired future will not happen simply because you dream about it. You have to intentionally pursue it. Use Opportunity Desk to search, apply, learn and position yourself for the opportunities that align with the person you are becoming. The scholarship, fellowship, grant, job, internship or programme you discover today could become the door that leads you into the future you have been imagining. Your desired future may be one opportunity away. Go for it. For more opportunities, visit OD Blog.

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
For many talented young Africans, the challenge is not a lack of ambition or academic ability, but access to the resources, networks and opportunities that can turn that potential into impact. The Mastercard Foundation Scholars Program was created to help address that gap. Since its launch in 2012, the programme has developed into much more than a traditional university scholarship. Through partnerships with universities and organisations in Africa and internationally, it supports young people, particularly those who have faced barriers to education, to pursue higher education while developing their leadership capacity and preparing to contribute to their communities and the continent. Financial support can include tuition, accommodation, books and educational materials, alongside mentoring, counselling, leadership development and, where necessary, return travel. Importantly, however, the Mastercard Foundation Scholars Program is not administered through one universal application. Each partner institution determines its own programmes, eligibility requirements, selection process and deadlines. (Mastercard Foundation) Explore the Mastercard Foundation Scholars Program. University of Edinburgh Mastercard Foundation Scholars Program 2027/2028 One of the major opportunities prospective applicants should currently be watching is the Mastercard Foundation Scholars Program at the University of Edinburgh. For the 2027/2028 academic year, Edinburgh is offering both on-campus and online postgraduate scholarship routes. The on-campus scholarship supports a one-year, full-time master’s degree and covers approved tuition, accommodation, travel, study materials and a living-cost stipend. Online scholars receive full approved tuition fees, an academic stipend to support access to a laptop and reliable internet, an opportunity to attend an in-person gathering, and participation in the University’s wider Climate Leadership Programme. (Global) What particularly sets Edinburgh’s programme apart is its emphasis on climate leadership. Applicants must demonstrate experience or ambition in addressing the climate crisis, and all Mastercard Foundation Scholars at Edinburgh participate in a Climate Leadership Programme. The University describes the wider programme as developing talented, entrepreneurial and compassionate African leaders equipped to contribute to sustainable transitions. (Global) There is also considerable flexibility in how scholars can study. Eligible on-campus programmes include Africa and International Development, Entrepreneurship and Innovation, Environment and Development, Food Security, Planetary Health, Sustainable Energy Systems, Climate Change Finance and Investment, Environmental Sustainability, Data, Inequality and Society, and Operational Research. Online options include programmes such as International Development, Global Food Security and Nutrition, One Health, Social Justice and Community Action, Digital Education and Data Science Technologies. (Global) Who can apply to Edinburgh? Applicants must be citizens or refugees of an African country and resident in Africa. The WTO Youth Talent Incubator Programme builds on the legacy of the Youth Trade Summit on Gender, which brought together fifty young professionals from academia, research, and government in November 2023. Cost The programme will be held and delivered entirely online and is cost-free. Eligibility Open to young professionals with the skills needed to advance gender equality in global trade. The program aims to provide scholars of Southeast Asia with opportunities for training, networking, and field research to improve competitiveness for the academic and non-academic job markets. TITLE: Olympic Studies Centre PhD Students & Early Career Academics Research Grant Programme 2027

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: September 22, 2026 Applications are invited for the Olympic Studies Centre PhD Students & Early Career Academics Research Grant Programme 2027. The Olympic Studies Centre (OSC) organises an annual research grant programme intended for PhD Students and Early Career Academics engaged in scholarly research on the Olympic Movement, its history and ideals, and the impact of the Olympic Games on the various aspects of contemporary society and culture. The objectives of the programme are as follows: Support PhD Students and Early Career Academics and foster excellence in Olympic related research with a humanities and/or social sciences perspective. Facilitate a research and study visit at the Olympic Studies Centre in Lausanne, Switzerland (the Olympic Capital), and the consultation of the OSC’s collections (including primary sources and the IOC historical archives). Support the next generation of scholars in the field of Olympic studies. Grant Successful applicants will receive a research grant of a maximum of USD $6,000. The total amount to be awarded will be decided by the Grant Programme Selection Committee after full consideration of all elements of the application. Eligibility Students enrolled in a PhD degree programme, with a humanities and/or social sciences perspective, with Olympism, the Olympic Movement or the Olympic Games as, at least, one of the research foci. Students must remain enrolled in the PhD degree programme for the entire duration of the grant, from submission of the application to delivery of the final report. The project presented should demonstrate a clear contribution to the candidate’s doctoral thesis. Academic staff and postdoctoral fellows who completed their doctorate or equivalent highest degree with a humanities and/or social sciences perspective (including masters, depending on the field) in or after 2024 (named or referred to in this programme as “Early Career Academics” (ECA)). ECA applicants must hold a university appointment covering the period of the grant (from submission of the application to delivery of the final report). Application Applications and all supporting documentation must be submitted in either French or English, the two official languages of the Olympic Movement. Completed application files must include the following documents: Official application form duly completed Proof of registration covering the period of the grant (from submission of the application to delivery of the final report), issued by the university administration on institutional letterhead: for PhD students: current proof of doctoral enrolment; for ECA: current proof of a university appointment, including academic/research status. Letter of recommendation written on institutional letterhead, signed and sent by the applicant’s supervisor (for PhD students) or mentor (for ECA). The Selection Committee is particularly interested in the supervisor’s/mentor’s assessment of the following points: the scholarly significance of the research project; the methodology and original nature of the study; the impact of the project on the Olympic Movement; the candidate’s training, abilities, achievements to date and motivation for the research proposed; and the likelihood that the applicant will complete the project on time. If the research proposal includes interviews, surveys or any other methodologies that involve human subjects, human data and/or fieldwork, or as required by the applicant’s home institution, a certificate stating that the project has been approved by the university’s ethics committee must be included. TITLE: Call for Applications: African Food Baskets Country Researchers Program 2026

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: September 6, 2026 Applications are open for the African Food Baskets Country Researchers Program 2026. The Alliance for Food Sovereignty in Africa (AFSA) invites applications from qualified African researchers to support the first phase of the African Food Baskets initiative. Ten Country Researchers will be selected—one from each participating country—to document the foods, dishes, beverages, recipes, food sources, menus, stories, proverbs and cultural knowledge that shape their country’s food heritage. The initiative forms part of the TAFS Project, funded by Sida, and contributes to AFSA’s My Food Is African campaign. It aims to preserve and promote African food knowledge while building a continental resource for advocacy, research, education, communication and policy engagement. Scope of Work The selected Country Researcher will: Attend the AFSA online training on the African Food Baskets Toolkit and complete the practice exercises. Prepare a short country workplan identifying the communities or food territories to be documented, the knowledge holders to be engaged and the fieldwork schedule. Conduct community entry, explain the purpose of the initiative and obtain consent from communities and individual participants before any documentation begins. Collect data using the KoboToolbox modules, meeting at least the minimum country data package set out. Collect and caption photographs and other media in line with the consent recorded in Form 7. Complete the Field Data Quality and Validation Checklist and validate the findings with the communities concerned before final submission. Submit the complete country data package to AFSA together with a short narrative report of no more than eight pages covering the process followed, the people engaged, the main findings, foods identified as being at risk, and recommendations. Benefits Each selected researcher will receive USD $1,000 as facilitation for the assignment. This amount is paid after the complete country data package has been submitted and accepted by AFSA, and it covers the researcher’s time, local travel, communication and community engagement costs. Eligibility Applicants must: Be a national of, or be resident and actively working in, the country they are applying to document. Hold a background in research, preferably in food systems, agriculture, agroecology, nutrition, anthropology, sociology, development studies, environmental studies, cultural heritage or a related field. A postgraduate qualification is an advantage, but strong demonstrated field research experience will also be considered. Have practical experience of qualitative fieldwork, community interviews or participatory documentation. Be able to work in at least one of English, French or Portuguese, and be able to communicate in the main local language of the communities to be documented, or arrange reliable interpretation. Have access to a smartphone, tablet or computer and be willing to learn KoboToolbox. Prior experience with KoboToolbox or similar mobile data collection tools is an advantage. Be able to take clear, well composed photographs of foods, dishes and food environments, or work with someone who can. Be available for the full period. Application Submit the following in a single email: A curriculum vitae of no more than two pages with at least two referees. A country concept note of no more than three pages setting out the communities or food territories you would work with, why you have chosen them, the knowledge holders you would engage, how you would obtain consent, and how you would manage fieldwork within two months. One example of previous relevant work, such as a report, article, thesis chapter or documentation product. Where applicable, the name of the AFSA member organisation you are affiliated with. Applications must be submitted to afsa@afsafrica.org by 6 September 2026 and may be submitted in English, French or Portuguese. For more information, visit African Food Baskets Country Researchers.

The Africa Research Excellence Fund (AREF) Towards Leadership programme aims to empower talented, emerging scientists in Africa to compete successfully for UKRI MRC and other major funding opportunities in global health research. Together they are investing in talented African scientists in Africa, enhancing their global health research and leadership potential. The programme will run in March 2027 consisting of two residential workshops (opening and closing) and one virtual workshop. The curriculum is designed to support engage and enhance the participants’ capabilities and to empower talented, emerging scientists in Africa to compete successfully on a level playing field for UKRI MRC and other major funding opportunities in global health research. The programme is directed towards to winning grant funding, empowering effective teams, collaborating internationally, influencing stakeholders, and building rewarding research careers. The Effective Researcher develops the individual’s ability to envision, plan and action career goals and development trajectory through personal development planning, time management, and mentorship. The Researcher as a Communicator augmenting the individual’s leadership, authorship & authority skills through the use of effective presentations, storytelling and messaging while refining their engagement with research users. TITLE: Swiss Government Excellence Scholarships 2027-2028 for Foreign Scholars & Artists

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: Varies Applications are open for the Swiss Government Excellence Scholarships 2027-2028. Each year the Swiss Confederation awards Government Excellence Scholarships to encourage international exchange and research cooperation between Switzerland and over 180 other countries. Recipients are selected by the awarding body, the Federal Commission for Scholarships for Foreign Students (FCS aka ESKAS). Swiss Government Excellence Scholarships are mainly intended for talented early career researchers (ECRs) from abroad who have already completed their Master’s degree. The scholarship programme is currently open to applicants from 183 countries. Scholarship Types Research: These scholarships are available to postgraduate researchers in any discipline wishing to pursue research at any Swiss cantonal university, university of applied sciences, either of Switzerland’s two federal institutes of technology (ETHZ or EPFL) or at one of the four research institutes within the ETH Domain (PSI, WSL, Empa, Eawag). Prerequisite: the scholarship application must be backed by an academic supervisor in Switzerland who is willing to direct and guide the applicant’s proposed research. Open to PhD Students from 183 countries Required: Master’s Degree and Supervisor Duration: 12 months PhD: Open to PhD Students from 183 countries Required: Master’s Degree and Supervisor Duration: 36 months Art: Art scholarships are open to students wishing to pursue an initial Master’s degree in an artistic field in Switzerland. This scholarship is available to students from a limited number of countries only. Open to Art Students from 26 countries Required: Bachelor’s Degree and Admission or proof of application Duration: 21 months Scholarship Benefits Scholarships: Amount and additional benefits Research fellowships, PhD scholarships and art scholarships: CHF 2,450 per month to cover basic living expenses of one person. Please note: This scholarship is not a salary. No funding is provided for fieldwork and participation in conferences Additional benefits: Health insurance: FCS covers the premiums for compulsory health insurance for scholarship holders from non-EU/EFTA countries. Scholarship holders from EU/EFTA countries must cover these costs themselves. One-time grant of CHF 600 for rental deposit. Half-Fare Travelcard for public transport In addition, the coordinating body organises excursions and activities for federal scholarship holders. Return flight allowance: Scholarship holders from non-EU/EFTA countries receive a return flight allowance (amount determined by country of origin). This allowance may be used up to two months after expiry of the scholarship exclusively for the purpose of returning to the country of origin. Costs to be paid by scholarship holders: Tuition fees: The Federal Excellence Scholarship does not cover tuition or semester fees. In some cases, universities, universities of applied sciences or federal institutes of technology require scholarship holders to pay semester fees (approx. CHF 600 to CHF 2,000 per semester) or reduced tuition fees. In some cases, PhD fees are not waived. Scholarship holders must cover these fees themselves. Conferences: The costs of participating in international conferences are borne by the scholarship holders. Field research: PhD scholarship holders may request to do field research for up to six months (without additional funding). All associated costs are borne by the scholarship holders. Travel expenses: Scholarship holders from EU/EFTA countries must pay their own travel expenses. Eligibility and Application Information on application deadlines and scholarship available by country of origin. Applications are submitted to Swiss diplomatic representations. The FCS assesses scholarship applications according to three criteria. Candidate profile Quality of the research project or artistic work Synergies and potential for future research cooperation By the end of May at the latest, the FCS will announce its decisions regarding the scholarship awards for the following academic year. Click here to find more details and apply. For more information, visit Swiss Government Excellence.

Benefits The Leon Levy Scholarship is a three (3)-year award. Scholars will receive: Annual stipend equals 125% of the National Institutes of Health (NIH) postdoctoral rate, according to the postdoctoral year Fringe benefits at the host institution’s rate for postdoctoral Scholars US$2,000 flexible technology and travel allowance as a one-time award Annual supplement of up to US$10,000 to support care costs (e.g. dependent care) Indirect support to the host institution will be allowed at the standard published rate if less than 20% and capped at 20%. 3-year Membership to The New York Academy of Sciences Participation in a structured Mentorship Program for Leon Levy Scholars Access to leadership and skills-building workshops through The New York Academy of Sciences Access to the community of past and present Leon Levy Scholars and Fellows Grant writing support Eligibility Applicant’s Eligibility By the time of appointment on September 1, 2027, the applicant must: Hold a doctoral degree (PhD, DPhil, MD, DDS, DVM, etc.) Hold a full-time postdoctoral position at an eligible institution, or an institution that has obtained eligibility prior to the closing of the application period, in one of New York City’s five boroughs. TITLE: Global Prize for Innovation in Water (GPIW) 2026

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: September 30, 2026 Applications for the Global Prize for Innovation in Water (GPIW) 2026 are now open. The Global Prize for Innovation in Water (GPIW) is the largest of its kind in the world. It was launched in 2023 as an initiative by the Saudi Water Authority, reaffirming the Kingdom’s pioneering role in promoting research, fostering innovation, and adopting new breakthroughs in the water sector. The prize aims to honor participants and support pioneers from around the globe. Categories The Global Prize for Innovation in Water honors innovative solutions that drive the water sector toward sustainability and efficiency, covering 6 main categories: Advanced Water Production and Desalination Technologies Water Reclamation, Circular Economy, and Zero Liquid Discharge (ZLD) Water Efficiency, Conservation, and Consumption Management Digitalization, Automation, and Smart Water Management Environmental Sustainability and Water Resource Conservation Accessible and Cost-Effective Wastewater Solutions Awards The GPIW offers a financial prize purse, dedicated recognitions, and selected piloting support to advance the development, validation, and market adoption of high-potential water innovations. Awards are distributed as follows: Grand Prizes – USD $100,000 per winner: Two winners in total, one winner from Track A (TRL 1-3) and one winner from Track B (TRL 4-7) Impact Medals – USD $50,000 per winner: Twelve winners in total, six winners from Track A (TRL 1-3) and six winners from Track B (TRL 4-7) Special Mentions – non-monetary recognition: Up to 6 winners in total under Track C (TRL 8–9), with up to two recognitions in each category. Eligibility The GPIW is designed to be open, inclusive, and accessible to a broad range of applicants working to advance innovation in the water sector. Applications are welcomed from, among others: Early-stage startups and venture-backed scale-ups; Multinational corporations and small-to-medium enterprises (SMEs); Universities, public or private research institutes, and laboratories; Non-Governmental Organizations (NGOs) and civil society groups; Public-Private Partnerships (PPPs), municipal water utilities, and utility consortia; Individual innovators, research teams, and project teams. Applicants must ensure that their submission is aligned with at least one Prize track and category and complies with all eligibility requirements set out in these Guidelines. Application The application is organized into 8 sections and can be completed at your own pace: your progress can be saved as a draft, allowing you to leave the form and return at any time before the submission deadline. Applications are only considered once formally submitted; saving a draft does not constitute submission. Before beginning, applicants are encouraged to prepare the required supporting materials and to review the relevant track and category guidance in this document, as the questions presented will vary according to the Technology Readiness Level (TRL) track selected. The application is structured as follows: Applicant Information — Contact details and information about the applicant and their organization. Innovation Overview — A high-level description of the innovation, the selected TRL track and prize category, and the water challenge addressed. Technical Questions — Questions on the scientific, technical, and developmental basis of the innovation, tailored to the selected TRL track. Impact & Market — The scale of the challenge, expected or demonstrated impact, target beneficiaries, competitive landscape, and barriers to adoption. Team & Organizational Maturity — Team expertise, intellectual property status, funding history, and development milestones. Supporting Materials — Upload of the required documents and video presentation (see below). Review — A summary of all responses, which applicants can review and edit before proceeding. Declaration & Submit — Confirmation of accuracy and agreement to the Terms and Conditions before final submission. TITLE: Finding Yourself in a Busy World

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
We live in a world that is constantly moving. There is always somewhere to be, something to achieve, someone to respond to and another goal waiting to be reached. Social media makes it even easier to compare our lives with other people’s progress, careers, relationships and achievements. In all this noise, it is possible to become so busy living that you lose touch with yourself. Finding yourself does not necessarily mean disappearing to somewhere quiet or completely changing your life. Sometimes, it simply means creating enough space to understand who you are, what matters to you and the kind of life you genuinely want to build. Slow Down Enough to Listen Busyness can become a distraction. When every moment is filled with work, messages, meetings and responsibilities, there is little room to reflect. Creating moments of silence can help you reconnect with yourself. This could mean taking a walk without your phone, journalling, praying, sitting quietly or simply spending time away from constant notifications. Ask yourself important questions. Am I happy with the direction of my life? What gives me energy? What drains me? What am I doing because I truly want to, and what am I doing because other people expect it? The answers may not come immediately, but asking the questions matters. Stop Measuring Your Life Against Others Comparison is one of the easiest ways to lose yourself. Someone will always appear to be moving faster, earning more, travelling more, achieving more or living a more exciting life. But you rarely see the complete picture of another person’s journey. Your life does not have to follow someone else’s timetable. Instead of constantly asking whether you are ahead or behind, focus on whether you are becoming the person you want to be. Progress is deeply personal. Remember What Makes You Feel Alive Think about the things that once brought you joy before life became filled with responsibilities. Perhaps you loved writing, painting, dancing, volunteering, reading, travelling, creating things or simply spending time with people you love. Growing older does not mean abandoning the parts of yourself that make life meaningful. Make room for them again. Sometimes finding yourself is not about discovering someone new. It is about returning to parts of yourself you neglected while trying to survive, succeed or meet everyone else’s expectations. Learn to Say No Finding yourself also requires boundaries. You cannot say yes to everything and still have enough time and energy for what truly matters. Not every invitation must be accepted. Not every opportunity is right for you. Not every relationship deserves unlimited access to your time. Saying no can sometimes be an act of self-respect. Protect your time, your energy and your peace. Accept That You Are Still Becoming There is no final version of you. Your priorities may change. Your dreams may evolve. Things that mattered deeply five years ago may no longer feel important. That does not mean you are lost. Growth often involves letting go of identities, relationships, expectations and ambitions that no longer fit who you are becoming. Give yourself permission to change. Spend Time With the Right People The people around you can either help you become more yourself or make you feel as though you constantly need to perform. ay attention to the relationships where you feel safe enough to be honest, imperfect and fully present. Healthy friendships and communities remind you of your values, challenge you when necessary and encourage your growth without asking you to become someone else. Sometimes finding yourself also means recognising the environments where you can truly flourish. Define Success for Yourself

It also advises against measuring one's life against others and encourages individuals to focus on becoming the person they want to be. The guide suggests remembering what makes one feel alive, making room for meaningful activities, learning to say no, accepting that one is still becoming, and spending time with the right people.

TITLE: Finding the Right Investors for Your Business

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Finding an investor is not just about finding someone with money. The right investor should understand your business, believe in your vision and bring value beyond capital. A strong investor can open doors to new markets, introduce you to useful networks, provide strategic advice and strengthen the credibility of your business. This is why choosing the right investor is just as important as raising the money itself. Know What You Need Before approaching investors, be clear about why you need funding and what the money will achieve. Do you need capital to develop a product, hire staff, increase production, enter new markets or improve technology? Investors are more confident when entrepreneurs can clearly explain how the investment will be used and what results it is expected to produce. Choose the Right Type of Investor Different investors support different kinds of businesses. Angel investors often support early-stage companies, while venture capital firms usually invest in businesses with strong growth potential. Impact investors may be interested in businesses that combine financial returns with social or environmental impact. Research potential investors and focus on those whose interests, sectors and investment stage match your business. Show Evidence That Your Business Can Grow Investors want more than a good idea. They want evidence. This could include paying customers, growing revenue, partnerships, successful pilots, repeat customers or increasing demand for your product. Even if your business is still young, showing progress demonstrates that there is a real market for what you are building. Develop a Strong Pitch Your pitch should clearly explain the problem, your solution, target market, business model, traction, competitive advantage and growth potential. You should also state how much you are raising and what the investment will help the business achieve. Keep your pitch simple, compelling and supported by realistic numbers. Build Relationships Do not wait until you desperately need funding before speaking to investors. Attend business events, accelerator programmes, industry conferences and investment forums. Use professional platforms such as LinkedIn to connect with investors and entrepreneurs in your sector. Warm introductions through mentors, founders and business networks can also increase your chances of getting noticed. Look Beyond the Money The best investors bring more than capital. Consider whether an investor can introduce you to customers, future investors, industry experts, partners or new markets. You should also ask whether their values and long-term expectations align with yours. An investor may become part of your business for several years, so choose carefully. Research the Investor Too Investors will investigate your business before investing. You should also investigate them. Speak with founders they have previously supported. Find out how they work with companies, especially when things become difficult. You should also understand investment terms, including equity, voting rights, valuation and board representation, before signing any agreement. Keep Building Fundraising can take time, so continue developing your business while searching for investors. Keep improving your product, speaking to customers, generating revenue and building partnerships. Progress makes your business more attractive and shows investors that you are capable of creating momentum. Find a Partner, Not Just a Funder The right investor should help accelerate your vision, not control it. Instead of asking only, “Who can give me money?”, ask, “Who can help me build the business I want to create?” The right investment partnership can provide the capital, networks and expertise needed to take your business to the next level.

TITLE: Nzalakanda-Noble Dabri Loic from the Republic of the Congo is OD Young Person of the Month – September 2026

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Nzalakanda-Noble Dabri Loïc is a young social entrepreneur from the Republic of the Congo and Co-Founder of AquaPlay, an innovative platform using technology and gamification to transform environmental education and inspire action for ocean conservation. Driven by the belief that technology can do more than entertain, Loïc is working to make learning about marine ecosystems engaging, accessible and action-oriented, particularly for young people. Through AquaPlay, he is demonstrating how locally developed digital solutions can help build a new generation of environmentally conscious citizens. Background and Work Loïc’s work sits at the intersection of technology, youth engagement and environmental conservation. Growing up in the Republic of the Congo, a country rich in natural resources and home to coastal communities whose livelihoods are closely connected to the ocean, he became increasingly concerned about the limited understanding of marine biodiversity and environmental protection among many young people. At the same time, he observed how deeply technology, mobile devices and digital platforms were becoming embedded in the everyday lives of young people. Rather than seeing this growing digital engagement simply as a form of entertainment, Loïc began thinking about how technology could become a tool for education and social action. That thinking ultimately led to AquaPlay. AquaPlay transforms environmental education into an interactive experience. The platform combines learning with gamification to help users understand marine ecosystems while encouraging them to participate actively in protecting them. Through interactive challenges, marine species recognition activities, citizen reporting tools and a community platform, users can learn about biodiversity, identify environmental issues and become part of a wider community taking action for the ocean. At the centre of AquaPlay is a simple idea: environmental education becomes more powerful when people are not only told about a problem but are given practical and engaging ways to become part of the solution. How It Started The idea for AquaPlay grew from a question Loïc kept returning to:What if technology could be used not just to entertain young people, but to educate them and inspire environmental action? For Loïc, the disconnect between young people and environmental issues presented both a challenge and an opportunity. Although conversations around climate change, pollution and biodiversity are becoming increasingly visible globally, environmental information can sometimes feel distant from the everyday experiences of young people. Traditional approaches to environmental education may also struggle to compete with the interactive digital platforms that increasingly shape how young people communicate, learn and spend their time. Loïc wanted to bridge this gap. Together with his co-founder, he began developing AquaPlay as a platform where environmental learning could become interactive, practical and enjoyable. Instead of positioning young people merely as recipients of environmental information, AquaPlay encourages them to become learners, observers, reporters and active participants in protecting marine ecosystems. Successes So Far AquaPlay’s journey has already gained recognition within both the innovation and environmental communities. The project won second place at the Ocean Hackathon in Pointe-Noire, an innovation event bringing together participants to develop solutions to challenges facing the ocean. For Loïc and the AquaPlay team, the recognition provided important validation that a technology-driven approach to marine education and conservation could offer a meaningful response to environmental challenges. AquaPlay reached another major milestone when it was selected among the 12 global finalists of the Opportunity Desk Impact Challenge 2025. Being recognised on a global platform strengthened Loïc’s conviction that solutions developed by young African innovators can respond to local challenges while carrying relevance far beyond their immediate communities. But for Loïc, awards are not the ultimate measure of success. What matters most is AquaPlay’s potential to help young people see themselves differently:

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: November 7, 2026 Applications are open for the Schlumberger Foundation Faculty for the Future Fellowships 2026-2027. The Schlumberger Foundation is an independent non-profit organization that supports education in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM). ​Recognizing the link between science, technology, and socio-economic development – as well as the key role of education in realizing individual potential – the Foundation has focused since its inception on funding a variety of scientific educational programs all over the world.​ Since 2004 the Schlumberger Foundation’s flagship program has been Faculty for the Future. Committed to gender parity in science, the long-term goal of the program was to accelerate gender equality in STEM by creating the conditions that enable more women to pursue scientific careers. ​By accelerating gender equality in STEM, the talent and capacities of these women can be developed for the benefit of their local communities, their regions, and for the wider world. Grant Faculty for the Future grants are based on actual expenses to be incurred by the student only. This typically includes university tuition and bench fees, accommodation costs and a living allowance (e.g., food, a small allowance for books and supplies, medical insurance, childcare, transport costs) in addition to a budget for initial travel to the host country, visa charges as well as conference expenses. Grants can be up to USD $50,000 per year for PhD courses and a maximum of USD $40,000 for post-doc research programs. In addition, and at the discretion of the Schlumberger Foundation, an exceptional childcare grant may be awarded (per eligible child) to a grantee when certain conditions are met. These conditions are provided in the financial section of the application form. Eligibility You are eligible if you: are a female and are a citizen of a low or middle income country where women are underrepresented in Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM) disciplines. You are not eligible to apply if you hold dual citizenship of which one is citizenship of a developed (N.B. If you have been awarded a Faculty for the Future grant and after the award you obtain citizenship of a developed country, the grant will be discontinued as of the date of such additional citizenship); are preparing for a PhD degree or post-doctoral research in a STEM discipline. The Faculty for the Future program does not fund Master level studies; are enrolled, admitted or have applied to a host university/research institute abroad that is well ranked and recognized for strong research in your field. Applications are not accepted where a candidate has not yet applied to a university. If you are applying for a sandwich course the final degree must be awarded by the Host University abroad or jointly (ie., but not solely from the home country university); hold an excellent academic record; are willing to go back to your home country or region upon completion of your studies to contribute to its socio-economic development; have a proven record of teaching experience in your home country and can demonstrate your commitment to going back home to: i) an academic or research position in a STEM faculty; ii) and/or to using your knowledge to become a STEM entrepreneur to help resolve regional challenges in your local community/region; iii) and/or to demonstrating leadership by contributing to the public sector using your scientific skills to help provide evidence-based support for STEM policy making; can demonstrate leadership skills, active community outreach and have a track record in encouraging young people, particularly girls and women into STEM. Schlumberger employees are not eligible to apply for Faculty for the Future grants. Selection Criteria A successful application

TITLE: Vital Impacts Environmental Photography Fellowships and Mentorships 2027

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: December 1, 2026 Applications are open for the Vital Impacts Environmental Photography Fellowships and Mentorships 2027. The Vital Impacts Environmental Photography Fellowships and Mentorships support visual storytellers undertaking long-term documentary photography projects that explore environmental and conservation challenges and, importantly, the people and communities working toward solutions. The program has a dual purpose: to provide financial support and mentorship to photographers developing significant bodies of work while fostering meaningful collaboration with communities and organizations engaged in environmental and wildlife conservation. They are particularly interested in stories that move beyond documenting environmental problems to illuminate the people, communities, and initiatives working toward meaningful solutions. Benefits In 2027, Vital Impacts will award: One $20,000 fellowship to an established environmental photographer; Six $5,000 fellowships to emerging photographers from around the world; and Ten mentorships to photographers whose work demonstrates strong potential and would benefit from additional guidance and professional support. Eligibility Vital Impacts is particularly interested in photographers who have a meaningful, established relationship with the people, places, and issues they are documenting. They believe the strongest environmental stories often emerge from photographers who have taken the time to listen, build trust, understand context, and return to a story over time. They strongly encourage applications from photographers documenting environmental and conservation stories in their own communities. Local photographers bring perspectives, knowledge, access, and relationships that can offer a depth and authenticity that outsiders may not have. At the same time, they recognize that meaningful relationships with a community or issue can take many forms. You do not have to live permanently in a place to have a genuine connection to it. They will also consider photographers who can demonstrate sustained knowledge and engagement through recurring travel, long-term collaboration, professional or academic experience, or other meaningful relationships with the community or issue they propose to document. Applicants should clearly demonstrate why they are the right person to tell this story: what they know, whom they know, what relationships they have built, and what perspective they bring that will allow them to tell the story with depth, context, and care. They are looking for photographers who are committed to long-term storytelling rather than short-term access—photographers willing to invest the time necessary for trust to develop, relationships to deepen, and more nuanced stories to emerge. Application All applicants must: Submit up to 20 JPEG images representing one or two bodies of work or photo stories. Applicants may submit 10 images from one project and 10 from another, or, if preferred, up to 15-20 images from a single project. The selection should demonstrate the applicant’s experience and ability in documentary storytelling, rather than simply present a collection of individual photographs. Submit a 25-word synopsis of the proposed project. Submit a 500-word project statement that describes the project, the environmental issue it explores, and the personal connection that drives the work. The statement should articulate what the photographer hopes the project will reveal, communicate, or change—and the impact they hope it will have on audiences, communities, or conservation efforts. Submit a biography of up to 1,500 characters. Provide requested social media information. Agree to abide by the Vital Impacts Code of Ethics. Agree to and sign the Vital Impacts Environmental Fellowship or Mentorship Agreement if selected. Click here to apply For more information, visit Vital Impacts Environmental Photography Fellowships and Mentorships.

TITLE: Center for Democracy & Technology (CDT) Non-Resident Fellows Program 2026

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: September 18, 2026 Applications for the Center for Democracy & Technology (CDT) Non-Resident Fellows Program 2026 are now open. The Center for Democracy & Technology (CDT)’s Non-Resident Fellows (NRF) Program brings leading scholars and academics into direct engagement with CDT’s policy work. The program provides Fellows with opportunities to share their research and expertise with CDT staff, engage in policy discussions, and help inform the organization’s thinking on emerging technology and its impact on society. Fellows represent a diverse range of academic disciplines, institutions, and areas of expertise, reflecting the increasingly interdisciplinary nature of technology policy. From law and political science to computer science, sociology, economics, and beyond, NRFs bring perspectives that help CDT better understand the complex ways technology shapes — and is shaped by — their institutions, communities, and everyday lives. Through this engagement, the program seeks to bridge the gap between academic research and public-interest technology policy, creating meaningful opportunities for scholars and practitioners to learn from one another and translate research into actionable insights. Fellows also become part of a broader community of researchers and technology policy experts, providing opportunities to build relationships, exchange ideas, and collaborate on issues at the forefront of technology and democracy. Benefits At the start of their program, CDT conducts an orientation program that includes details on how Fellows work with CDT, how CDT promotes Fellows’ research, and how to participate in the tech policy process. CDT commits to providing regular updates on key tech and internet policy developments, engaging fellows in relevant working groups, and offering expert insights on Fellows’ research interests. All Fellows are invited to attend certain CDT-branded public events and webinars, including our Annual Dinner, Tech Prom, as guests of CDT. As a CDT Non-Resident Fellow, you’ll be an active part of our community, with invitations to events and programs over the course of the program. You’ll also engage directly with our experts. In turn, you will have the chance to provide feedback and suggestions to CDT, contributing to our work on developing trends and issues. Eligibility Qualified applicants commit to a two-year, nonresident engagement and must hold a full-time position at an academic institution. Candidates should have published impactful work in peer-reviewed academic venues and have experience working on tech policy issues relevant to CDT’s areas of work, with a particular emphasis on U.S. and EU developments. The program is not open to current students or post-doctoral researchers, and candidates ideally possess a terminal degree (Ph.D., J.D., etc.) or equivalent experience in their respective field of study. Application Send a full CV, a relevant writing sample and a cover letter, describing your interest in the position and your experience/qualifications for such work, by clicking the “apply for this position”. These materials should be compiled into one PDF or document for submission. For more information, visit CDT Non-Resident Fellows Program.

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: November 16, 2026 Applications are open for the Wallace Fellowships 2027-2028 at Harvard University. The Wallace Fellowships are designed for scholars who explore the historiography and impact of the Italian Renaissance in the Modern Era (19th-21st centuries). They are made possible by a generous grant from The Lila Wallace – Reader’s Digest Fund. Projects could address a range of topics from historiography to the reaction to, transformation of, and commentary on the Italian Renaissance and its ties to modernity. Also, welcome are projects on museum and collecting history and on the survival of the Renaissance in modern art and architecture (including photography and landscape architecture), in literature and music, and in philosophy and political thought. I Tatti offers Fellows the precious time they need to pursue their studies with a minimum of obligations and interruptions together with a maximum of scholarly resources—a combination that distinguishes the Harvard Center from similar institutions. Each year, a limited number of activities organized at I Tatti are reserved for the Fellows, and they are expected to join the wider community at conferences, lectures, and concerts. This is a residential fellowship of 4 or 6 months in length. Up to four fellowships will be awarded every year. Benefits The grant is USD $5,200 per month, plus a one-time supplement (maximum USD $1,800) towards relocation expenses. In light of the residential nature of the fellowship Fellows must live in the Florence area and spend at least three days a week at the center. When possible, an apartment will be set aside for the Fellow’s use, rent free, but with charges for utilities. If an apartment is not available, a housing subsidy will be offered to help offset rental costs. Eligibility At the time of application, scholars must have a PhD in hand and will be asked to upload a scan of the certificate. They may not be working on a second PhD at the time of application. They should work solely on the project with which they applied and are not permitted to work simultaneously on editing other book or article projects. The proposed research project may represent a segment of a larger project. Applicants must be conversant in English and have familiarity with Italian. Priority will be given to early and mid-career scholars. Projects can address the historiography or impact of the Renaissance on any field, including art and architecture, landscape architecture, history, literature, material culture, music, philosophy, religion, and science. It must be possible for applicants to carry out most of their research in Florence. I Tatti welcomes applications from scholars from all nations and gives special consideration to candidates without regular access to research materials and facilities in Italy. TITLE: How to Use the Internet to Make Money

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The internet has completely changed how people work, build businesses and earn money. Today, you do not necessarily need a physical office, large capital or connections to begin creating an income. With a smartphone or computer, internet access, useful skills and consistency, you can connect with people and organisations willing to pay for what you know, create or can do. However, making money online is not magic. The internet is simply a marketplace connecting people who have skills, knowledge, products and solutions with people who need them. The most important question is therefore not simply, “How can I make money online?” but “What value can I provide that someone is willing to pay for?” 1. Freelancing: Turn Your Skills into Income Freelancing is one of the easiest ways to begin earning money through the internet. A freelancer provides services to individuals, businesses or organisations without necessarily becoming a permanent employee. Writing, graphic design, video editing, website development, social media management, virtual assistance, research, data analysis, translation, voice-over work, grant writing and presentation design are examples of skills that can be offered online. Platforms such as Upwork and Fiverr have made it possible for freelancers to connect with clients across different countries. You do not have to wait until you consider yourself an expert. Start with something you can already do reasonably well, create samples of your work and continue improving. Your first few projects can help you build experience, testimonials and a portfolio that makes it easier to attract better-paying clients. 2. Become a Virtual Assistant The growth of remote work has created significant opportunities for virtual assistants. Entrepreneurs, executives, organisations and small businesses increasingly need people who can provide administrative support without being physically present in an office. A virtual assistant may manage emails, schedule meetings, conduct research, prepare documents, organise calendars, respond to customers or support social media activities. If you are organised, reliable and comfortable using digital tools, this can be a practical way to begin earning online. As you gain experience, you can specialise in areas such as executive assistance, project management, social media support or customer service. Specialisation can help you become more valuable and increase what you can charge. 3. Create Content and Build an Audience Social media is not only for entertainment. It can also become a business platform. YouTube, TikTok, Instagram, Facebook, podcasts, blogs and newsletters allow ordinary people to build audiences around their knowledge, experiences and interests. You could create content about education, careers, fashion, technology, food, entrepreneurship, development, parenting, travel or almost any subject you understand well. As your audience grows, opportunities may emerge through advertising, sponsorships, partnerships, consulting and the sale of your own products or services. You do not necessarily need millions of followers to make money. A smaller community that trusts your knowledge and recommendations can sometimes be more valuable than a very large audience with little connection to your work. Focus first on creating useful content and building trust. 4. Sell Digital Products One of the most interesting opportunities created by the internet is the ability to create something once and sell it many times. Digital products require no physical shop and can often be sold to customers anywhere in the world. You could create an e-book, online course, template, educational guide, business toolkit, budgeting resource, workbook or other downloadable product based on something you understand well. For example, someone who is good at writing CVs could provide individual CV-writing services while also creating a professional CV template and guide that people can purchase online. Deadline: September 19, 2026 Applications are open for the UNDP Responsible Digital Transformation: Impact Assessments for AI & Data Governance Course 2026. UNDP is launching Responsible Digital Transformation: Impact Assessments for AI and Data Governance, a 4-week online course designed to help public-sector professionals translate responsible AI principles into practice. As governments accelerate digital transformation, the use of AI and data-driven systems in public services is rapidly expanding. These technologies are reshaping service delivery while introducing new challenges around fairness, transparency, accountability, and inclusion. This course equips policymakers and practitioners to move beyond general principles and awareness, and apply practical impact assessment tools to real governance decisions involving AI, digital public infrastructure and data-driven public services. Building on UNDP’s Human Rights Impact Assessment (HRIA) methodology, the course guides participants through a structured process to scope a use case, identify risks and impacts, and develop mitigation and governance recommendations. By the end of the course, participants will have developed a draft impact assessment and mitigation plan for a real-world digital or AI governance use case relevant to their institutional contexts. Costs With the generous support of the Global Gateway strategy of the European Union, this course is free for selected participants. Eligibility Participants should have a basic understanding of digital systems and AI, and ideally two or more years of experience in digital policy/transformation, ICT, or governance, dealing with various governance frameworks for digital systems. Those who have a strong interest in applying practical risk assessment tools are particularly encouraged to apply. Important additional requirements: Applicants must hold an undergraduate degree in a relevant field or have a minimum of three years of experience in the above-mentioned areas if they do not hold a university degree. Possess a fluent level of English. Complete the application questionnaire, provide a motivation letter and attach an up-to-date CV. Government officials and policymakers from developing countries, particularly women, are encouraged to apply. Application Selection will be conducted by the course organizers, who will consider the above entry requirements along with an analysis of the application questionnaire and the motivation of each applicant. TITLE: Cybersafe x SANS AI Security Fellowship 2026 (Fully-funded)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: September 10, 2026 Applications are open for the Cybersafe x SANS AI Security Fellowship 2026. The CyberSafe X SANS AI Security Fellowship is a fully funded, nine-month advanced training and certification programme for experienced African women in cybersecurity who are ready to specialise in securing AI systems and applications. Over the course of the fellowship, participants move from foundational AI security literacy to advanced application security and automation practice, building the technical depth to defend, build, and automate secure AI systems. The programme brings together two complementary strengths: CyberSafe Foundation‘s pipeline of capable women across the African cybersecurity community, built over years through programmes like CyberGirls, and SANS Institute‘s curriculum, labs, and certification path. It’s a direct answer to a widening gap. AI security is one of the fastest-growing and least-staffed disciplines in cybersecurity, and this fellowship is designed to put its fellows at the front of that demand curve, not the back of it. Benefits The fellowship is fully funded. SANS provides the training and certification pathway as an in-kind contribution, and fellows do not pay tuition. Other benefits include: Specialised AI security expertise: Move beyond general cybersecurity knowledge into practical skills covering LLMs, generative AI applications, RAG systems, AI threat modelling, application security, and security automation. Hands-on practice: Build, secure, analyse, and defend systems through labs designed around real AI security challenges. Globally recognised certifications: Preparation for the GIAC AI Platform Security (GAIPS) and GIAC AI Security Automation Engineer (GASAE) certifications. Instruction from leading practitioners: Courses are taught by working AI security consultants, researchers, and course authors. Mentorship and Structured support Eligibility This fellowship is designed for experienced cybersecurity professionals who are ready to specialise. You may be a strong fit if you can say yes to all of the following: You are a woman older than 21. You are African, speak English, and currently reside in an African country. You have at least three years of hands-on cybersecurity experience. You have a genuine interest in AI security. You can commit to the full fellowship, including dedicated exam preparation windows. You are willing to complete the prerequisite AI security course as part of the application process. This fellowship is for you if you have already built cybersecurity experience and are asking what comes next: you want to understand the security implications of AI systems, gain practical exposure to emerging AI attack surfaces, and develop expertise that sets you apart in a fast-changing market. TITLE: Machine Alignment Transparency & Security (MATS) Residency Program 2027

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: October 31, 2026 Applications are open for the Machine Alignment Transparency & Security (MATS) Residency Program 2027. The MATS Program seeks individuals who are deeply motivated by AI alignment, transparency, and security, and who are equipped with the skills and mindset to contribute to cutting-edge research. The Residency is for people who have already produced research-caliber work, not for those hoping to begin. They look for at least one substantial piece of work in which you took a hard, open-ended problem, applied rigorous methods, and produced a result you were meaningfully responsible for, whether a paper, a technical report or evaluation, a serious empirical or policy analysis, or a research-grade modeling or software project. That work need not be published, in AI safety, or done in a role with ‘researcher’ in the title: confidential work, unpublished work, and rigorous research done inside industry, policy, or other settings all count, provided the rigor plausibly transfers to safety-relevant problems and you can make that case. What matters is the research itself, so a career outside research, on its own, is not the same evidence: if your strongest work has not involved sustained, self-directed inquiry into a difficult problem, the Residency is probably not the right fit yet. Support MATS provides visa support for those relocating from abroad. Eligibility They assess the quality and seriousness of your work, not the titles or credentials on your CV. You do not need a PhD, a role with “researcher” in your title, an extensive publication record, or a prior background in AI safety to be a strong applicant. The Residency is looking for talented individuals capable of producing outstanding AI safety research, including many whose best work is confidential, unpublished, or outside traditional research roles. Application All applicants submit the following materials through the online application: A short profile and eligibility section: Your contact details, current affiliation, CV (maximum 2 pages), office preference, availability for the intake, work-authorization status, highest degree, and any previous MATS involvement. This takes a few minutes, is mostly for routing and logistics, and is not itself assessed. Track choice: Your chosen track, and a two-to-three-sentence note on why it fits. Reviewers use this note to spot early on whether a different track might suit you better. References: Submit two references who can speak directly to the quality of your work. If your strongest work is confidential or was completed as part of a larger team, your referees may attest to your contribution in place of publicly available evidence. Some tracks have additional requirements for referees. See the track-specific requirements below. Representative work sample: Submit one work sample that best represents your strongest or most relevant work. This might include a paper, repository, technical report, evaluation, policy analysis, or another substantial research output. Written responses: Complete two short written responses and a brief counterfactual question about what you would do if you were not offered a place in the Residency. Applications are reviewed by the MATS Residency team with input from the program’s advisors where appropriate. You will hear about the outcome of your application by the end of November 2026. Shortlisted applicants will then be invited to an interview or a paid work test in the first week of December 2026, depending on track and research area. Information about the interview and the panel members will be shared beforehand. Selected Residents will be informed by the end of 2026, with a plan to start in early 2027. Click here to apply For more information, visit MATS Residency Program.

TITLE: Berenson Fellowship 2027-2028 at Harvard University (Funded)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: November 16, 2026 Applications are open for the Berenson Fellowship 2027-2028. This Fellowship, made possible by The Lila Wallace – Reader’s Digest Fund, is designed for scholars who explore “Italy in the World.” Projects should address the transnational dialogues between Italy and other cultures (e.g. Latin American, Mediterranean, African, Asian etc.) during the Renaissance, broadly understood historically to include the period from the 14th to the 17th century. It is named after Bernard Berenson, who in his 1956 statement ‘On the Future of I Tatti’ expressed the hope that not only would scholars come from many countries, but that they would also travel in “what was the ancient Oecumene, not going farther East than the Euphrates and not farther South than Egypt and the great desert of North Africa” and be intimately acquainted with the Mediterranean countries and their “Hinterland.” Taking a broad geographic view of the Renaissance more than half a century ago, Berenson was a pioneer of the geographically expansive approach to the early modern world that this Fellowship wishes to encourage. Scholars working in all the fields supported by I Tatti—architecture and the arts, history, philosophy, literature, music and history of science—are encouraged to apply. I Tatti offers Fellows the precious time they need to pursue their studies with a minimum of obligations and interruptions together with a maximum of scholarly resources—a combination that distinguishes the Harvard Center from similar institutions. Each year, a limited number of activities organized at I Tatti are reserved for the Fellows, and they are expected to join the wider community at conferences, lectures, and concerts. This is a residential fellowship of 4 or 6 months in length. Up to four fellowships will be awarded every year. Benefits The grant is USD $5,200 per month, plus a one-time supplement (maximum USD $1,800) towards relocation expenses. In light of the residential nature of the fellowship, Fellows must live in the Florence area and spend at least three days a week at the center. When possible, an apartment will be set aside for the Fellow’s use, rent free, but with charges for utilities. If an apartment is not available, a housing subsidy will be offered to help offset rental costs. Eligibility At the time of application, scholars must have a PhD in hand and will be asked to upload a scan of the certificate. They may not be working on a second PhD at the time of application. They should work solely on the project with which they applied and are not permitted to work simultaneously on editing other book or article projects. The proposed research project may represent a segment of a larger project. Applicants must be conversant in English and have familiarity with Italian. Priority will be given to early and mid-career scholars. It must be possible for applicants to carry out most of their research in Florence. I Tatti welcomes applications from scholars from all nations and gives special consideration to candidates without regular access to research materials and facilities in Italy. Application Applications can be written in English or Italian and must be submitted electronically by midnight (Cambridge, MA time) on November 16, 2026. Scholars can apply for only one type of fellowship at I Tatti Fellowship per academic year. Click here to apply For more information, visit Berenson Fellowship.

TITLE: New_ Public Entrepreneur in Residence Program 2026 ($22,500 stipend)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: September 9, 2026 Applications are open for the New_ Public Entrepreneur in Residence Program 2026. New_ Public is a launchpad for mission-driven entrepreneurs building the future of human connection. This fall, they are piloting an entrepreneur in residence program — a virtual residency that includes a stipend, expert advice, a community of ambitious peers, and time to go from early hunch to conviction and clarity. If you want to build better social technology and have a hunch you want to explore. If you are interested in creating platforms that increase social trust, agency, and belonging, rather than atomize and enrage us, apply. The residency is structured around one goal: move from early hunch to clear idea and conviction in three months. Explore widely and be your most productive self. With a stipend and an open calendar, you have self-directed time to prototype your ideas, test your assumptions, and get something real out into the world. Participate fully in the residency. That means regular check-ins with your New_ Public point of contact, engagement with other residents and our broader team, and openness to candid feedback on your product and strategy. Engage seriously with go-to-market questions. Who is your user? How will they find you? What’s the path to sustainability? We will push on these questions and help you find answers based on evidence, not assumptions. Help build this program. As the first cohort, your experience will directly shape how the entrepreneur in residence program works going forward. They will ask for your honest feedback on what’s useful, what isn’t, and what’s missing — and they will adjust in real time. If you need a fully polished program with every detail locked in on day one, this isn’t the right fit. But if you thrive in environments where you’re helping build the thing you’re participating in, they want to talk. At the end of the three months, each resident will have a clear picture of where their product stands: what’s working, what isn’t, and what it would take to reach the next stage. Benefits $22,500 stipend plus $1,500 toward an AI coding tool of your choice Hands-on product and strategy support through office hours with senior New_ Public staff and advice from outside experts Access to five years of New_ Public’s research on moderation, governance, community stewardship, and platform design Introductions to New_ Public’s network — spanning major platforms, startups, academic researchers, and philanthropic partners — to help with early user testing, community partnerships, product feedback, and possibly fundraising The pilot cohort will also kick off together at an in-person New_ Public retreat in Philadelphia in October. Eligibility Open to applicants based in the United States, Canada, or Mexico. As they establish this program, they want the cohort to be in similar time zones and be able to stay closely connected with the New_ Public team, most of whom are on the West Coast. They are looking for people with entrepreneurial drive who are ready to build their next thing. Application The deadline to apply is 11:59pm PST on Wednesday, September 9, 2026. Click here to apply For more information, visit New Public Entrepreneur in Residence.

TITLE: Asian Development Bank-Japan Scholarship Program 2026

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: December 1, 2026 Applications for the Asian Development Bank-Japan Scholarship Program 2026 are now open. The Asian Development Bank – Japan Scholarship Program (ADB-JSP) provides support for Master’s degree study in ADB-JSP approved fields of study at the University of Hawai‘i at Mānoa (UHM), and for participation in the educational, residential, and leadership development programs at the East-West Center (EWC). The ADB–JSP scholarship was established in April 1988 with financing from the Government of Japan to strengthen human resource capacity in Asian Development Bank developing member countries. It aims to provide an opportunity for well-qualified citizens of ADB’s developing member countries to undertake graduate studies in economics, management, science and technology, and other development-related fields at participating academic institutions in the Asian and Pacific Region. After completing their studies, scholars are expected to return to their home countries to apply and share their new knowledge and skills to promote socioeconomic development. Benefits The ADB-JSP scholarship provides the following support for Master’s degree study at the University of Hawaii at Manoa: Full tuition and fees, Roundtrip travel to Honolulu from the applicant’s home country, Housing in East-West Center residence facilities, Monthly stipend, Funds for textbooks, Health insurance, US visa sponsorship (J-1 Exchange Visitor). Eligibility Be a citizen and current resident of a developing member country of the Asian Development Bank and not more than 35 years old at the time of application. Have a 4-year bachelor’s degree or the equivalent of a 4-year Bachelor’s degree, at the time of application. (An equivalent could be a 3-year Bachelor’s degree plus a 1-year Master’s degree, or a 2-year bachelor’s degree plus a 2-year Master’s degree. This is subject to review.) Have at least 2 years of full-time professional work experience after a university degree at the time of application. Take one of the English proficiency tests; the minimum acceptable scores are 550 for the paper-based TOEFL; 213 for the computer-based TOEFL; and 79-80 for the internet-based TOEFL iBT; 95 for the DUOLINGO; or 6.5 for the IELTS. Results must be taken from a test within the past two years. Application Click here to apply For more information, visit Asian Development Bank-Japan Scholarship Program.

TITLE: WFP Innovation Accelerator x Adaptation Fund Climate Innovation Accelerator (AFCIA) 2027

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: September 6, 2026 Applications are open for the WFP Innovation Accelerator x Adaptation Fund Climate Innovation Accelerator (AFCIA) 2027. Extreme weather events are placing growing pressure on food systems around the world. Droughts, floods, storms and rising temperatures are disrupting food production, threatening livelihoods and increasing food insecurity for vulnerable communities. Latin America and the Caribbean is one of the world’s most climate-vulnerable regions. Increasingly frequent shocks and environmental degradation are putting additional strain on livelihoods and food systems, making it harder for communities to adapt and thrive. Yet across the region, innovators are developing new ways to build resilience and help communities adapt to the new realities. To support these efforts, the World Food Programme (WFP), in partnership with the Adaptation Fund, launched the Adaptation Fund Climate Innovation Accelerator (AFCIA). Through its third edition in Latin America and the Caribbean region, WFP implemented AFCIA aims to identify, support and scale innovative solutions from across the region, or those with strong potential for implementation there, that strengthen resilience, improve food security and help vulnerable communities adapt. Eligibility Your organization must be an established legal entity (for-profit, not-for-profit, social business, NGO, INGO). Your organization should have a presence in one of the three countries of implementation (Dominican Republic, El Salvador and Peru). This could take the form of a country office or other permanent presence, subsidiary, long-term operations or partnerships in the country. Your innovation addresses at least one of the above-mentioned priority areas related to pressing challenges faced in the climate adaptation space of the country of implementation. Your innovation must be at least in the seed stage. Solutions that are still at the idea, research or early pre-seed stage are not eligible. Your innovation should have a clear pathway to scale, adequate resources and a proposed plan to implement during the nine-month Sprint with the available funding. Applicants are expected to have strong intentions to collaborate with relevant humanitarian stakeholders, build relationships with the country offices, and connect with the innovation ecosystems. Evaluation Criteria Following the requirements mentioned on the left, your application will be evaluated according to the following criteria: Level of innovation/innovativeness: The solution is novel, innovative and has a strong climate adaptation regarding the mentioned themes. Relevance to the context: The solution addresses at least one of the above-mentioned priority areas, is suitable for at least one of the three country contexts, and provides concrete solutions to end-users or the ecosystem. Financial sustainability and scalability: The solution showcases a clear business model and a robust sustainable revenue model relative to its maturity stage. Team expertise and capabilities: Proven competence, technical coherence, commitment, motivation, entrepreneurial mindset and a diverse and inclusive team. Climate adaptation: The solution effectively enhances resilience to climate impacts, promotes sustainable practices, improves resource efficiency and facilitates adaptive measures to address climate-related challenges. Level of Impact: Evidence of tangible historical and projected impact towards solving a defined challenge related to climate adaptation, demonstrating long-term, sustainable change beyond the grant period. Environmental and social sustainability: The solution adheres to the environmental and social principles of the Adaptation Fund. Established in 2010 with generous support from the Malú and Carlos Alvarez Family, the Student Scholars Program offers 25 undergraduate students from Council communities the opportunity to attend the National Conference at no cost.
