TITLE: Africa No Filter Voices for Climate Justice Program 2026 (up to $4,000)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: September 25, 2026 Applications are open for the Africa No Filter Voices for Climate Justice Program 2026. Across much of Africa, climate finance is arriving as debt rather than as the grants it should be. Instead of receiving support that reflects the continent’s minimal contribution to the crisis, African nations are being pushed further into debt through loans, with many governments spending more on debt repayment than on health or climate adaptation combined. Africa No Filter is looking for journalists, content creators, podcasters, vloggers, muralists, data visualizers from Mozambique, Uganda, Nigeria, Angola, Chad, the Republic of Congo, Tanzania, South Sudan, Malawi, and Zambia to take part in the Voices for Climate Justice initiative. They are looking for creative ideas that can help explain how climate change, debt, gender, and fossil fuels affect people and communities across Africa; whether you tell stories through video, podcasts, articles, murals, data visualization, they want to hear from you. Selected storytellers will receive training in climate justice, data storytelling, and narrative framing before working with researchers and partners to develop accurate, engaging stories based on research. Benefits The 12-month program is delivered in partnership with Comic Relief, and will support 15–20 storytellers with training, mentorship, content amplification and grants of up to US$4,000 to create powerful stories that spark public conversation and inspire action. Eligibility You must: Must be a storyteller ( journalists, content creators, podcasters, vloggers, muralists, data visualizers) aged 18 and above; Applicants must be based in Mozambique, Uganda, Nigeria, Angola, Chad, the Republic of Congo, Tanzania, South Sudan, Malawi, and Zambia; Applicants must have an active and engaged platform ( podcast, YouTube channel, TikTok, Facebook, Instagram, publication, data visualization portfolio) with that has been active and highly engaged for more than a year; Applicants must commit to sharing a minimum of four gender, debt, and fossil fuel content for a period of not less than 6 months; Content creators and data visualizers must have a combined audience of 5,000 or more followers on Instagram, TikTok, Facebook, Twitter/X and Snapchat. (Journalists may instead demonstrate reach through publication circulation); Content creators must be unsigned (not represented by an agent). Journalists may be affiliated with a publication, or outlet provided the submitted work and content rights remain their own; All applicants’ proposed ideas must be focused on the campaign’s core themes of climate justice, gender, debt, and fossil fuels in Africa; Only individual applicants can apply (no organizations or agencies) Demonstration of commitment to ANF’s principles and to ethical, survivor-centered storytelling on gender-based impacts. Application Step 1 – Prepare a pitch deck of not more than 5 slides or a video of not more than 60 seconds highlighting your storytelling idea that connects gender, debt, and fossil fuels in Africa. Step 2 – Submit an online application on the application portal, links to your platforms (social media, publication, or community network), and a short description of the audience/community you plan to reach. All content shall be delivered in English, or French. Click here to apply For more information, visit Voices for Climate Justice.

TITLE: Leading Change Fellowship 2026-2027

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: September 7, 2026 Applications are open for the Leading Change Fellowship 2026-2027. The Leading Change Fellowship is designed for young professionals and emerging leaders aged 19 to 35 across Canada who are motivated to create positive environmental and social change in their workplaces and communities. The Fellowship is particularly valuable for people who are early in their careers, navigating a career transition, or looking to deepen their ability to create impact. They believe leadership takes many forms, and they welcome changemakers from different industries, educational backgrounds, communities, and lived experiences. What matters most is your commitment to making a difference, your curiosity, and your openness to learn, grow, and contribute alongside others. The Fellowship brings together three interconnected learning areas: Environmental Prosperity and Resilience: Explore climate solutions, adaptation, resilience, wellbeing, nature and pathways toward a just and sustainable future. Financial Wellbeing: Build your understanding of financial resilience and explore how money, finance, climate, and sustainability intersect. Cooperation in Business: Explore cooperative and purpose-driven approaches to business grounded in democracy, equity and shared prosperity. Eligibility The Fellowship may be a strong fit if you: are aged 19–35 and reside in Canada; care about creating positive environmental or social change; are early in your career, navigating a career transition, or looking to grow your capacity as a leader; are curious about how sustainability connects across sectors and systems; want to turn learning into action; and are excited to learn alongside people whose perspectives and experiences may differ from your own. Application The Leading Change Fellowship is a virtual, cohort-based learning experience running from fall 2026 to February 2027. OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: October 12, 2026 Applications are open for the Zukunftskolleg Postdoctoral Fellowships 2026. The Zukunftskolleg offers postdoctoral researchers independence for their research, interdisciplinary and intergenerational exchange as well as intra-university integration and international contacts. Each fellow is a member of both a university department and the Zukunftskolleg. Additionally, fellows of the Zukunftskolleg can be affiliated to the Clusters of Excellence at the University of Konstanz: “Politics of Inequality” or to the “Centre for the Advanced Study of Collective Behaviour”. The target group consists of excellent early career postdoctoral researchers who demonstrate scientific excellence, research independence, and a strong capacity for teamwork, indicating high potential for a successful academic career. Responsibilities Develop and implement your research project Build up your own research profile You are expected to participate actively in the regular weekly meetings of the Zukunftskolleg and to contribute to the Zukunftskolleg in creating a team of exciting interdisciplinary postdoctoral researchers Have your place of residence in Konstanz or its surroundings Benefits Postdoctoral Fellows profit from all support measures available at the Zukunftskolleg: they receive an annual research allowance e.g. for funding research assistants or equipment; they are eligible to apply for co-funding; Senior Fellowships and the Mentorship Programme give them the opportunity to invite distinguished colleagues to Konstanz; they can go on a temporary Research Visit abroad or nominate international early career researchers for a Research Visit at the Zukunftskolleg; they are eligible to apply for funding for cooperative initiatives or for funding for particular career stages; they receive non-monetary support like coaching, professional career counseling or in grant proposal writing; they get financial support to organise and run a scientific retreat. Eligibility You should be in possession of a doctoral degree granted between 30 September 2024 and 1 October 2026. Earlier graduation dates may be accepted in case of maternity/paternity leave, or working contracts outside academia. Candidates must not hold a permanent professorship, or have a habilitation or equivalent (Venia legendi). Candidates with their own position funded by another programme, which can be transferred to Konstanz, are also eligible. Applicants must propose a research project that ties in with a discipline represented at the University of Konstanz. They are invited to include in their motivation letter a reflection note on how their research relates to the 17 SDGs of the UN. Applicants should contact potential local host among the researchers at the University of Konstanz in order to ensure appropriate affiliation. Support from a department strengstens the application. International experience in teaching or research, and a strong interest in interdisciplinary topics are an asset. The working language is English. Proficiency in English is required. OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: September 15, 2026 Applications are open for the Max Planck Institute for Social Anthropology Dissertation Writing-up Fellowships 2027. The Law & Anthropology Department offers a stimulating interdisciplinary forum where both anthropologists and legal scholars can engage with one another and conduct cutting-edge, policy-relevant research linked to the intensification of exchanges and encounters among and between legal systems, countries and communities in today’s societies. With this comes a growing demand for empirically grounded (ethnographic) knowledge and its translation – to the extent possible – into normative thinking at various levels of decision-making. The Department prioritizes research proposals that address this demand for translation in the increasingly plural European context. The Law & Anthropology Department is offering positions for Dissertation Writing-up Fellowships. Benefits The grants will be awarded for a period of maximum 4 months. The Institute provides successful candidates with a monthly living stipend that is not taxable and is free of social security obligations. Eligibility Open to doctoral candidates in the final stage of their programme. Priority will be given to applicants working towards PhDs in anthropology. The Max Planck Society strives to ensure gender equality and diversity. Note: The fellow should be prepared to participate in the activities of the Department during the fellowship period, and is expected to submit a working paper that addresses the topic of his or her research. A presentation of the doctoral research will be included in the Department’s seminar series. A clear understanding must be reached in advance between the Director of the Department and the candidate’s principal supervisor regarding how the candidate can take fullest advantage of this period and how the home university and the Max Planck Institute can collaborate in the best interests of the candidate and of both institutions. Application Applicants are asked to submit the following materials: cover letter; curriculum vitae; writing sample (chapter of the PhD dissertation); 1–2-page summary of the PhD work; photocopies of university degrees and transcripts; a letter of recommendation from the principal supervisor confirming that the applicant is advanced enough to finalize the doctoral manuscript within the period financed by the Law & Anthropology Department (to be sent directly to the Department at: marencakova@eth.mpg.de) Click here to apply For more information, visit Dissertation Writing-up Fellowships.

TITLE: Mitacs Globalink Research Award (GRA) Program 2026

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: Unspecified Applications are open for the Mitacs Globalink Research Award (GRA) Program 2026. Grow your potential, expand your innovation horizons, build new or strengthen international research collaborations with another university, through the Globalink Research Award (GRA) program. The Mitacs Globalink Research Award (GRA) program supports research collaborations between Canada and eligible countries and regions through intern(s) international mobility. Under the joint supervision of a home and host professor, successful senior undergraduate students, graduate students, and postdoctoral fellows can do one or two 12-24 weeks internship(s). The program is offered through two streams: Allocation stream: Participating Canadian universities receive a set number of internship units per year. Each university will manage their allocation. Rules and conditions may vary. Contact your local Mitacs advisor for details, before starting to develop a project. Quantum stream: Open to all Canadian universities. The project must be in the quantum sector (includes but not limited to: Quantum computation (hardware), algorithms, and software – Quantum communication, networks, and cryptography – Quantum metrology, sensing, imaging, and materials.). No limit of projects per Canadian university and does not count in the university’s allocation. Funding Each intern will receive $6,000 per internship unit (IU): $6,000 research award to conduct one 12- to 24-week research project in the other country. This is one internship unit (IU). $12,000 research award to conduct one 24- to 48-week research project or two 12- to 24-week research projects in the other country. This is two internship units (IUs). Eligibility Intern Must be registered as full-time senior undergraduates, graduate students, or postdoctoral fellows at an eligible Canadian institution or eligible international institution and remain as such throughout their Globalink Research Award. Postdoctoral fellows may apply if their date of graduation from a PhD program is no more than five years prior to the proposed start date of the research project and they have postdoctoral status at an eligible institution. Cannot undertake a research project at an institution where they have previously completed a degree. Cannot undertake a research project in a country where they hold citizenship. Permanent residents or citizens of Canada who are enrolled in an eligible country other than Canada and who wish to do a project in Canada are eligible to apply. Permanent residents or citizens of Canada who are enrolled in a Canadian institution and who hold citizenship in an eligible country may apply to do a project there. Must be the legal age of majority in Canada (18 years of age or older). Must meet travel requirements for their intended destination, including visa and/or immigration requirements and associated documentation. Cannot hold more than two Globalink Research Award or Mitacs-JSPS Summer Program Award per academic lifetime. Interns may not participate in more than one MITACS internship at the same time. Supervisor Must hold a faculty position at an eligible university. Must be eligible to supervise graduate students. Supervisors at Canadian institutions: Must be eligible to hold Tri-Agency funding. Application Note the application process may vary depending on the Canadian university and its internship unit allocation. Check with your local Mitacs Advisor to determine if your project fits the funding requirements for your institution and to request the link to the GRA Application Portal. Awards are offered in partnership with Mitacs’s academic partners and are subject to available funding. It is recommended applicants apply at least 16 weeks prior to the planned start date. For more information, visit Mitacs Globalink Research Award (GRA) Program.

Foreign currency investment can offer investors an opportunity to diversify their portfolios, gain exposure to growing economies and potentially benefit from movements in exchange rates. However, currencies can move quickly in response to economic, political and global events, making it important to approach foreign currency investment with research rather than speculation. Finding the right foreign currency investment begins with understanding what drives the value of a currency and determining whether the opportunity fits your financial goals, investment horizon and tolerance for risk. Understand What You Are Investing In Investing in a foreign currency is different from simply exchanging money before travelling. An investor is effectively taking a position on how one currency may perform relative to another. For example, someone holding British pounds who invests in US dollar-denominated assets has exposure to movements between the pound and the dollar. Even when the underlying investment performs well, changes in the exchange rate can increase or reduce the investor’s eventual return. This means that investors should consider two things: the quality of the investment itself and the potential movement of the currency in which it is denominated. Look at the Strength of the Economy A country’s economic condition can have a significant influence on its currency. Before investing, examine indicators such as economic growth, inflation, employment, government debt, trade performance and consumer confidence. A growing economy does not automatically mean that its currency will appreciate, but understanding these indicators provides useful context. Investors should also consider the country’s longer-term economic prospects. Is the economy becoming more productive and competitive? Is it attracting international investment? Is it heavily dependent on a single commodity or industry? These questions provide a broader picture than simply looking at today’s exchange rate. Pay Attention to Interest Rates and Inflation Central banks play an important role in currency markets. Decisions about interest rates can affect how attractive a currency is to international investors. Higher interest rates can sometimes increase demand for a currency because investors may seek better returns on deposits and fixed-income investments. However, the relationship is not always straightforward. Very high interest rates may also indicate serious inflation or economic instability. Inflation is equally important. Persistent high inflation reduces purchasing power and can place downward pressure on a currency over time. Investors should therefore examine interest rates alongside inflation rather than treating either indicator in isolation. Consider Political and Institutional Stability Currencies respond not only to economics but also to politics. Elections, conflicts, changes in government policy, trade disputes, sanctions and political instability can significantly affect investor confidence. Countries with credible institutions, predictable economic policies and relatively stable political environments may present different currency risks from countries experiencing frequent policy changes or political uncertainty. Before investing, consider what could realistically change within the country during your intended investment period. Decide How You Want to Gain Currency Exposure Buying physical foreign currency is only one way of gaining exposure. Depending on the investor’s circumstances and jurisdiction, foreign currency exposure may also come through foreign-currency bank accounts, international bonds, overseas shares, funds, exchange-traded funds and other financial instruments. For example, an investor who believes strongly in the long-term prospects of the US economy may decide that investing in carefully selected US assets is more appropriate than simply holding dollars. The important question is not merely, “Which currency should I buy?” but “What investment gives me the most appropriate exposure to this currency and economy?” Understand Currency Pairs Currencies are valued relative to other currencies. TITLE: Wege Prize 2027 for Innovators ($65,000 total prize)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: October 4, 2026 Applications are open for the Wege Prize 2027 for Innovators. Wege Prize is an annual competition that ignites game-changing solutions for the future by inspiring college/university students around the world to collaborate across institutional, disciplinary, and cultural boundaries to redesign the way economies work. Part design competition, part global learning lab—Wege Prize challenges transdisciplinary teams of university students to develop real-world solutions to complex, “wicked” problems through the framework of the circular economy. The Challenge: Designing Circular Solutions The circular economy transforms our throwaway linear system into one where materials never become waste and our activities replenish the natural world. It gives us the tools to redesign every element—from how we manage resources, to how we make and use products, to what we do with the materials afterwards—creating an economy that thrives on resilience instead of consumption. Wege Prize challenges teams to use circular design to develop products and services that create unique value, solve real-world problems, and benefit people, businesses, and the environment. Represent three (3) or more academic disciplines – Based on current program of study. Previously completed degree programs are not considered. Represent two (2) or more institutions of higher education – Includes schools within a larger university, i.e. Example University’s School of Engineering and School of Earth Sciences would be considered different. Individuals To be eligible to join a Wege Prize team, individuals must: Be currently enrolled in an undergraduate, graduate, or post-graduate degree program anywhere in the world. Teams can be composed of a mix of undergraduate, graduate, and post-graduate students if they so choose. Be enrolled full-time for the majority of the competition. TITLE: AU Enterprise Africa Network (EAN) Fellowship Programme 2026/2027 [Cohort 2]

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: September 30, 2026 Applications are invited for the AU Enterprise Africa Network (EAN) Fellowship Programme 2026/2027 [Cohort 2]. The Enterprise Africa Network (EAN) Fellowship Programme is an AUC Startup Acceleration Initiative and the African Union’s flagship programme for the development of micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs). Implemented by the AU Commission’s Department of Economic Development, Trade, Tourism, Industry and Minerals (ETTIM), the programme provides Africa’s most promising entrepreneurs with structured training, expert mentorship, intellectual property support, and direct market access opportunities across the continent and beyond. The EAN’s inaugural cohort (2024/25) trained 56 fellows from 30 African countries and produced over USD 1 million in deals and contracts. Cohort 2 (2026/27) will expand the programme to 100 fellows drawn from all 55 AU Member States, targeting USD 2 million in new attributable revenue and 500 new jobs. Fellowship Sectors Cohort 2 covers seven sectors organised into two clusters aligned with the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA): Products Cluster (goods for intra-African trade): Manufacturing, Agro-processing, Creative Industries Services Cluster: ICT/Digital, Fintech, Health, Logistics/Transport Benefits All fellows receive twelve months of structured training across ten modules differentiated by sector and tier; expert mentorship through African Union Partners, access to the African Trade Observatory (ATO) and AfCFTA market intelligence tools; and participation in continental events. Tier 1 and 2 fellows participate in virtual market-entry sessions across ten AfCFTA pilot countries; Tier 3 fellows participate in B2B matchmaking sessions. Eligibility Open to youth- and women-led small enterprises that are: registered and operating in an AU Member State; Formally registered as a business entity; Operating for at least two years; and Employing a minimum of three full-time staff. Applications are particularly encouraged from women-led enterprises and businesses from underrepresented AU regions and small island Member States. Application The application form collects business registration details, sector, years of operation, employee count, countries currently trading, revenue range, IP status, and access to formal finance, together with a written pitch of up to 800 words describing the enterprise, its main market challenge, and the applicant’s objective for the fellowship. Shortlisted applicants will be asked to provide one supporting document verifying finance access (bank statement, mobile money statement, or equivalent). This is not required at application stage. Click here to apply For more information, visit AU Enterprise Africa Network (EAN) Fellowship.

TITLE: Pulitzer Center Local Letters for Global Change Contest 2026

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: November 1, 2026 Applications are open for the Pulitzer Center Local Letters for Global Change Contest 2026. Make your voice heard this fall by writing a letter to a local elected representative that explains the global issue you want them to prioritize, shows how it connects to your local community, and proposes a solution. Through this contest, students can practice global citizenship, civic action, and persuasive writing, all while exploring the underreported issues that matter to them through Pulitzer Center news stories. The Pulitzer Center wants to read and share your letters: tell them, and the world, what’s most important to you. Prizes They will select one first place winner and up to four finalists for each issue category. First place winners will receive: $300 to support global community engagement in your classroom (prize distributed to your class teacher) Publication of your letter, photo, and bio on the Pulitzer Center website Finalists will receive: $75 to support global community engagement in your classroom (prize distributed to your class teacher) Publication of your letter, photo, and bio on the Pulitzer Center website All entrants will be invited to participate in a Pulitzer Center town hall event, held virtually in November, to share their solutions with other students from around the world. Eligibility They welcome entries from all current K-12 students across the globe. Letters may be written in English and/or Spanish. Letters should address a topic within one of the Pulitzer Center’s five focus issues: Climate and Environment (Includes climate change, pollution, extractive industries, and more) Global Health (Includes health inequities, food security, mental health, water and sanitation, and more) Human Rights (Includes racial justice, gender equality, migration and refugees, Indigenous rights, and more) Information and Artificial Intelligence (Includes technology and society, misinformation, and more) Peace and Conflict (Includes war, conflict, and peacebuilding efforts) Application Go to the Suggested Stories tab above and choose a story that gives you new information about an issue that matters to you. (All eligible stories are available here) Write a one-page letter to a local decisionmaker that answers the following questions: What issue do you want the local decisionmaker to address? Why is this issue important globally? (Remember to cite evidence from the Pulitzer Center-supported story! You are encouraged to cite additional sources throughout your letter, too.) Why is this issue important to your local community, and/or to you personally? Why are you writing to this person? What power and/or responsibility do they have? What do you want this person to do? Offer a solution, and cite evidence that your solution will be effective. You do not have to answer the questions in this order, but your letter should answer all five questions. For support writing your letter, use this graphic organizer, or see the Resources for Teachers and Students tab above. Submit your letter using the contest entry form. It will request some basic personal and contact information; the name and contact information for one of your teachers; and you can copy/paste your letter directly into the form. After submitting your letter to the Pulitzer Center, consider mailing or emailing your letter to the decisionmaker directly. For more information, visit Pulitzer Center Local Letters for Global Change Contest.

TITLE: AWARD Leadership Program for Emerging African Women in Science 2026

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: September 20, 2026 Applications for the AWARD Leadership Program for Emerging African Women in Science 2026 are now open. The AWARD Leadership Program for Emerging African Women in Science is a customized learning experience for young African women in science under 35. The program will equip participants with the skills and confidence to lead and innovate in the scientific world. The underrepresentation of women in leadership roles ultimately affects progress toward sustainable development and achieving global sustainable development goals. To ensure women’s effective participation in leadership, women must access learning opportunities to gain skills that will equip them to lead effectively. The AWARD Leadership Program for Emerging African Women in Science is tailored to address some challenges that impede young women’s growth into leadership in science. Programme Structure The Program comprises highly interactive training sessions on leadership, mentoring, proposal writing, communication skills, and one-on-one coaching sessions. Participants will get a deeper understanding of: Effective leadership styles and developing their leadership potential How to define their career path and leverage networks to advance their careers How to develop personal brands to build confidence in pitching their research ideas to potential funding agencies and collaborators The necessary tools and skills to successfully manage teams, navigate organizational dynamics, build alliances, and take risks Costs The program does not offer stipends, sitting allowances, or subsidies. However, all training materials and mentorship provided will be at no cost. Eligibility The program is available to high-potential female applicants under 35 years old who work in science and agriculture and have at least five years of full-time sector experience. Applicants must have a minimum of a B.Sc. degree or equivalent in any agricultural science discipline from a recognized university. Applicants must demonstrate their commitment to growth, clearly articulate their career goals, and demonstrate their ability to take on leadership responsibility. Applicants must reside in Africa and be currently actively engaged in agriculture-related professional work. Applicants must not be a Fellow or Laureate of any other Fellowships offered by AWARD. Application Click to Apply in English or French For more information, visit AWARD Leadership Program.

TITLE: UN FAO Young Professionals Programme (YPP) 2026

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: September 7, 2026 Applications are open for the UN FAO Young Professionals Programme (YPP) 2026. The Young Professionals Programme (YPP) is a recruitment initiative targeted at talented, qualified young professionals who are mainly nationals of non or underrepresented members. Priority consideration will be given to candidates from Small Island Developing States (SIDS), Least Developed Countries (LDCs) and Landlocked Developing Countries (LLDCs) and developing countries in general, to start a career as an international civil servant with FAO. Under the supervision of a senior staff member, Young Professional Officers work with international and national staff and are involved in the identification, design, implementation, monitoring and evaluation of FAO activities. Purposes of assignments vary and may have a country-specific, regional, sector-based or thematic focus. Young Professional Officers are offered two years fixed term contracts subject to a one-year probationary period. They will generally be employed at P-1 step 1 level on initial appointment and will move to P-1 step 2 level for the second year of their assignment. Eligibility Candidates for the YPP are selected on a highly competitive basis. The qualifications below are required for consideration: Candidates should be 32 years of age or younger as of 31 December of the year of application; Academic qualifications: Advanced university degree (Master’s, Ph.D. or equivalent) in a field relevant to the work of FAO; A minimum of one year of professional experience in a field relevant to the work of FAO; Working knowledge of English and limited knowledge of another FAO official language (French, Spanish, Arabic, Chinese or Russian); Candidates must not bear any of the following relationships to staff members of the Organization: son, daughter, brother or sister. Application Visit the list of YPP opportunities currently available in the Organization (for vacancies, click the YPP (Young Professionals Programme) link from the banner at the left of the newly opened page). Kindly note that the application and selection process will be conducted in English. For more information, visit UN FAO Young Professionals Programme.

TITLE: Africa Fellowship for Young Energy Leaders (AFYEL) – Cohort 6

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: September 4, 2026 Applications are open for the Africa Fellowship for Young Energy Leaders (AFYEL) – Cohort 6. The AFYEL is a six-month, no-cost fellowship that trains early-career professionals across four renewable energy technologies and pairs classroom learning with a one-month internship, a capstone project addressing a real local energy problem, and a virtual summit connecting fellows with mentors and industry leaders from across the continent. The fellowship is run by the Renewable Energy Technology Training Institute (RETTI), through RETTI Virtual University, in partnership with government agencies, academic institutions, and private sector companies working across Africa’s energy value chain. AFYEL exists because the renewable energy sector in Africa needs a trained, capable workforce faster than universities alone can produce. Close to 600 million Africans still lack reliable access to electricity. Closing that gap means giving young engineers, economists, and finance professionals the technical and commercial skills the sector runs on, and keeping that talent working on African energy problems. Tracks Every applicant selects one track to specialize in. Each track runs expert-led lectures, real case studies, one-on-one mentoring, and ends in a track-specific capstone project. Solar PV — Small-scale, large-scale, and utility-scale solar systems, from household installations to grid-connected plants. Onshore Wind — Wind resource assessment, turbine technology, and project development. Bioenergy — Biomass and biogas systems, feedstock supply chains, and rural energy applications. Hydropower — Small and large hydro systems, feasibility, and grid integration. Benefits Practitioner-led training in your chosen technology track, taught by working professionals in that field, not just academics. A one-month internship placement with a partner organization. A capstone project you design and carry out, addressing an actual energy access problem in your own community or country. A virtual summit connecting you with international mentors, past fellows, and industry and grant partners. Ongoing access to the AFYEL alumni network and continued opportunities after the fellowship ends. Eligibility Recent graduates in Physics, Electrical/Electronic Engineering, Mechanical Engineering, Building/Construction Engineering, Economics, Mathematics, Accounting, Finance, or Solar Energy (or a closely related field). Aged 21–35. A citizen or resident of any African country. Able to read, write, and speak English at a working level — all training, mentoring, and group work happens in English. Able to commit fully to the six-month fellowship and the one-month internship that follows it. This isn’t a side project; partial participation isn’t an option. Application Click here to apply For more information, visit AFYEL.

TITLE: World Bank Group Global Program on GovTech & Public Sector Innovation 2026 (Fully-funded)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: October 2, 2026 Applications are open for the World Bank Group Global Program on GovTech & Public Sector Innovation 2026. The World Bank, the Republic of Korea’s Ministry of the Interior and Safety (MOIS), and the National Information Society Agency (NIA) invite government institutions worldwide to apply for the GovTech Bootcamp on AI in Governance and Public Administration. This initiative targets government institutions in low- and middle-income countries that are developing, piloting, or deploying AI-enabled solutions to strengthen public administration, service delivery, transparency, efficiency, and citizen engagement. Participants will learn directly from practitioners who design, operate, and scale Korea’s public AI systems, engage with Korean and World Bank experts, and develop practical implementation roadmaps for their own AI initiatives. Following the bootcamp, participating teams will be able to receive follow-up support and technical feedback to help advance their initiatives, depending on the strength and viability of their proposals and the expert advice provided during the program. Benefits Up to five government teams will be selected to participate in a fully funded, five-day technical bootcamp in Seoul. Eligibility Open to government agencies from low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), as classified by the World Bank’s income group methodology. The applying institution must be developing, piloting, or deploying an AI tool or application for the public sector that addresses a specific governance or administrative challenge. Upper-middle-income countries are classified as LMICs under the World Bank’s income group methodology and are therefore eligible to apply. Only government institutions may apply. The proposal must be led by and submitted on behalf of a government agency with direct institutional authority over the initiative. Multiple agencies from the same country may submit separate proposals. However, only one team per country will be selected for the bootcamp. Prior participation in World Bank programs does not disqualify an applicant. Proposals at the concept, prototype, pilot, or deployment stage are all eligible. However, proposals that demonstrate concrete institutional backing and a specific, actionable plan will be prioritized over purely conceptual submissions. Application Information sessions for prospective applicants will be offered across three time zones. Applicants will be asked to describe the public sector challenge being addressed, the proposed AI solution, technical and data readiness, institutional support, implementation risks, learning objectives, and planned next steps following the bootcamp. Applicants may also submit supporting materials, such as endorsement letters, technical diagrams, policy documents, budget commitments, or other relevant documents. Click here to apply For more information, visit Global Program on GovTech & Public Sector Innovation.

TITLE: U.S. Department of the Treasury International Affairs Junior Fellowship 2027-2029

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: October 31, 2026 Applications are open for the U.S. Department of the Treasury International Affairs Junior Fellowship 2027-2029. The Junior Fellowship program is a highly selective, fixed two-year program for new college graduates to work shaping international economic policy for the United States in Treasury’s Office of International Affairs. Fellows have left the program to pursue a range of opportunities, including employment at Treasury and elsewhere in the U.S. government, work in the private sector, and graduate study (e.g., law, public policy, international relations, and finance and business). Junior Fellows have exposure to multiple policy issues and opportunities to enhance their knowledge and skills. They typically perform a variety of tasks that include developing policy proposals, analyzing international economic and financial developments, and conducting analytical studies. Fellows also support bilateral and multilateral meetings for senior Treasury officials engaging counterparts at the IMF, World Bank, G7, and G20 – to name a few. Junior Fellows often participate in such meetings and may have opportunities to travel abroad. Junior fellows will be placed in either a regional or functional office. Regional offices oversee Treasury’s engagement with counterpart finance ministries and treasuries across the world. Functional offices oversee Treasury’s engagement with international financial institutions and structure broader Treasury policy on issues ranging from international trade to export credits, to foreign exchange. Benefits Junior Fellows are usually hired at the GS-9 level and receive standard Treasury benefits. Eligibility Applicants must be U.S. citizens. Strong candidates will have recently received – or will soon receive – a bachelor’s degree with relevant coursework in economics, public policy, finance, international relations, or related fields. Note that due to the structure of the program, preference is given to undergraduates. Application Email a cover letter, resume, one recommendation letter, and transcript(s) attesting to academic qualifications and career potential to IAFellows@treasury.gov by October 31, 2026. In the email, candidates must also: indicate a desired start date; confirm they hold U.S. citizenship (must be able to provide documentation); note veterans’ preference, if applicable; and include a resume that demonstrates 52 weeks (2,080 hours) of paid or unpaid work, volunteer, or extracurricular experience relevant to the duties described above. Note that resumes should not exceed two pages. Expand on duties performed for each professional or extracurricular job or activity listed (volunteer work, work study, etc.) to demonstrate requisite experience. Also include the time period when the job or activity took place with the number of hours per week, (e.g., June 1, 2025 to August 31, 2025, 30 hours per week). Candidates passing a first round of screening will be asked to respond to two short essay questions. Applications will be evaluated in December 2026 for Fellows to start in summer 2027 (or at a mutually agreed alternative time). Candidates must be able to obtain and maintain a national security clearance. For more information, visit International Affairs Junior Fellowship.

TITLE: Caribbean Climate Leaders Fellowship 2026 (Fully-funded)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: August 21, 2026 Applications are open for the Caribbean Climate Leaders Fellowship 2026. The Caribbean Community Climate Change Centre (CCCCC), with funding from the Caribbean Development Bank, invites applications for the Caribbean Climate Leaders Fellowship — a fully funded professional development opportunity placing two emerging Caribbean professionals within the CCCCC delegation at COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye. COP31 will bring governments, climate experts, development partners, advocates and stakeholders from around the world together to advance global climate action. For the Caribbean, these discussions are especially important. Decisions surrounding adaptation, climate finance, loss and damage and the Global Goal on Adaptation have direct implications for the future of Small Island Developing States. Through the Caribbean Climate Leaders Fellowship, the CCCCC is investing in the next generation of professionals who will help carry the Caribbean’s climate agenda forward. The Leaders Fellowship is designed to give two young professionals meaningful exposure to the UNFCCC process, CCCCC’s regional coordinating role and CARICOM’s climate priorities, while allowing them to make an active contribution to the region’s COP31 programme. Benefits They provide economy airfare from your home country to Antalya, Türkiye. Hotel accommodation throughout the conference period. Daily allowance covering meals and incidental expenses. Official observer accreditation through the CCCCC delegation. Guidance from experienced members of the CCCCC delegation before, during and after COP31. Pre-COP preparation, role definition and post-conference knowledge-sharing activities. Eligibility Open to Caribbean nationals between the ages of 18 and 30 who are early-career, mid-career or emerging professionals with a strong interest in climate change and sustainable development. Applicants should also be currently enrolled in tertiary education, employed, or actively involved in one or more of the following areas: Youth organisation Non-governmental organisation Community-based organisation Private-sector organisation Public-sector institution; or Other organisation working in climate, development or public engagement. Evaluation Criteria Applications will be evaluated primarily on the strength, clarity and credibility of the three required statements. Particular consideration will be given to: The applicant’s commitment to the Caribbean’s climate agenda The potential professional value of the fellowship The quality of the proposed institutional knowledge-transfer plan The strength of the applicant’s climate-literacy contribution The applicant’s ability to communicate climate information effectively; and The potential for the fellowship to create impact beyond COP31 Shortlisted applicants will be invited to participate in an interview with a CCCCC selection panel. Application Your CV should clearly outline your education, professional experience, volunteer involvement, climate-related work and relevant skills. You must have a written application of 1,200–1,500 words. Your written application must address the following three areas: Professional development: Explain how the fellowship will contribute to your professional development. Identify the skills, knowledge, experience and career trajectory it will support, and explain why this is the right moment for you to participate. Institutional impact: Explain how your participation will benefit your institution or organisation. Include a realistic plan for sharing the knowledge, insights and professional networks gained through the fellowship with your colleagues or community. Caribbean climate literacy: Describe how your COP31 participation will translate climate discussions into accessible information that strengthens climate literacy and public engagement across the Caribbean. A short supporting statement from your institution or organisation is encouraged. Click here to apply For more information, visit Caribbean Climate Leaders Fellowship.

TITLE: ITU Robotics for Good Youth Challenge 2026-2027

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: April 1, 2027 Applications are open for the ITU Robotics for Good Youth Challenge 2026. The ITU launched the Robotics for Good Youth Challenge in April 2024 to promote AI and robotics education among youth worldwide and to help ensure that no one is left behind in the robotics and AI revolution. It is inspired each year by a global challenge in which robots are developed to deliver innovative and practical solutions to real-world problems. As an educational, platform-agnostic robotics championship, it gives participants full freedom to design, build, and program their robots without relying on a mandatory kit, while also allowing them to source hardware locally. In doing so, it aims to democratize access to robotics and AI education, help bridge the digital skills gap, and promote sustainable practices through the use of recycled materials, the reuse of robots across seasons, and the development of environmentally efficient robotic solutions. TITLE: Choosing the Right University and Course for Your Study Abroad Degree

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Studying abroad is a major investment in your education, career and future. Beyond earning an international degree, it can expose you to new cultures, professional networks, opportunities and ways of thinking. However, with thousands of universities and courses available across the UK, United States, Canada, Australia, Europe and other destinations, deciding where and what to study can quickly become overwhelming. It is easy to begin with university rankings or familiar names such as Edinburgh, Oxford, Harvard,Toronto or Melbourne. But a famous university is not automatically the right university for you, and a popular course is not necessarily the course that will move you towards your goals. The best choice is one that connects your interests, career ambitions, finances and the opportunities you hope to access after graduation. 1. Start With Where You Want the Degree to Take You Before searching for universities, think about what you want your degree to help you achieve. You do not need to know exactly what job you will have in five years, but you should have some idea of the sector, profession or problem you want to work on. For example, imagine that you are passionate about improving healthcare in your country. Your first thought might be to study Public Health. However, if your ambition is specifically to influence national health policies, a programme combining Public Health and Health Policy might be more useful. If you want to manage large health programmes for international organisations, Global Health or International Development with a health specialisation might be a better fit. The same applies to someone who wants to work in international development. You may encounter master’s degrees in Development Studies, International Development, Public Policy, International Relations and Social Policy. Although these programmes overlap, they can lead you towards different skills and career pathways. Instead of asking only, “What do I want to study?”, ask, “What do I want to be able to do after studying this?” 2. Look Beyond the Course Title One of the easiest mistakes to make is choosing a programme because its title sounds impressive. Suppose you receive offers for an MSc International Development from two different universities. At first glance, they may appear almost identical. However, when you examine the modules, one programme may focus strongly on economics, quantitative methods and development policy, while another emphasises gender, politics, inequality and community-led development. The same principle applies to courses such as Data Science, Business Analytics or Artificial Intelligence. One programme may expect significant previous programming experience, while another may be designed for students transitioning from non-technical backgrounds. Always examine the compulsory modules, optional courses, assessment methods and dissertation requirements. If a university offers ten modules and eight of them do not genuinely interest you, the attractive course title should not persuade you otherwise. 3. Research the University’s Strength in Your Field University rankings can be helpful, but overall rankings should not make the decision for you. Imagine choosing between University A, which is ranked highly overall, and University B, which has a particularly strong research centre in your area of interest. If you want to specialise in climate finance and University B has academics researching climate finance, partnerships with relevant organisations and regular industry events, that environment may be more valuable to your career than the difference between the universities’ overall rankings. This becomes even more important for master’s and doctoral students. If you hope to research gender-based violence, for example, finding a university with academics and research centres working specifically on gender, violence, feminist policy or human rights could provide access to supervision, networks and opportunities directly connected to your interests.

RESTRICTIONS

TARGET GROUP
- Individuals considering studying abroad

FUNDING / BENEFITS

APPLICATION

OTHER IMPORTANT CONDITIONS

SUMMARY
Studying abroad is a significant investment in education, career, and future. It offers an international degree, cultural exposure, professional networks, and new ways of thinking. However, choosing the right university and course can be overwhelming. Key steps include: 1) Starting with where you want the degree to take you, considering career ambitions and specific skills needed. 2) Looking beyond the course title, examining modules, assessment methods, and dissertation requirements. 3) Researching the university's strength in your field, considering research centers, partnerships, and industry events. University rankings can be helpful but should not be the sole decision factor.

TITLE: Kleinhans Fellowship for Community Forestry Research 2027 (up to $20,000)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: February 28, 2027 Applications are open for the Kleinhans Fellowship for Community Forestry Research 2027. Recognizing that sound scientific inquiry can help to guide technical assistance for local development, the Kleinhans Fellowship supports research that seeks solutions to the challenges faced by the community forestry model. The fellowship provides funds for research that is oriented toward solving real-world problems as defined by community forest enterprises (CFEs). Moreover, the planning, implementation and dissemination of research results will be carried out in participatory manner to ensure that it has practical value for communities and helps to inform their action plans. Research Topics The Kleinhans Fellowship provides a two-year stipend of US$20,000 per year to support research that addresses one of the following topics: Markets for lesser-known species and non-timber forest products (NTFPs). Most community forestry products are unlikely to reach international markets, but domestic markets in many tropical forest countries are being flooded with illegal wood products, making it hard for legitimate operations—especially CFEs—to compete. The absence of markets for lesser-known species and NTFPs further impedes optimal forest management and is a critical hurdle that must be overcome if CFEs are to become economically viable. The fellowship supports research that systematically documents and analyzes the creation and maintenance of domestic markets for diversified forest products, helps determine what drives success and recommends future actions. Biodiversity management practices. Sustainable forest management requires practices that conserve biodiversity, such as the protection of High Conservation Value Forests and the creation of riparian buffers. The Kleinhans Fellowship supports research that explores the feasibility of implementing such practices at the community level and their effects on the economic viability of CFEs. Social organization and governance. Technical assistance programs are often limited in their ability to invest in organizational capacity building. The fellowship supports research that investigates modes of social organization and highlights both problems and innovative, replicable solutions for CFE governance. Topics of interest include equitable participation and transparency in decision-making and benefit-sharing; human resource management and business training; and governance aspects such as CFE bylaws, compliance and legal status. Multi-community enterprises. Without access to financing, CFEs often get mired in debt, are beholden to high-risk, high-cost lenders and cannot invest in developing their businesses. CFEs are often encouraged to work together to aggregate supply, invest collectively and access financing, but it can be difficult to put these strategies into practice. The fellowship supports research that examines multi-community enterprises, documents and analyzes their successes and failures, and makes recommendations for future investment in the development of such ventures. Award The fellowship provides a grant of $20,000 per year for two years. Note that the fellowship will not subsidize academic tuition or fees, nor will it cover the cost of purchasing transport vehicles or equipment that is unnecessary or unreasonable. Eligibility Applicants must have a master’s degree in forestry, ecology, botany, environmental science or an appropriate related field. Doctoral candidates or post-doctoral researchers are preferred, although applicants may substitute relevant experience for higher-level degrees. Application Applications will be accepted starting six months before the deadline, on February 28, 2027: A proposal that does not exceed seven typed pages in length. The proposal should include an abstract, a review of the relevant literature, detailed methodology and a discussion of the project’s practical applications A budget A copy of the candidate’s curriculum vitae or resume Two letters of recommendation A list of past, current and potential funding sources for both the applicant and the project Applications can be submitted in English, Spanish or Portuguese. Applicants are required to submit their completed application by email to Elena Degli Innocenti at

This is an ambitious business growth and investment readiness programme designed to support high-potential women entrepreneurs across Southern Africa. Delivered by WomHub, in partnership with AfricaGrow Technical Assistance Facility, KfW DEG Impact, and the Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ), the programme supports women-led businesses operating within the STEM sectors (Science, Technology, Engineering and Manufacturing) to become investment-ready, scale sustainably, and access catalytic funding. The programme is designed for women entrepreneurs who are building innovative, revenue-generating businesses with strong potential for growth and impact. Through a combination of expert-led training, mentorship, technical assistance, business diagnostics, and investor engagement, participants will strengthen their business foundations, enhance their growth potential, and prepare to attract investment. Phase 3: Capital Deployment – Businesses that successfully complete the investor readiness journey and due diligence process will become eligible to pitch for catalytic funding, with between five (5) and ten (10) businesses receiving investment together with ongoing post-investment support. Benefits Beyond funding, participants will gain access to a dynamic network of mentors, industry experts, ecosystem partners, and investors committed to supporting the growth of women-led STEM enterprises across the region. The programme seeks to create lasting impact by strengthening founder capabilities, improving investment readiness, enabling access to capital, driving revenue growth, creating quality jobs, and accelerating innovation within the STEM ecosystem. TITLE: Whitley Awards 2027 for Grassroots Conservation Leaders (£50,000 prize)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: October 30, 2026 Applications are open for the Whitley Awards 2027 for Grassroots Conservation Leaders. Awarded annually, Whitley Awards recognise grassroots conservation leaders, providing funding to support and scale up proven, science-based solutions that deliver lasting impact for both people and nature. Whitley Fund for Nature (WFN) is a fundraising and grant-giving nature conservation charity. Established in 1993, it has channeled £23 million to 200 conservation leaders in 80 countries across the Global South, benefitting wildlife, landscapes, and people. They offer long term, laddered support to courageous changemakers leading local solutions to the global biodiversity and climate crises; they are acting on the latest science and igniting projects with passion. Through these award winners they support work rooted in communities that creates lasting benefits for wildlife, landscapes and people. Award Whitley Awards are worth £50,000 GBP in project funding over one year. In addition to £50,000 in project funding, winners receive: International recognition and profile-raising opportunities. Professional communications and media support. Peer learning, training and collaboration opportunities. Eligibility for future Continuation Funding and the Whitley Gold Award. Eligibility Open to grassroots conservation leaders who are nationals of the country where they work (i.e. you were born there or have lived there long term and obtained national status) and are embedded in local communities. Work based in at least one eligible country. Eligible countries are those not classified as a High-Income Economy by the World Bank. Wildlife conservation projects that are delivering measurable positive impacts for threatened ecosystems and biodiversity at the landscape or seascape level, while providing tangible benefits to Indigenous peoples and local communities. Applicants who work for a locally incorporated NGO, charity, not for profit, or university. WFN will fund: Strong communicators and passionate people who inspire others and importantly, collaborate effectively and share their learnings and results. Note that applicants must be able to communicate in English. Whilst total fluency is not required, applicants must be able to communicate verbally in English without a translator. This ensures winners can benefit fully from the Whitley Awards week which involves interviews, networking events, training, and media opportunities. Leadership and teamwork. Whitley Awards recognise individuals backed by an experienced team or organisation that can demonstrate past success and an evidence-based approach. Individuals working in isolation, as well as team or joint entries, are not eligible. Ecosystem level projects are preferred. Genuine flagship species projects are accepted, but not if results are purely species-specific. Community-led conservation projects are encouraged, and all projects must demonstrate how they empower, engage and benefit the Indigenous peoples and communities with which they work. Grassroots, pragmatic conservation work that is realistic, but ambitious too. They look for applicants on the cusp of achieving significant impact, with projects that are replicable or scalable. Actions that will have clear, measurable outcomes. They look for applications that have given careful consideration to the indicators that will be used to evidence impact. Sustainable projects that will continue well beyond the Whitley Award. Successful proposals will demonstrate long-term planning. Projects that demonstrate value for money and ability to manage funding at the Whitley Award level (£50,000). Projects for which a Whitley Award will make a significant difference. Priority will be given to applicants that can clearly demonstrate need. Work that would benefit from greater visibility, particularly projects that could gain momentum through media exposure and wider recognition. Application Applications for the 2027 Whitley Awards are currently open and close at midnight GMT on 30 October 2026. Click here to apply For more information, visit Whitley Awards.

TITLE: ACLS Digital Justice Seed and Development Grants 2026-2027

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: November 3, 2026 Applications are invited for the ACLS Digital Justice Seed and Development Grants 2026-2027. Generously funded by the Mellon Foundation, this program supports digital projects across the humanities and social sciences that critically engage with the interests and histories of people of color and other historically marginalized communities through the ethical use of digital tools and methods. The program seeks to address the inequities in the distribution of access to tools and support for digital work among scholars across various fields, those working with under-utilized or understudied source materials, and those in institutions with less support for digital projects. It promotes inclusion and sustainability by extending the opportunity to participate in the digital transformation of humanistic inquiry to a greater number of humanities scholars and projects. Additionally, all grant recipients can receive general financial planning coaching from the Nonprofit Finance Fund to plan for the long-term stewardship and sustainability of their projects. Grant The program offers two kinds of grants: Digital Justice Seed Grants for start-up projects, ranging from $10,000-$25,000 Digital Justice Development Grants, ranging from $50,000-$100,000, for projects that have advanced beyond the proof-of-concept phase Eligibility Project’s principal investigator must be a scholar in the humanities and/or the interpretative social sciences. Projects must be made as widely available as intellectual property constraints allow, ideally with the most liberal open-source and Creative Commons license that is appropriate for the underlying content. An institution of higher education in the United States must administer any awarded grant funds. For Seed Grants: Project must be within the start-up or prototyping phase of development. For Development Grants: Projects must demonstrate evidence of significant preliminary work as well as a record of engagement and impact with scholarly and/or public audiences. Application Completed applications must be submitted no later than 5:00 PM EST on November 3, 2026. Click here to apply For more information, visit ACLS Digital Justice Seed and Development Grants.

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: September 11, 2026 Applications are open for the AKO UAL Storytelling Research Fellowship 2026/2027. The Storytelling Research Fellowship is a programme from the UAL AKO Storytelling Institute, in partnership with the Power of Pop Fund at Comic Relief. It supports original research into how popular culture creates social and environmental change— across creative media including television, film, games, music, social media, podcasts, comics, publishing and digital content. The programme aims to build a stronger evidence base for understanding how, when and why popular culture creates meaningful social change. Research should be rigorous and practically useful — primarily to creatives, and secondarily to funders, broadcasters, civil society organisations and campaigners. The objectives of the Fellowship are to: Deepen understanding of how popular culture influences beliefs, behaviours, attitudes and public discourse Support original research into the mechanisms and conditions through which stories contribute to social and environmental change Produce insights useful to those producing cultural content, and to those in social justice organisations, commissioning, funding and research Encourage research that combines intellectual rigour with accessible, public-facing dissemination Bring fellows together through workshops, research guidance and a closing symposium to share learning across cause areas Benefits They offer a nine-month employment contract for two days per week (0.4 FTE), starting in November 2026, at an annual salary of £48,563 (pro rata). The salary payable for the nine-month contract is £19,425, subject to PAYE and National Insurance contributions. Eligibility All applicants must: Have the right to work in the UK for the duration of the Fellowship. Be in London for the kick off meeting and mid-point workshop in-person. Be able to commit to the whole programme. Propose an original research project and have an interest specifically in the impact of popular culture and in making a difference with their work. All research outputs should not have been previously published. Be fluent in English. Application Application should include: CV Record of research outputs (provide links where available) Research proposal maximum 1000 – 1200 words Supporting statement including at least one example of a research project you’ve designed and delivered. TITLE: How I Won a Fully Funded Study Abroad Scholarship and How You Can Too

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
A scholarship can be the door you have been waiting for. A year ago, I received a fully-funded Mastercard scholarship, and I did that after receiving 17 rejections. Now, I will show you how I did that and how you can too. First, picture this: there are 15,000 people and 50 people need to be selected for a scholarship worth £80,000. Why should that scholarship body decide to invest in you? Why are you the best person to be invested in, and why should they invest in you now? Why should you be one of the 50 people selected? Don’t think they must invest in you just because you want to get it. Think about it as a journey in which you have already made a lot of progress. You need to get the door open. Here is how I opened mine, and here is what I would do differently if I was starting from rejection number one again. 1. Know Your Story Before Anyone Else Does Many scholarships would need you to share your story. Your past, your present, and your future, especially as it relates to your career. Your understanding of your own personal journey, story, life, and trajectory would be a shaping force for you to define where you are headed. This isn’t just about writing a nice paragraph for the personal statement. It’s about actually sitting down, sometimes for weeks, and asking yourself hard questions: Where did I start? What shaped my choices? What am I really working towards, and why? For me, that meant going back to why I even chose my field in the first place, tracing it through the projects I had taken on, the setbacks, and connecting all of that to the future I wanted the scholarship to help me build. If you can’t tell your own story to yourself in a way that makes sense, you won’t be able to convince a panel of strangers either. 2. Do the Work, Not Just the Application You don’t want to go around lying about things you did not do. You want to reflect on what you have done and how that leads you to a future, and how, with a scholarship, you would leverage that to be and do even more. Make sure you are telling an authentic story of your own work. Make sure it is verifiable, and make sure you are doing it from a place of something you are truly invested in and not because you just want a scholarship. After applying 17 times over three years, I realised that my courage for the work I was doing had not waned because of rejections, and even now, I find the need to leverage all I am learning to do and be more. What kept me going wasn’t the scholarship itself, it was the work. I kept publishing, kept volunteering, kept building, even after rejection number 10, number 14, number 17. By the time I got that yes, I had a body of work that could speak for itself, not because I planned it that way, but because I never stopped. Get the work done! 3. Show, Don’t Tell It’s very sweet to write a beautiful story, but make sure that as you are telling stories, you are showing what you have done and adding the numbers, the impact, the journey, and everything. An example is saying “I led a project” versus “I led a project that reached 500 students and raised £10,000.” The second one gives the panel something to picture and something to verify. Go through your own CV

Deadline: August 25, 2026 Applications are open for the Commonwealth Fellowship Programme 2026/2027. From 2026/27, the CSC has launched a new ‘Commonwealth Fellowship Programme’ featuring two strands: the current Professional Fellowships alongside a new strand of Academic Fellowships. Commonwealth Academic and Professional Fellowships are for citizens of Commonwealth countries to spend a period of time in the UK at an organisation working on a programme of professional or academic development which will have a developmental impact upon their return home. Benefits Each fellowship provides: Approved return airfare from the Fellow’s home country to the UK. Reimbursement of the standard visa application fee. Stipend (living allowance) payable monthly (or pro rata) for the duration of the award at the rate of £2,218 per month, or £2,753 per month for those at organisations in the London metropolitan area (rates quoted at 2025/26 levels). If a Fellow declares a disability, a full assessment of needs and eligibility for additional financial support will be offered by the CSC. Arrival allowance of up to £1,247.09 (rates quoted at 2025/26 levels), including an element for warm clothing. Additional fees can be agreed for costs associated with Fellows attending short courses/conferences as well as travel to visit other UK organisations where this forms an integral part of the programme. Programmes from six weeks to two months can claim up to £1,000 and programmes of two months to three months can claim up to £2,000. These costs will be paid directly to the host organisation. Eligibility To be eligible for these Fellowships, prospective Fellows must: Be a citizen of or have been granted refugee status by an eligible Commonwealth country, or be a British Protected Person. Be permanently resident in an eligible Commonwealth country. Prospective Fellows should not have indefinite leave to remain in the UK. Professional Fellows: have at least five years’ full-time, or equivalent part-time, relevant work experience, in a profession related to the subject of the Fellowships programme, by the proposed start of the fellowship – voluntary work experience will not be counted towards this minimum. Academic Fellows: hold a PhD and be employed by a university in a Commonwealth country other than the UK. Be in employment at the time of application at an organisation that they will return to upon completion of the fellowship. Provide at least two references, one of which must be from their current employer. Any applications for which references are not received will be considered ineligible. Not have undertaken a Commonwealth Fellowship within the last five years (at the time of taking up the award). Be available to undertake their fellowship from the prescribed start date. OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: August 16, 2026 Applications for the Kenneth Myer Innovation Fellowships 2027 are now open. The Kenneth Myer Innovation Fellowships aim to support breakthrough solutions to Australia’s most pressing social and environmental challenges. A Fellowship offers a unique opportunity for recipients to take 12 months, supported by $180,000, to focus on their existing projects that have the potential to achieve positive outcomes for society and the environment, supporting initiatives that align with one or more of the program themes of inclusion & equality, sustainability & environment including climate change, or human, civil & legal rights. Fellows receive a combination of time, resources and a program of support to help progress their existing work, and grow and scale their impact. Benefits Up to $180,000 is available to each Fellow for their 12-month Fellowship comprising a stipend of $140,000 and up to $40,000 for approved project expenses. Project expenses are those directly related to the Fellowship from its commencement such as renting a separate workspace (if required), travel and contracting of external expertise, and available on a reimbursement basis. During the 12-months, Fellows have access to a range of supports including a panel of experts, who meet quarterly, a mentor and the network of past Fellows. Eligibility The applicant must: be an Australian citizen or permanent resident; reside in Australia for the majority of the Fellowship period; be prepared to take a sabbatical from their current role for 12 months; have a proven track record of achievement; pursue out-of-the-box thinking and be a risk-taker; have an ability to turn well-formulated ideas or new approaches into action (that is, your idea must have substance to it; a good idea on its own is not sufficient); have well-developed networks within an area of the proposed project. The proposed project must: be based in Australia; be aligned with one or more of the program themes of Inclusion & Equality, Sustainability & Environment including climate change, or Human, Civil & Legal rights; have been in development for not longer than three years. Application Applications are due by 11.59pm AEST on Sunday, 16 August 2026. Expressions of Interest received after the closing time will not be accepted (for example, due to technical, personal or other challenges). There are no exceptions. They do not accept further information from applicants once the deadline for submissions has passed. Click here to apply For more information, visit Kenneth Myer Innovation Fellowships.

TITLE: EJN Virtual Media Workshop on Mining, Environment and Human Rights Reporting in Africa 2026

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: September 6, 2026 Applications are open for the EJN Virtual Media Workshop on Mining, Environment and Human Rights Reporting in Africa 2026. Internews’ Earth Journalism Network (EJN) is hosting a three-day virtual media workshop from November 3-5, 2026, to strengthen the capacities of journalists in four African countries—Ghana, Uganda, Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and South Africa—to report on issues related to mining, the environment and human rights. It is expected that by the end of the workshop, participants will have: Gained a better understanding of the environmental impacts and potential implications of different types of mining (including artisanal, small-scale, and large-scale industrial mining, as well as legal mining versus illegal mining); Increased knowledge regarding water, soil and air contamination – including an improved understanding of the science behind mining-related contamination, and how to go about finding and analyzing data for stories; Learned about land rights, community displacement and free, prior and informed consent (FPIC); Reviewed potential threats and risk mitigation strategies for ensuring physical safety and digital security while reporting on potentially sensitive issues, from mining sites and within conflict-affected areas; Learned about investigative tools and techniques for covering extractive industries. The workshop sessions will be structured as part-presentation and part-discussion. Journalists will learn from researchers, environmental scientists, mining law experts, human rights advocates, civil society organizations and local communities working at the intersection of mining, environment and human rights in Africa. Benefits To ensure these workshops are accessible, EJN will offer a limited number of communications stipends to those with an unstable internet connection in remote areas. Participants who attend all sessions will receive a certificate of completion from EJN and will also receive special consideration should they choose to apply for a story grant to produce journalistic content following the workshop. Eligibility Applicants can be from Ghana, Uganda, DRC or South Africa. For the purposes of this training opportunity, they will only be accepting applications in English and French. Unfortunately, they do not have the capacity to consider applications in any other languages at this time. Applicants must have a working understanding of English or French to participate in and fully benefit from the workshop. Applications are open to journalists working in any medium (online, print, television, radio) as well as social media content creators with experience covering mining, environmental and/or human rights issues. They welcome applications from freelance reporters and staff from all types of media organizations – community-based, local, national and international. They especially encourage women, rural, Indigenous and early-career journalists to apply. Applicants are required to be transparent about the use of generative AI tools, if any, to revise their proposals. EJN reserves the right to disqualify applicants from consideration if they have been found to have engaged in unethical or improper professional conduct, including, but not limited to, submitting AI-generated content as their own. Application Click here to apply For more information, visit EJN Virtual Media Workshop.
