The ideal candidate takes a systemic approach to social change, leading with humility, openness, and a collaborative approach. They are ready to utilise the Oxford MBA and the Skoll Centre community to enhance and expand social impact. Selection Criteria Entrepreneurial experience Minimum three years of experience building and leading a social venture, with demonstrated evidence of significant social impact. Changemaking qualities Demonstrates curiosity, humility, and persistence in seeking to understand the systemic roots of social or environmental challenges. Has lived experience with the issue they seek to address or has meaningfully engaged with the issue through long-term work, research, or collaboration with those directly affected. Leveraging the Oxford MBA to contribute to systemic change Demonstrates a clear intention to pursue a career aligned with long-term, systemic social or environmental impact. Articulates how being part of the University of Oxford, the Saïd Business School MBA programme, and the Skoll Centre community would advance their professional growth and their ability to create systemic social or environmental impact. TITLE: Chevening Scholarship to Study in the UK 2027-2028 (Fully-funded)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: October 6, 2026 Applications are open for the Chevening Scholarship to Study in the UK 2027-2028. Chevening is the UK Government’s global scholarship programme that offers future leaders the unique opportunity to study in the UK. These scholarships are awarded to outstanding professionals from all over the world to pursue a one-year master’s degree in any subject at any UK university. Chevening provides fully-funded scholarships, leaving you free to focus on achieving your academic goals and enjoying the experience of a lifetime. You will live and study in the UK for a year, during which time you will develop professionally and academically, grow your network, experience UK culture, and build lasting positive relationships with the UK. Scholarship As Chevening Scholarships are fully-funded, your award includes the following: university tuition fees a monthly stipend travel costs to and from the UK an arrival allowance a homeward departure allowance the cost of one visa application a travel grant to attend Chevening events in the UK Eligibility To be eligible for a Chevening Scholarship you must: Be a citizen of a Chevening-eligible country or territory. Commit to returning to your home country for at least two years after your scholarship ends. Have at least two years of work experience (2,800 hours). Hold an undergraduate degree that qualifies you for a UK master’s programme. Apply to three different and eligible UK university courses. You must have received an unconditional offer from at least one of these course choices by the references and education documents deadline listed on the application timeline. You are not eligible for a Chevening Scholarship if you: Hold British or dual British citizenship (unless you are a citizen of a British Overseas Territory or hold BN(O) and are applying from Hong Kong). Hold refugee status in a country not eligible for Chevening. However, if you are a citizen of an eligible country and hold refugee status in another eligible country, you are eligible for a scholarship. Are an employee, former employee, or relative of an employee of the UK government, British Embassies/High Commissions, the British Council, the Association of Commonwealth Universities, or sponsoring UK universities. Employees, former employees, or relatives* of an employee of Chevening Partner organisations are eligible to apply, but if the employment took place within the last two years, you cannot receive a Chevening Partner Award from the organisation from which you work, previously worked, or are affiliated with through relatives. Have previously studied in the UK on a UK government-funded scholarship. Note that having a master’s degree does not prevent you from applying for a second master’s degree in the UK, providing you can articulate how it aligns with your career goals and will help you to drive positive change in your home country. Application To apply, find the awards available in your country/territory. Begin by selecting your country of citizenship. You can then refine your search depending on if you are applying for a scholarship or a fellowship. Click here to apply For more information, see FAQ and visit Chevening Scholarship.

TITLE: African Academy of Sciences (AAS) Fellowship 2026

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: September 9, 2026 Applications are open for the African Academy of Sciences (AAS) Fellowship 2026. The African Academy of Sciences (AAS) recognizes scientific excellence by electing to its membership outstanding scholars who have attained the highest level of excellence in their scientific field and have made significant contributions to the advancement of science regionally and globally. AAS Fellows are elected for life through a rigorous peer review process on the basis of excellence in their publications record, innovations, leadership roles and contribution to policy and society. There is no age limit and AAS encourages nomination of female scientists and deserving scholars from under- represented disciplines. Candidates may be nominated from all scientific disciplines grouped into ten AAS scientific clusters: Agricultural & Nutritional Sciences. Biosciences. Chemical Sciences. Cultural Humanities & Social Sciences. Engineering, Technology & Applied Sciences. Mathematical Sciences. Geological, Environmental, Earth & Space Sciences. Medical & Health Sciences. Physical Sciences. Policy Sciences. Eligibility Have obtained a PhD or equivalent qualifications no less than 10 years before the year of nomination Have an H-index of 20 and above in either of (Scopus, Google Scholar, Web of science and ResearchGate) and not necessarily all. However, this is NOT applicable to social scientists. Have at least one journal article with 100 or more citations. Be a first author, senior or corresponding author or last author in at least 50% of the 10 submitted articles. Candidates for Associate Fellows who are members of an Academy in their home country or region will have an added advantage. Candidates for Associate Fellowship must: Demonstrate contributions that they have made to Africa. For example, they can demonstrate supervision of several African masters and doctoral students and published papers based on research in Africa with a substantial number of the African research papers having African first authors. Special consideration will be made to the associate fellows who are Social Scientists regarding publishing of papers. (See Annex 1) Be currently active and if not, clearly state on the form, what contribution they would make to the advancement of science and/or scholarship in Africa. Demonstrate outstanding scientific leadership and citizenship and, if applicable, contribution to policy. Demonstrate evidence of recognition by their peers in the field such as active peer review of journal articles, membership of scientific advisory committees, invited lectures, awards, prizes, membership in other academies or professional bodies. Peer review for Social Scientists will not be limited to journal articles. Application Click here to apply For more information, visit AAS Fellowship.

TITLE: Climate Resilience Awards for Business 2026

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: September 30, 2026 Applications are open for the Climate Resilience Awards for Business 2026. Resilience against climate change is becoming a strategic priority for businesses worldwide. Yet resilience projects and solutions often receive less visibility, recognition, and investment than climate mitigation initiatives. To help shift this reality, the World Business Council for Sustainable Development (WBCSD) and the Global Resilience Partnership (GRP) launched the Climate Resilience Awards for Business. Following a successful first edition in 2025, the initiative returns for a second year to further spotlight business leadership and innovation in climate adaptation and resilience. The Climate Resilience Awards for Business aim to: Recognize business leadership in climate resilience and adaptation Establish the state-of-play of business resilience action today Showcase credible and measurable resilience outcomes Share lessons learned by publishing high-quality case studies to inspire others Accelerate resilience solution implementation across sectors and geographies Strengthen the business case and strategic importance for resilience for business Categories Businesses can submit case studies under four categories. Building Climate-Proof Infrastructure: This category celebrates projects that strengthen the resilience of the built assets, facilities, energy systems, transport systems, industrial operations and other critical infrastructure of businesses, municipalities, and communities against acute and chronic climate change-related hazards. Promoting Water Stewardship: This category highlights businesses’ efforts put into managing water stress and ensuring water security by addressing flood, drought, and water management, in particular with solutions that prevent water-related disruption or improve the security of water supply for business and communities. Safeguarding Agriculture & Food Systems: This category recognizes companies that build resilience across agriculture and food systems, from agricultural production to processing, storage, logistics, and distribution, helping ensure food security and nutrition in the face of climate-related physical risks and supply chain disruptions. Protecting People First: This category focuses on projects that strengthen the capacity of workers, customers, value chain partners and communities to cope with, adapt to, and transform in response to climate change. Benefits Receive independent recognition for your organization’s leadership in climate resilience and adaptation through a robust and credible evaluation process and by a globally acclaimed jury. Showcase your project to business leaders, investors, policymakers, resilience practitioners, media audiences, and potential partners. Highlight measurable resilience outcomes and communicate the value your project creates for business, people, nature, and climate. Compare your approach against leading practices and learn from organizations advancing resilience across sectors and geographies. Connect with a growing network of businesses, experts, and practitioners committed to accelerating climate resilience action for business. Share lessons learned, contribute to the evidence base for resilience, and help shape emerging best practices for business resilience action worldwide. Eligibiliity Applications are open to business organizations of all sizes, sectors, and geographic locations. Both of the following applicant types are welcome: Resilience & Adaptation Implementers: Organizations improving the resilience or adaptive capacity of their operations, assets, people, infrastructure, within and beyond their value chain. Resilience Solution Providers: Organizations offering products, services, technologies, financing, or advisory support as part of their business model that help their clients, customers or other beneficiaries become more resilient against climate change. Solution providers are encouraged to submit applications that provide information on project implementation and resilience impact from their client’s perspective to demonstrate the resilience outcomes in practice. Application Click here to apply For more information, visit Climate Resilience Awards for Business.

TITLE: Berlin Prize at the American Academy in Berlin 2027-2028 ($5,000 stipend)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: September 25, 2026 Applications are open for the Berlin Prize at the American Academy in Berlin 2027-2028. The American Academy in Berlin is an independent, nonprofit institute for advanced study in the arts, humanities, social sciences, law, journalism, and public policy. Its primary mission is to strengthen the cultural and intellectual ties between the United States and Germany. Each year, following a rigorous selection process, the Academy awards roughly two dozen semester-long fellowships to individuals who demonstrate excellence in their respective fields. Benefits Berlin Prize Fellows receive monthly stipends of $5000, roundtrip airfare, accommodation at or near the Hans Arnhold Center, partial board, access to in-house library services, and professional networking opportunities. Fellows present their work to audiences in and around Berlin via lectures, readings, public discussions, performances, and film screenings. They should also be willing to engage with relevant German institutions, organizations, and the media. These activities are integral to the Academy’s mission of fostering transatlantic dialogue. Eligibility The Academy welcomes applications from a broad range of disciplines in the humanities, social sciences, law, journalism, and various areas of public policy. Berlin Prize recipients include both established and emerging scholars, writers, artists, journalists, and policy experts who wish to engage in independent study within an interdisciplinary residential community. Emerging scholars should hold a PhD and a strong record of peer-reviewed work beyond the dissertation. The Academy will not consider projects that have not advanced significantly beyond the candidate’s dissertation project. Independent scholars who satisfy the general eligibility requirements are welcome to apply. Applicants working in most other fields—such as journalism, filmmaking, or public policy—must have a significant record of publication or production. Writers of fiction and nonfiction must have published at least one book with a reputable press at the time of application. Note that they do not accept project proposals in mathematics or the natural sciences, and that we select visual artists and composers through invitation-only competitions. Fellowships are restricted to citizens and permanent residents of the United States. Candidates must explain any limited periods spent outside the United States, such as sabbaticals or foreign assignments. While project proposals need not focus on topics related to Germany, candidates should explain how a residency in Berlin would enhance their work. The Academy accepts proposals for collaborative projects. Candidates who wish to pursue a joint project must submit separate applications. External reviewers will consider the merits of each candidate alongside their joint project. Previously unsuccessful candidates are welcome to reapply. They strongly encourage re-applicants to update their application materials and revise their project proposals substantially. A number of Academy fellows have applied more than once before selection. Individuals who have already received a Berlin Prize are not eligible to apply for another, except under exceptional circumstances. Application The application deadline for the 2027-28 Berlin Prize is Friday, September 25, 2026, at 12:00 p.m. ET/6:00 p.m. CET. Fellowship candidates must complete the online application form and upload PDFs of the following materials (in English): project proposal of 1500 to 1750 words, plus a short bibliography (maximum one page), combined into a single document; curriculum vitae (maximum 10 pages); two writing samples, with a combined total not exceeding 60 pages. Applicants must also provide the names and contact information of three referees. Referees will receive an automated email via the application portal SlideRoom with instructions for submitting their letters of recommendation. Click here to apply For more information, visit Berlin Prize.

TITLE: OHCHR Indigenous Fellowship Program 2027 (Funded)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: September 6, 2026 Applications for the OHCHR Indigenous Fellowship Program 2027 are now open. The Indigenous Fellowship Programme was launched in 1997 by the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) in the context of the first International Decade of the World’s Indigenous People. The aim of the programme is to give indigenous persons the opportunity to gain knowledge about the UN system and mechanisms dealing with human rights issues in general and indigenous issues in particular. Trained participants are better equipped to assist their organisations and communities in protecting and promoting their rights. This training programme is available in 4 languages: English, Spanish, French and Portuguese. Fellows from all 4 language components of the programme are trained together with simultaneous interpretation over 4 weeks in Geneva. The date of the training programme usually coincides with the annual session of the Expert Mechanism on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (June/July each year), allowing the fellows to participate more actively in that Mechanism. Benefits The selected candidates are entitled to a return flight ticket, living expenses and basic health insurance for the duration of the training. Eligibility The candidate must be indigenous (non-indigenous persons will not be taken into consideration, even if they have close links with indigenous communities and/or organizations). Indigenous candidates, including women, LGBTQI+ individuals, and persons with disabilities, are strongly encouraged to apply. Age should not be a limitation to participation in the programme. Formal education should not be a limitation to participation in the IFP given the socio-economic barriers confronted by many indigenous peoples that limit access to formal educational institutions. Candidates should agree to train other indigenous persons after the return to their respective communities/organizations. The candidate should be proposed, and his/her candidacy supported by his/her indigenous organization and/or community. It is desirable that the sponsoring organization has a firm constituency or membership and that it is representative. The candidate should have a good working knowledge of the language in which the programme is imparted. OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: Unspecified Applications are open for the IWMF Fault Lines Reporting Fund 2026. Hate-based storylines have emerged from dark channels, fringe media, and special interest groups across the U.S. to mainstream narratives promoting religious intolerance and gendered discrimination. This racist, antisemitic, Islamophobic, and misogynistic rhetoric is filled with dis- and misinformation, fueling violence toward marginalized communities. The International Women’s Media Foundation’s Fault Lines Reporting Fund supports journalists reporting on the forces driving racism, antisemitism, Islamophobia, misogyny, and other forms of intolerance promoting hate in the United States. Successful applications will examine how false, divisive, and harmful narratives – such as stories that promote or normalize hate, discrimination, and the dehumanization of individuals and communities – take hold, including what is fueling them, where they are most pronounced, the scope of their impact, and where individuals and communities are making real progress in combatting these hate-based agendas. The three-year program will provide grants to staff and freelance journalists planning well-researched, investigative, and evidence-based reporting within the United States. Grant Grant awards will range from $2,500 to $10,000. Larger awards will be considered on a case-by-case basis. Grant funds may be used to cover travel, logistics, security, insurance, and other reporting-related expenses. Eligibility Applicants must report in the United States. The applicant’s primary profession must be journalism. Applications will be accepted from freelance, staff, or content-based journalists. Applicants must have 3+ years of professional journalism experience outside of internships. Applicants must present a strong track record of exceptional journalism or show proof of interest from an editor. Application Grants will be distributed on a rolling basis to meet time-sensitive needs. Submissions will be answered within 6–8 weeks of receipt. TITLE: Wongani Mulanga from Malawi is OD Young Person of the Month – August 2026

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Wongani Mulanga is a Malawian Environmental Scientist and the Co-Founder and Executive Director of Green Minds Malawi, a youth-led organisation working at the intersection of climate education, clean energy access, and community engagement. She also runs Her Climate Lab, a girl-led climate education programme at a secondary school in Mangochi. Background and Work Growing up, Wongani watched students around her work hard with very little to show for it, not because they lacked ability, but because they lacked electricity to study by, resources to learn with, and spaces that reflected their potential back at them. She carried that observation through school and into university, and when she finished her BSc in Environmental Science, she decided she was not going to wait for a job before doing something about it. Together with three other young people, she co-founded Green Minds Malawi and launched the Green Ed Initiative almost immediately after finishing university. Green Ed is built on the conviction that educational inequality and environmental degradation share the same root. Students studying by kerosene lamp are breathing harmful fumes and falling behind academically because the light is poor, and both problems have the same solution. Through the initiative, Green Minds distributes solar lamps to students from households without reliable electricity, works with schools to establish environmental clubs, introduces waste management through bin donations and clean-up campaigns, and plants trees. Young people are treated as thinkers who are already part of the climate story, not as passive recipients waiting to be educated. The initiative has engaged over 100 students across four partner schools, three primary schools and one secondary school, through environmental education, club activities, and clean energy access. The work has also extended beyond Green Minds. Through Her Climate Lab, Wongani facilitated a session on solar energy and clean technology with a group of young women studying at a secondary school in Mangochi, connecting climate science to the energy choices their families make every day. How It Started There was no single dramatic moment, it was just an accumulation of things observed over years, students relying on kerosene to read at night, environmental issues treated as secondary in communities already carrying too many burdens, young people left out of conversations about changes affecting their lakes, their farms, and their futures. What pushed Wongani to act was recognising that the gap was not in awareness. Most people already know the environment is under pressure. The gap was in practical tools and platforms that would allow young people to do something about it, and she did not want to be someone who wrote reports about that gap without trying to close it. Successes So Far Green Minds has distributed solar lamps to students from households without electricity, enabling them to study at night while adopting clean energy in ways that feel personal and immediate rather than abstract. Four school partnerships have produced environmental clubs, clean-up campaigns, waste management initiatives, and tree planting activities. The organisation has also been documenting climate stories from communities living on the shores of Lake Malawi, capturing flood experiences and recovery through its Climate Witness project. Challenges and How They Were Faced Like most youth-led startups, the hardest thing has been funding. Green Minds is still largely self-funded, with the founding team working voluntarily and relying on personal contributions alongside a small pool of dedicated volunteers to keep operations running. There is no comfortable budget to fall back on, and every activity requires finding creative ways to make limited resources go further. OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: September 7, 2026 Applications are open for the NourishNext West Africa Youth Agrifood Innovation Challenge 2026. This is a regional innovation challenge, led by the Global Alliance for Improved Nutrition (GAIN) in partnership with the Scaling Up Nutrition (SUN) Movement and national implementing partners across Benin, Côte d’Ivoire, Nigeria, and Senegal. The initiative is implemented with the support of the Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation (SDC) and the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS). NourishNext identifies, supports, and accelerates youth-led innovations that strengthen nutritious fruit and vegetable value chains across West Africa. The Challenge seeks innovative solutions that improve how fruits and vegetables are processed, preserved, packaged, transported, marketed, distributed, purchased, prepared, and consumed, contributing to more resilient, inclusive, and nutrition-sensitive food systems. Competition Categories Value addition and processing innovations that enhance fruit and vegetable value chains Integration of Local Produce of fruits and vegetables in Public Nutrition and Social Protection Systems Strengthened market and supply chain solutions for fruits and vegetables, that improve their supply, safety, and desirability Consumer Demand and Healthy Diet Behaviour Change for increased consumption of fruits and vegetables Benefits Selected innovators will receive USD $5,000 in seed funding, tailored technical mentorship from industry experts, capacity-building opportunities, and access to national and regional networking and showcasing platforms. Finalists will have the opportunity to present their innovations at the NourishNext West Africa Regional Showcase in Dakar, Senegal, in 2026, connecting with policymakers, investors, development partners, and private sector leaders. Eligibility Open to youth-led enterprises and innovators aged 18 to 35 years, who are based in and primarily operating within Benin, Nigeria, Senegal, or Côte d’Ivoire. This age limit is flexible for women-led enterprises/ set-ups, for women up to the age of 40 years. Your innovation must directly address at least one of the four competition categories mentioned and operate within or in direct support of fruit and the vegetable value chains. Application You need a completed online application form (all sections), proof of age of the lead applicant (national ID, passport, or birth certificate), and evidence of operational stage — photos, customer testimonials, financial records, or a pilot report etc. Click here to apply For more information, visit NourishNext West Africa Youth Agrifood Innovation Challenge.

TITLE: City Bureau Civic Information Fellowship 2026 (stipend available)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: August 11, 2026 Applications are open for the City Bureau Civic Information Fellowship 2026. The City Bureau’s Civic Information Fellowship is a paid, six-month, two-phase program for Chicagoans who want to grow their skills in community engagement, civic participation and journalism. With support from City Bureau staff, fellows will use these skills to design and implement group projects that help improve their neighbors’ access to information. Their work prioritizes the South and West sides of Chicago. Fellows attend weekly learning and co-working sessions to build their skills. Fellows work individually and in teams to deeply understand the information needs of their communities, gather information, build relationships over time, and tell compelling stories about civic issues. City Bureau emphasizes racial equity and community engagement, and participants can expect to have critical conversations about how people create, receive and share information; and how they participate in civic life. The Horn of Africa (HoA) is home to one of the world’s youngest populations that are aspiring to shape political dialogue, civic action, and democratic change across the region. Yet despite their demographic strength, many remain excluded from meaningful engagement in governance, face shrinking civic space in the national landscape, and have limited opportunities to collaborate across borders. To contribute to addressing these challenges, the Horn Center for Democracy (HCD) is launching the Youth Leadership for Democracy and Solidarity (YLDS)-a regional leadership initiative that brings together emerging youth leaders committed to promoting democratic governance and cross-border cooperation. This initiative is part of HCD’s multiyear strategy-youth development program-composed of digital civic education and youth leadership cohorts. This program aims to advance youth engagement in democracy, foster cross-border collaboration, and increase the resilience of pro-democracy actors throughout the HoA region. Through intensive learning, peer exchange, leadership development, and collaborative action, the program will support a new generation of young leaders equipped to lead democratic transformation across the region. About the Youth Cohort The inaugural cohort will bring together 15 emerging youth leaders from across the HoA region and will take place in Addis Ababa from October 11-18th, 2026. Participants will engage in: A week-long intensive residential leadership training; Immersive online learning sessions (Hybrid guided model) Interactive workshops led by regional experts, democracy practitioners, and academics Peer learning and dialogue, collaborative problem-solving, and innovation labs Continued mentorship, networking opportunities, and engagement through an alumni network The program is designed not only as a training opportunity but as the foundation of a regional network of democratic leaders committed to long-term collaboration and solidarity. TITLE: International Science Council (ISC) Civic Science Fellow Program 2026 (Funded)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: August 16, 2026 Applications are open for the International Science Council (ISC) Civic Science Fellow Program 2026. The International Science Council (ISC) is seeking applications from outstanding early- to mid-career researchers to serve as a Civic Science Fellow with a focus on science communication. Hosted virtually by the ISC, the 18-month Fellowship provides an opportunity to explore how multilateral organizations can communicate evidence more effectively in international policy processes and strengthen the role of science in multilateral decision-making. Working at the interface of science, policy and communication, the Fellow will work with the ISC Secretariat, its global membership and international partners to analyze current practices, develop practical guidance and test new approaches to communicating scientific evidence in complex policy environments. Responsibilities The Fellow will contribute to a programme of work that includes: Mapping existing science communication practices, channels and audiences across selected international partners. Conducting research on the information ecosystem in which scientific evidence is communicated and the factors that influence how science is communicated, interpreted and used in international policy contexts. Identifying barriers and enablers for the uptake of scientific evidence in decision-making processes. Analysing how evolving digital information environments, including misinformation and disinformation, shape engagement with scientific evidence. Drawing on communication, behavioural and social science to identify effective approaches for communicating evidence to diverse audiences. Developing practical guidance and resources to improve communication across science–society interfaces for scientific and multilateral organizations. Supporting the piloting and evaluation of communication approaches through selected ISC initiatives and partnerships. Producing high-quality analytical reports and publications. Supporting outreach and engagement of relevant academic and practitioner networks. Funding A monthly stipend of about USD $5,000. This Fellowship is fully funded through the Rita Allen Civic Science Fellows program. Eligibility Applicants must: Hold a PhD (or expect to have completed one before the Fellowship start date) in a relevant discipline. Be able to undertake the Fellowship on a full-time basis for its full 18-month duration from September 2026 with a letter of support expected from the organization where the Fellow may be currently employed. It will be the responsibility of the Fellow to ensure that she/he can commit for the full duration of the fellowship and to make the necessary arrangements with his/her employer as necessary. Sign a tripartite collaboration agreement with the Rita Allen Foundation and the ISC. The ISC will also enter into a contractual arrangement directly with the Fellow and the stipend will normally be paid to the Fellow directly. Hold a valid passport and be able to undertake international travel as required by the Fellowship. Be eligible to obtain visas for international travel where necessary. The Fellowship will involve occasional travel to international meetings and events, including in countries such as the United States. Be available weekly on Tuesdays for 18 months from noon to 2:00 pm ET to participate in Learning Labs with the other Civic Science Fellows of the cohort, convened by the Rita Allen Foundation. Applicants should demonstrate: A strong track record of high-quality research and publications relevant to the Fellowship. Demonstrated expertise in science communication, particularly in relation to public policy, international governance or the science–policy interface. Experience working with, or advising, governments, international organizations, scientific organizations or other policy actors A proven ability to translate research into practical guidance, tools or recommendations for policy and practice. Excellent written and spoken English, with excellent communication and facilitation skills. The ability to work independently while engaging effectively with a wide range of international stakeholders. Experience leading interdisciplinary or international research collaborations, designing capacity-building activities, or working in multilateral contexts would be highly desirable. TITLE: France-South Africa Scholarship Programme 2026

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: October 8, 2026 Applications are invited for the France-South Africa Scholarship Programme 2026. The France-South Africa Scholarship Programme is directed to students who intend to study in universities or higher education institutions in France for their Master’s degree or PhD. Campus France is an agency of the French Ministries of Europe and Foreign Affairs and of Higher Education, Research and Innovation. Its goal is to promote French Higher Education and facilitate academic international mobility and exchange. The Campus France South Africa office assists candidates in identifying study programmes aligned with their academic background and personal project. The central Campus France agency in France is responsible for managing all aspects of scholarships for selected laureates. Scholarship The scholarship provides a monthly allowance to pursue studies in France (covering living expenses). It also includes social security coverage for the whole stay in France, priority access to accommodation in CROUS student residences and one round-trip air ticket to France. The full scholarship does not include tuition fees. The monthly allowance granted is approximately 900€ for master students and 1 850€ for PhD students. Eligibility To be eligible for the France-South Africa Scholarship Programme, applicants must be: Born on or after 1 January 1997. A citizen of South Africa, Lesotho or Malawi. Dual French citizens are not eligible. Have achieved a minimum average of 60% in their most recently completed degree. For Master’s applicants: plan to enrol in a French higher education institution to pursue a Master’s degree. Applicants are not required to have secured admission at the time of submitting their scholarship application. For PhD applicants: plan to pursue a PhD at a French higher education institution and have identified a prospective supervisor or research laboratory in France. Applicants are not required to have a formal admission offer at the time of submitting their scholarship application. Selection Process Applicants will be shortlisted on the basis of the quality of their file. Candidates whose applications have been pre-selected will be interviewed. In order to identify grant recipients, the Advisory board will consider: The candidate’s skills and merit as indicated by his/her academic record and professional background. The quality of his/her study project, its coherence with his/her background, as well as the clarity and quality of his/her future career plans. For PhD applicants, the Advisory Board will favour PhDs under co-supervision and commitment of South African and French supervisors will be decisive. The level of proficiency in foreign languages and its adequacy with the chosen study programmes. Application The application file is to be submitted online only and must include: A complete application form (online). A passport copy (or ID if passport is not yet available). An up-to-date CV that also states the candidate’s entire academic history. A cover letter explaining motivations and interests in the planned academic project. Copies of all previous academic degree certificates. University transcripts (academic marks) of at least three years of studies. Click here to apply For more information, visit France-South Africa Scholarship.

The Resilient Futures Call is a co-funded initiative by the Better Politics Fund, the European Climate Foundation, Naia Trust, and the Vibe Fund to support non-partisan initiatives working at the intersection of democratic political leadership and climate resilience globally. The total available funding is USD $700,000 across two funding streams: Ideation Grants and Incubation Grants. The Resilient Futures Call supports non-partisan initiatives working at the intersection of political leadership and climate resilience, across three areas: Pathways. Helping climate scientists, advocates, and affected communities work more effectively with political and/or governance decision-makers so that good evidence and local knowledge shape policy, and so that policy gets carried through at every level of government, from town councils to national parliaments. Leadership. Supporting programs that integrate a critical climate lens into democratic leadership development, strengthening ethical communication, policy design, effective implementation, and strategic coalition-building at all levels of governance. This includes initiatives that open doors and build pipelines for leaders from underrepresented backgrounds to engage in climate-related political processes. Cross-Sector Leadership. Backing leadership on the issues climate touches most directly — energy, housing, transport, food, security, health, and conservation — and helping reform political systems and institutions so that leaders and new ideas in these areas can succeed. Deadline: August 17, 2026 Applications are open for the ProPublica Emerging Reporters Program 2026-2027. The Emerging Reporters Program is specifically designed for talented aspiring journalists who find investigative journalism inaccessible for financial reasons. ProPublica has a vested interest in developing more journalists from a wide range of backgrounds, particularly those who are economically disadvantaged. They consider it crucial to the future of the industry and to their own ability to fulfill their mission, which is to expose abuses of power and produce journalism that provokes change. Without the voices and points of view of more journalists from diverse backgrounds, there is every reason to believe that important stories are being overlooked. Barriers that keep aspiring journalists from entering the field include financial constraints and lack of access to mentors and training. The Emerging Reporters Program is aimed at lowering those barriers and encouraging the next generation of journalists. Benefits The Emerging Reporters Program provides $9,000 stipends, along with mentoring and a trip to a journalism conference, such as the Investigative Reporters & Editors conference. Accommodations and other expenses for the conference will be covered by ProPublica. The dates of the conferences are to be determined. Eligibility Open only to students who are eligible to file U.S. taxes and are able to provide a completed W-9 form, including U.S. citizens or U.S. residents. The W-9 form requires that each participant provide a valid Social Security number or individual taxpayer identification number. They will not make any exceptions to this rule. All students who will be undergraduate juniors or seniors in college this academic year are eligible to apply, and students from groups that are traditionally underrepresented in journalism are especially encouraged to do so. Application This year’s program will run from late September to June, during which time mentors and program participants will be in contact by phone and email. TITLE: How to Start a Career in Mental Health Counseling

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Mental health counseling is a meaningful career for people who want to help others through some of life’s hardest moments. Counselors support individuals facing anxiety, grief, trauma, depression, relationship conflict, and other challenges that can affect daily life. The profession calls for education, supervised training, licensure, and emotional commitment, but it can also offer purpose, flexibility, and long-term stability. For people drawn to listening, guidance, and personal connection, this field is worth serious consideration. Understanding what counselors do, what training is needed, and which career paths are available can help you decide whether this profession fits your strengths and goals. Getting Started Many people become interested in counseling because they want to make a direct difference in someone’s life. If you have already started exploring the education required to be a mental health counselor, you are already taking an important first step. Mental health counselors do much more than give advice. Their job is to help clients understand emotions, behaviors, and experiences while developing healthier ways to cope. Some clients seek counseling after a loss, divorce, or personal crisis. Others are dealing with long-term stress, unresolved trauma, or emotional pain that has built over time. One of the rewarding parts of this work is that progress looks different for every client. For one person, improvement may mean returning to work, school, or social activities. For another, it may simply mean getting through a difficult week with better coping skills. In counseling, both major breakthroughs and smaller steps forward matter. What Counselors Really Do At the center of the job is careful listening, thoughtful questioning, and guided conversation. Effective counselors are not passive observers. They help clients identify patterns, set realistic goals, and practice habits that support emotional well-being. On a typical day, a mental health counselor may meet with clients individually to discuss panic, anger, sadness, trauma, stress, or relationship struggles. They may teach coping strategies, help clients challenge harmful thought patterns, and encourage practical tools clients can use between sessions. The work also includes responsibilities beyond face-to-face counseling. Counselors document sessions, track client progress, maintain accurate records, and follow legal, ethical, and privacy standards. Depending on the setting, they may also coordinate care with family members, physicians, teachers, or community providers. This balance of empathy and structure is one of the profession’s defining features. Counselors create a safe space where clients feel heard, but they also guide them toward meaningful change. Skills That Matter You do not need to be perfect to become a strong counselor, but several qualities are essential. Empathy is one of the most important. Clients need to feel respected, understood, and emotionally safe, especially when discussing painful or deeply personal experiences. Patience matters as well. Progress in counseling is rarely quick or predictable. Some clients open up right away and make steady gains, while others need time to trust the process. A good counselor remains supportive even when progress feels slow. Communication skills are equally important. Counselors must know how to ask useful questions, explain ideas clearly, and pay attention not only to what clients say but also to what they avoid saying. Active listening, emotional awareness, and thoughtful responses help build a productive therapeutic relationship. Professionalism and resilience are also critical. Counselors hear difficult stories on a regular basis, so they need strong boundaries and healthy ways to manage stress. Caring deeply is part of the work, but protecting your own mental well-being is necessary for long-term success. TITLE: How Nurses Can Plan the Next Step in Their Career

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Many nurses eventually reach a point where they wonder what comes next. After building experience, it is natural to want growth, a stronger voice, or a larger role in improving patient care. Some nurses want to lead teams, mentor newer colleagues, teach, shape policy, or expand their clinical authority. The next step does not have to feel uncertain. With thoughtful planning, nurses can choose a path that fits their goals, schedules, and responsibilities. Why Advance Now Healthcare is changing quickly, and nurses are needed in broader, more influential roles across hospitals, clinics, and community settings. Employers increasingly value professionals who can lead teams, improve systems, solve complex problems, and advocate for better outcomes. That demand is one reason many working nurses explore online MSN to DNP programs. For nurses who want to keep working while continuing their education, these programs can offer a practical path. Advancing now can also prepare nurses for future opportunities before they become urgent. Leadership and advanced practice roles bring greater responsibility, but they also allow nurses to help shape decisions instead of only responding to them. In these positions, nurses may mentor colleagues, improve workflows, and influence patient outcomes on a wider scale. Career growth is not only about earning a new title or degree. It is also about expanding your voice, increasing your impact, and building a future in which your experience can influence healthcare more broadly. Career Goals First Before choosing a program, nurses should define what they truly want. The next career step should reflect personal interests, strengths, and long-term goals, not just what sounds impressive or what others suggest. Some nurses are drawn to leadership roles where they can oversee staff, improve department operations, and guide teams through change. Others want stronger clinical authority so they can play a larger role in patient care decisions. Teaching is another common goal. That may mean working with nursing students, leading staff development, or training teams within a healthcare system. Other nurses are interested in policy, quality improvement, or organizational change and want to influence care beyond the bedside. Financial advancement can also be part of the decision, and that is a valid reason to consider further education. A useful first step is to write down your top three career goals. Specific goals make it easier to evaluate options. Once goals are defined, it becomes much easier to identify the degree or program that supports them. Fit School Into Life For many nurses, the biggest challenge is not motivation but time. Long shifts, family commitments, charting, and everyday responsibilities can make school seem difficult to manage. Still, many nurses succeed because they build a plan around real life rather than waiting for a perfect moment. Start by looking honestly at your weekly routine. Identify where studying can happen consistently, whether that means a few evenings a week, early mornings, or a block of time on weekends. Small, regular study sessions are often more realistic and effective than trying to do everything at once. It also helps to talk with the people in your household before classes begin. Setting expectations about study time, shared responsibilities, and support during busy periods can reduce tension later. If you have children, childcare planning is especially important. Choosing a program format that fits your life from the beginning can make a major difference in stress and your ability to stay on track. The goal is not perfect balance. The goal is a routine that remains workable even when work is busy and life becomes unpredictable. What to Compare When researching programs, it is easy to focus on polished websites

TITLE: Why Nursing Careers Matter More Than Ever Today

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Nursing matters more than ever because healthcare is no longer built around brief doctor visits or simple treatment plans. People are living longer, managing more stress, and facing health concerns that affect daily life in complex ways. That shift has placed nurses at the center of care, education, and problem-solving. For anyone considering the profession, nursing stands out as one of the most direct ways to help others while building a stable and flexible career. Why Nursing Is Changing Healthcare is evolving quickly, and nursing is evolving with it. Hospitals, clinics, schools, long-term care centers, and community programs all need nurses who can do more than follow routines. Patients often have medical, emotional, and social needs that overlap, so care now depends more on prevention, education, and teamwork. The profession is shifting from a role focused mainly on treatment toward one built around leadership, prevention, and stronger preparation. Nurses are increasingly expected to guide patients, mentor peers, and shape how care is delivered across entire systems. These broad changes are exactly what people mean when they discuss the future of nursing, which is less about responding to illness after it appears and more about helping people understand their health before small concerns become serious problems. Technology has also changed healthcare, but it has not replaced the human side of nursing. Digital tools can track symptoms, organize records, and monitor vital signs, yet they cannot reassure a frightened family member or notice subtle confusion in a patient. Nurses are often the people who catch those small but important changes early. More Than Bedside Care Many people still picture nurses mainly at the bedside, checking vital signs and giving medication. Those duties remain essential, but they represent only part of a much broader field. Nursing now offers many paths instead of one narrow role. Nurses may teach families how to manage chronic illnesses like diabetes, support students in schools, coordinate services for older adults, or explain complicated treatment plans to patients who feel overwhelmed. Some work in public health and focus on prevention. Others advocate for people who feel anxious, confused, or unheard. This expanded role matters because healthcare can become complicated very quickly. One patient may need medication, transportation, follow-up care, mental health support, and clear instructions all at once. Nurses often help connect those pieces. In practice, they frequently act as caregivers, educators, coaches, and care coordinators at the same time. What Communities Need Now Communities today face serious and often overlapping health challenges. An aging population means more people are living with long-term conditions such as heart disease, arthritis, and memory-related disorders. Mental health concerns are also being discussed more openly, which is important because ignoring them has never made them disappear. Access to care remains another major issue. Some people live far from healthcare services. Others cannot afford regular visits, do not have reliable transportation, or simply do not know where to begin. Even health information can be hard to trust, especially when conflicting advice online leaves patients more uncertain than informed. Nurses help close these gaps in practical ways. They explain care in plain language, recognize warning signs early, and help patients stay on track with treatment. In many communities, nurses are the steady and trusted presence people rely on. That trust matters because people are more likely to ask questions, follow care plans, and seek help before a crisis when they feel heard and respected. TITLE: Horizon Fellowship 2027 for Emerging Tech Experts (Funded)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: August 30, 2026 Applications are open for the Horizon Fellowship 2027. The Horizon Fellowship helps emerging technology experts launch their careers in public service. The Horizon Fellowship places experts in AI, biotechnology, and other emerging technologies in federal agencies, congressional offices and committees, and leading think tanks in Washington, DC, for up to two years. Fellows receive comprehensive training, networking opportunities, and access to a supportive community of 100+ other fellows and alumni to launch their careers in public service. Emerging technologies like AI and biotechnology are rapidly reshaping many domains, from healthcare and science to national security and the economy. The US government plays a critical role in developing and governing these technologies, and it needs people who understand them. Horizon fellows supply that understanding across the institutions that shape technology policy. Programme Structure Successful applicants will go through training, matching, and placement phases from January to summer of 2027. Training (January to March 2027): The selected fellowship cohort completes a part-time, work-compatible remote training on policy work, including the mechanics of the federal government and applied skills like memo writing and policy analysis. The training culminates in an in-person weekend in Washington, DC, where fellows connect with dozens of emerging technology experts from across the policy world. The curriculum and networking prepare fellows to secure strong placement offers and perform high-quality work during their fellowship. Matching (April to May 2027): After training, fellows begin an individualized matching process. Fellows decide which host organizations to pursue; Horizon supports them with introductions, application feedback, and interview preparation. Most fellows receive multiple offers and choose the placement that best fits their goals. Horizon has a nearly 100% fellow matching rate. Placement (Spring/Summer 2027 onward): After successfully matching, fellows work with their chosen host organization to finalize a start date (typically during the summer). Horizon provides a full-time salary and benefits once their placement begins. Fellows’ work is fully supervised and directed by their host organization. Benefits The provide $78,000 base salary for junior fellows, $130,000 for fellows, and $190,000+ for senior fellows. All fellows also receive a $17,000 benefits-equivalent stipend, a $3,000 professional development stipend, and up to $3,000 for relocation to DC, if needed. Eligibility They are looking for people who want to put their expertise to work on the hardest problems in emerging technology policy. They value attitude, abilities, and knowledge more than formal credentials, and they welcome applicants from diverse and interdisciplinary professional backgrounds. The Horizon Fellowship has helped engineers, data scientists, historians, lawyers, doctors, and many other professionals transition into public service. Competitive candidates generally have demonstrated subject-matter expertise in their technology area of interest. This could include relevant coursework, work experience, research projects, policy writing, or deep self-study. Prior policy experience is not required. They support fellows at a range of career stages through three fellowship levels: Junior fellow: typically less than 3 years of full-time work experience and no PhD. Current students and recent graduates are welcome to apply. Fellow: typically 3+ years of relevant full-time experience or a PhD. Senior fellow (new this year): typically 12+ years of full-time experience, including extensive leadership experience. Senior fellows will typically be placed in roles with greater responsibility, such as leading workstreams and advising senior decision-makers. Application The bulk of the application consists of administrative questions and a set of brief (max. 100-word) short-answer responses. If you exit without submitting, the application will not save your answers. Click here to apply For more information, visit Horizon Fellowship.

TITLE: Google Academic Research Awards 2026 (up to $100k)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: August 7, 2026 Applications are open for the Google Academic Research Awards 2026. Google holds global open calls for proposals that support groundbreaking foundational and applied research in computing and technology. This funding cycle, Google is interested in topics focused on quantum computing. This call for proposals is open to professors (assistant, associate, etc.) at degree-granting institutions who are advising students and conducting research in the field of technology and computing. The 2026 cycle centers on two major research directions. The first is Early Fault-Tolerant Quantum Algorithms & Applications, which focuses on building useful algorithms for early fault-tolerant quantum systems and exploring practical applications that may work with relatively few logical qubits. The second is Quantum Computing Security, which covers the protection of quantum systems, vulnerabilities at the classical-to-quantum interface, and broader cybersecurity concerns around quantum infrastructure. Google is looking for research that can help make quantum computing safer, more dependable, and more usable in real-world environments. Awards Awards will be up to $100k, but they may consider larger amounts for exceptional proposals that demonstrate a clear and compelling rationale for the increased funding. Funds will be disbursed as unrestricted gifts to the university or degree-granting research institution and are not intended for overhead or indirect costs. Eligibility Open to professors (assistant, associate, etc.) at a university or degree-granting research institution. Applicants may only serve as Principal Investigator (PI) or co-PI on one proposal per round. There can be a maximum of 2 PIs per proposal. Proposals must be related to computing or technology. Review Criteria Faculty merit: Faculty is accomplished in research, community engagement, and open source contributions, with potential to contribute to responsible innovation. Research merit: Faculty’s proposed research is aligned with Google Research interests, innovative, and likely to have a significant impact on the field. Proposal quality: The research proposal is clear, focused, and well-organized, and it demonstrates the team’s ability to successfully execute the research and achieve a significant impact. TITLE: When Unexpected Costs Hit: Your Financial Options Explained

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Unexpected expenses can disrupt even the most carefully planned budget. A vehicle may need repairs before the next workday, a laptop may fail during an important semester, or a medical bill may arrive without much warning. These situations rarely happen when money is readily available. When unexpected costs arise, it is easy to focus on finding the quickest solution. Taking a little time to understand the available financial options, however, can make a meaningful difference. The best approach depends on the nature of the expense, the amount involved, and the resources already available. Understanding the available choices before making a financial decision can help reduce stress while limiting financial pressure in the months ahead. Building a Clear Picture of the Expense The first step is understanding exactly what the expense involves before deciding how to pay for it. Knowing whether the cost is urgent, essential, or flexible helps narrow the available financial options. Some expenses require immediate attention because delaying them can create larger problems. Emergency medical treatment, essential vehicle repairs, or a broken heating system during winter are common examples. Waiting may increase both the inconvenience and the eventual cost. Other expenses allow more flexibility. A home décor upgrade, elective purchase, or nonessential subscription may feel important in the moment, though postponing it often has little lasting impact. Recognizing that difference helps prevent unnecessary borrowing. It also helps to estimate the full cost before making a decision. Looking beyond the initial invoice to include taxes, repair fees, or related expenses provides a clearer picture of how much financial assistance, if any, is actually needed. Using Savings and Emergency Funds First Savings are often the simplest financial resource to use when unexpected costs arise. If money has already been set aside for emergencies, using those funds may eliminate the need to borrow altogether. Emergency savings exist because unexpected situations are part of life. Drawing from those funds for a necessary repair or medical expense allows the problem to be addressed without creating a repayment obligation that continues for months afterward. Not every household has a fully funded emergency savings account, making it important to consider all available financial options. Even a modest savings balance, however, may reduce the amount that ultimately needs to be borrowed, making future repayment easier. Using savings does not mean abandoning long-term financial goals. After the emergency has passed, gradually rebuilding an emergency fund can help prepare for future unexpected expenses without placing extra strain on the monthly budget. Exploring Payment Plans and Financial Assistance Borrowing is not always the first solution worth considering. Many organizations offer payment arrangements or financial assistance programs that allow essential expenses to be managed over time. Medical providers frequently offer payment plans that divide larger bills into smaller monthly amounts. Colleges and universities may offer tuition payment plans, while utility companies sometimes provide hardship programs for customers facing temporary financial difficulties. Students may also have access to emergency grants or institutional assistance, depending on their school. Asking about available resources before committing to a loan can sometimes uncover solutions that were not immediately obvious. Exploring these alternatives may take a little extra time, though it can reduce the amount that needs to be financed. Even if they do not fully cover the expense, they may work alongside other financial options to make the situation easier to manage. Personal Loans as a Financing Option Personal loans can become a practical option when savings are limited and an essential expense cannot reasonably wait. Unlike revolving credit, they typically provide a fixed amount that is repaid through scheduled monthly installments. This repayment structure

Deadline: October 15, 2026 Applications are open for the Human Rights Advocates Program (HRAP) 2027-2028. Founded in 1989, HRAP leverages the resources of Columbia University and those offered by NYC as a hub of NGOs and international organizations to provide human rights advocates with academic, skill-building, mentoring, and networking opportunities. Through seminars, participation in University courses, and workshops led by staff from leading human rights organizations as well as meetings with policymakers and funders, advocates share their experiences, reflect critically on their work, and plan future campaigns. More than 350 advocates from nearly 100 countries have attended the program since it was created in 1989. The cumulative reach of HRAP participants is extraordinary: alumni have worked with organizations whose memberships range from the thousands to the millions. Participants are selected on the basis of their previous work experience in human rights, commitment to the human rights field, and demonstrated ability to pursue graduate-level studies. Advocates must work at the grassroots level. Applicants from high-income countries will not be considered except for those representing marginalized communities. Fluency in English is required. TITLE: Doha Debates Ambassador Program 2026

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: August 24, 2026 Applications are open for the Doha Debates Ambassador Program 2026. The Doha Debates Ambassador Program is a virtual convening of young leaders from across the globe who are eager to change how we conduct public discourse. Over the course of 12 weeks, participants from around the world will develop intercultural communication, systems thinking and debate skills through expert-led training, mentored collaboration and an emphasis on personal storytelling and cross-cultural understanding. Program Details Ambassadors should expect to devote a total of 4–5 hours each week of the program. They will attend the program synchronously via 90-minute weekly Zoom meetings and engage asynchronously via the Doha Debates Learning Community. The program culminates in a special two-hour event called the World Majlis, in which small groups of ambassadors will apply their new skills to conduct virtual dialogues. Upon successful completion of the program, ambassadors will receive an official certificate from Doha Debates. Alumni of the program are invited to stay engaged with Doha Debates through events, conversations, workshops, debates and more. They may also be selected to serve as mentors for future cohorts. Benefits Throughout the course of the 12-week program, participants interact with expert facilitators, mentors and each other to practice the skills they’re learning, including: facilitating and participating in discussions of complex global issues effectively navigating intercultural communication articulating and understanding their own worldview and those of others effectively telling their own story to engage and motivate people developing and exploring personal connections to global issues better understanding others and the motivations behind their positions cultivating lifelong relationships with an international peer group and learning circle engaging with Doha Debates staff and events, making connections for continued work learning how to hold open, productive community discussions at home, school and work Eligibility Eligible candidates for the Doha Debates Ambassador Program must: complete the three-step application process by August 24, 2026. be between the ages of 18–26 at the start of the program on September 22, 2026. be able to access reliable internet for videoconferencing. be a fluent English speaker. be available for all Zoom meetings every Tuesday at 6:00 p.m. AST from September 22 – December 1, 2026. OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: September 15, 2026 Applications are open for the Sloan Research Fellowships 2027. Sloan Research Fellowships support fundamental research conducted by early-career scientists. The two-year $75,000 fellowships are awarded annually to early-career researchers whose creativity, innovation, and research accomplishments make them stand out as the next generation of leaders. The Alfred P. Sloan Foundation seeks nominations of outstanding early career researchers for the Sloan Research Fellowships in the fields of chemistry, computer science, Earth system science, economics, mathematics, neuroscience, and physics. Candidates should have a record of independent research accomplishments that demonstrate creativity, initiative, and the potential to become leaders in the scientific community through their contributions to their field. The Foundation strongly encourages the nomination of qualified candidates from all backgrounds. Candidates must be members of the faculty of a college, university, or other degree-granting institution in the U.S. or Canada. Candidates must be tenure-track, though untenured, as of September 15 of the nomination year. Candidate’s faculty position must carry a regular teaching obligation. Nomination The following materials are required for nomination: A letter from a department head or other senior researcher officially nominating the candidate and describing his or her qualifications, initiative, and research; The candidate’s curriculum vitae (including a list of the candidates scientific publications); Two representative articles by the candidate that highlight his or her independent research; A brief (one-page) statement by the candidate describing his or her significant scientific work and immediate research plans; Three letters from other researchers (preferably not all from the same institution) written in support of the candidate’s nomination. They welcome submissions in three categories: written essays, poetry, and audiovisual works, responding to the theme of Europe’s future and EU enlargement. TEPSA’s contest “What future for the European continent?” is an invitation to change that. Whatever your background, wherever you are from, if you have a vision for what Europe could become, they want to hear it. Share your ideas and visions through three creative categories: poetry, written essays, and audiovisual works, and contribute to a broader public conversation on the opportunities that a wider EU can bring. The Young Feminist AI School is a free, fully online UN Women programme for young people aged 18 to 30, with a strong focus on young women and girls. Over 12 weeks (August–October 2026), participants learn to use AI for advocacy, policy influence, elections and information integrity, and civic technology, and to handle its risks responsibly. OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: On Rolling Basis Applications are open for the Future of Life Institute Digital Media Accelerator 2026. The Digital Media Accelerator supports digital content from creators raising awareness and understanding about ongoing AI developments and issues. With AI companies recklessly racing unchecked to build increasingly powerful AI – including artificial general intelligence (AGI), despite having no way to control it – the rest of humanity is being hurtled towards a dangerous and uncertain future. Top AI experts agree that mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority – with AI company leaders themselves even explicitly addressing the dangers of the technology they’re building. It is not too late to change trajectory however. We can bring about a secure, prosperous future with controllable, reliable Tool AI – systems intentionally built to empower humans rather than replace us – if we’re willing to take decisive action now. However, public awareness and understanding remains limited. The FLI Digital Media Accelerator program aims to help creators produce content, grow channels, spread the word to new audiences. They are looking to support creators who can explain complex AI issues – such as AGI implications, control problems, misaligned goals, or Big Tech power concentration – in ways that their audiences can understand and relate to. By supporting various content formats across different platforms, they want to spark broader conversations about the risks of developing evermore powerful AI, and AGI. Eligibility They are keen to support creators who already have a following, and are interested in raising awareness about AI safety and risk; Have compelling ideas for impactful pieces of content to bring AI safety/risk awareness to new audiences; and, They are especially eager to support creators interested in discussing AI safety in their content on an ongoing basis, incorporating it into their regular output. TITLE: Why a Mastercard Foundation Scholarship May Be the Best Fit for You

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
I received the Mastercard Foundation Scholarship after facing 17 rejections. Seventeen rejection emails could easily have convinced me that perhaps I was not qualified, prepared or fortunate enough to receive a major international scholarship. But rejection did not end my story. It strengthened it. The day you open a rejection email can be just as sunny, bright or cold as the day you eventually open an acceptance email. The major difference is that, on the day the acceptance arrives, your perseverance, persistence and determination have finally created the opportunity you refused to stop pursuing. Today, I am studying Africa and International Development at the University of Edinburgh as a Mastercard Foundation Scholar. Looking back, I am grateful that I continued applying, learning and believing that there was still a place for me somewhere. While the core benefits are well-known, there are numerous unadvertised perks and community-driven dynamics that completely transform the student experience, rendering this one of the most comprehensive scholarships available globally. Financial Coverage and Secure Housing Foremost among the structural benefits of this scholarship is the comprehensive financial peace of mind it establishes from day one, allowing scholars to immerse themselves entirely in their academic pursuits without the looming anxiety of historical or ongoing educational debt. The foundation takes full responsibility for complete tuition fees, eliminating the substantial financial barriers that often prevent top-tier global talent from accessing world-class instruction. In tandem with tuition coverage, scholars receive a regular monthly stipend designed to comfortably meet the cost of living in Edinburgh. This ensures that textbook purchases, dietary needs, local transit, and daily incidentals are entirely taken care of. This financial framework extends directly to student accommodation, which is meticulously planned, fully paid for, and coordinated by the program administration before arrival. Rather than leaving international students to navigate the highly competitive and stressful local rental market from afar, the foundation secures housing in prime areas of the town. These residential spaces are selected with strict criteria in mind, ensuring a high level of physical security, modern domestic comfort, and a pristine, quiet study environment optimized for rigorous academic focus. Strategic Career Transitions and Executive Mentorship The true value of this scholarship lies in its forward-looking design, which actively rejects the idea that a funding package should merely cover a degree and then dissolve. From the very moment a scholar is handed their official admission letter, the Mastercard Foundation implements a strategic framework aimed at preparing the individual for life beyond graduation. Central to this effort is direct access to a dedicated transitions coordinator. This professional’s entire mandate is to help students think critically about their long-term professional trajectories, identify hidden career avenues, and strategically position themselves within the global workforce. This guidance prevents post-graduation panic by transforming the academic year into a continuous launchpad for future leadership. To facilitate a smooth departure from university life when the time comes, the program provides a comprehensive transitions fee. This is a lump-sum financial cushion explicitly intended to offset the immediate logistical costs of moving, relocating, or establishing a professional base. This remains true whether a scholar chooses to utilize their chance to remain in the United Kingdom or return immediately to their home country. Furthermore, scholars gain unparalleled, first-hand advisory access to highly successful team members working directly within the Mastercard network. These industry professionals, who have built illustrious careers across diverse corporate, technological, and developmental fields, offer direct mentorship. They share operational insights and provide a realistic view of what it takes to drive systemic change on a global scale. Cutting-Edge Technology and Entrepreneurial Support I won the scholars
